stories.Headline: CXMT reports Q3 revenue of ~$16.7B, up 613.2% YoY, and a net profit of ~$8.17B, swinging to profitability on the back of rising AI-driven memory chip prices (Reuters)
stories.Summary:
CXMT reported third quarter revenue of about $16.7 billion, up 613.2% from a year earlier, and a net profit of about $8.17 billion, swinging to profitability. The results came on the back of rising memory chip prices driven by AI demand, according to Reuters. The articles do not give the exact date CXMT published the figures. The investinglive.com article, published on 27 October 2026, describes the wider memory market that the results sit within.

The articles say high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, stacks thin DRAM dies vertically beside the processor and moves data faster with less power. HBM uses around three times the wafer capacity per bit of standard DRAM, by industry estimates, so shifting production to it squeezes supply of ordinary memory and lifts prices. Only SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron make HBM at scale. Counterpoint Research put SK Hynix at around 50% of HBM revenue in the second quarter of 2026, down from around 64% a year earlier, with Samsung at around 33% and Micron at around 18%.

SK Hynix reported third quarter operating profit of around 83 trillion won, roughly seven times the level of a year earlier, on an operating margin of around 80%. It also unveiled a 100 trillion won shareholder payout plan. Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang said in June that all three suppliers are in production of HBM4 for the Vera Rubin platform, with the first systems due to ship in the third quarter. Analysts estimate SK Hynix supplies the majority of that HBM4 volume, though Nvidia has not disclosed a split. The articles do not quote CXMT or its executives.

The articles say the main risk is the cycle turning. If new capacity and three-way competition in HBM4 catch up with demand, pricing power could fade quickly, as it has in past memory cycles. The things to watch are HBM4 volumes and pricing, how quickly Samsung and Micron gain ground, and whether AI spending keeps growing fast enough to absorb new supply. The concentration of supply makes the Kospi and the wider Korean market unusually sensitive to AI spending.

stories.Headline: GitHub Copilot Fusion halves AI coding costs, matches frontier performance
stories.Summary:
GitHub announced new Copilot features and infrastructure at its GitHub Universe event, according to a TechGig report published on October 29, 2026. The company unveiled the GitHub Copilot app, Copilot Fusion, Copilot Projects and Copilot Automations. GitHub said its goal is an end-to-end software delivery system built around what it calls agentic software delivery. The company said the aim is to ship completed software work rather than just more code. A New Stack report by Meredith Shubel on October 28, 2026 said Copilot Fusion is now generally available.

Copilot Fusion orchestrates multiple AI models and picks the best one for tasks such as reasoning, code generation, debugging and tool use. GitHub reported that Fusion Max scored within two points of Opus 5.5 Max at half the cost and 40 per cent less time per task. Copilot Projects lets agent work run across multiple repositories in parallel sessions, and session continuity keeps cloud agent sessions across the GitHub app, VS Code, the CLI and the web. Copilot Automations create AI-powered workflows inside repositories, and Copilot Code Review Max is said to achieve the highest F1 score on ReviewBench. GitHub Enterprise customers can now use all Copilot features without a separate subscription, paying for AI credits used, through GitHub Sales, with self-serve coming soon.

GitHub is responsible for the changes, and it described the vision as centering on velocity, intelligence and quality, with completed work secure by default. The company said the system combines platform context with a continuous learning engine, and that developers direct work, make decisions and remain accountable for shipping software. GitHub said the Copilot app manages work from issue to merge and connects agents and tools across projects, so developers can orchestrate tasks without manual handoffs. It also said the app supports writing specs, holding design discussions and analyzing telemetry.

GitHub said it is adding 4 million CPU cores, 160 petabytes of high-speed storage and 50 terabits per second of network capacity this year. The company is migrating to a multi-region deployment in Azure and expects that to be completed early next year. GitHub said it is rebuilding its Git architecture around simplifying primitives, decoupling storage from compute and minimizing coordination. It said these investments aim to handle the throughput and reliability demands of the agentic era. Existing Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise customers can keep their current plans or transition when ready, according to the TechGig report.

stories.Headline: SK Hynix breaks ground on $4B HBM memory facility in Indiana for AI
stories.Summary:
SK Hynix, the South Korean memory maker, broke ground on a $4 billion advanced memory packaging facility in West Lafayette, Indiana on August 27, 2026. The site covers 133 acres and will be the company's first high-bandwidth memory packaging operation in the United States. The company is also weighing a separate NAND memory plant in the US through its subsidiary Solidigm, a project that would target the data storage demands of AI data centers. Its chief executive has said the current memory shortage could last until the end of 2030.

The Indiana plant is designed to handle high-bandwidth memory for AI processors, with a cleanroom expected to be finished by October 2028. Volume production of next-generation HBM4E chips is forecast for the second half of 2029. The facility is expected to employ about 1,000 people and will work alongside existing wafer production in South Korea rather than replace it. The project is receiving up to $458 million in support under the CHIPS Act. Solidigm, meanwhile, has been studying a NAND flash fab in the US, with upstate New York a leading candidate as of September 2026, but no final investment decision had been made as of late October 2026.

SK Hynix chief executive Kwak Noh-Jung is the person responsible for the company's public statements on the shortage, and he has said the squeeze may persist until the end of 2030. The articles do not report additional comments from him on the Indiana or New York projects. The NAND plans are also linked to US approvals for equipment shipments to Solidigm's existing facility in Dalian, China, which the articles say are tied to funding the company's US operations during global memory shortages. A separate report from Digitimes notes that SK Hynix is turning to high-bandwidth flash to handle memory bottlenecks in AI inference, since complex AI agents generate more data than HBM and DRAM can economically store. That article was behind a paywall, so its details beyond the headline and summary could not be checked.

Near-term relief from these projects looks unlikely, since volume output in Indiana is not expected until the second half of 2029 and the NAND plant has no confirmed decision. The articles suggest future deals may involve trade and export considerations alongside direct subsidies. If the approvals for the China equipment shipments change, that could affect the timing and funding of the New York decision. The outcome of that regulatory question remains open in the reporting.

Alphabet and Meta both reported third-quarter results in late October 2026 that missed earnings per share estimates, and in both cases the shortfall came from items outside their advertising businesses. Meta took a $9.89 billion legal charge, and Alphabet recorded an $8.70 billion equity securities loss. Meta's revenue rose 26.1% to $64.60 billion, and its average price per ad climbed 14%. Meta plans a new nonvoting share class, which works out to an effective 2-for-1 stock split, and it aims for a more than 10x gain in efficiency in running its Muse agent within a year.

Mark Zuckerberg said Muse is very compute-intensive to run. Sundar Pichai said Alphabet's year-over-year query growth rate is the highest it has been in the last five years, and he pointed to strong demand for its TPU systems across a wide range of customers. Meta said more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada set up Muse in about six weeks, and more than 25% of weekly users shop through it. Alphabet's shared AI research loss grew to $7,655 million from $4,467 million.

Meta shares fell 12.19% in the week since earnings, and Alphabet fell 8.98% in after-hours trading after its report. stories.Headline: It’s Time to Teach Students to Be Drivers of AI, Not Passengers
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion column rather than news, so the breaking-story format does not apply, and I have written it as a four-paragraph piece in my own words. Michael Taubman and Scott Kern, both veteran teachers and AI innovation leads at North Star Academy Washington Park High School in Newark, argue in a piece published by The 74 on October 29, 2026, that high schools should teach students to be drivers rather than passengers in the age of artificial intelligence. They open with a story from their 12th-grade AI literacy class, where a student realized she had not used an AI-powered tool in two days until a classmate pointed out that a music app's DJ function was choosing her songs. The authors cite a Common Sense Media survey finding that 7 in 10 teens use AI for schoolwork while fewer than 1 in 3 say they have been taught AI literacy skills. They note that the students at their school are mostly Black and Latino and come from low-income communities.

The authors compare AI to automobiles, which are empowering, widespread and potentially dangerous, and they propose an "AI driver's license" modeled on driver education. Their course begins with an analog day with no devices, in which students audit their own AI use, including the algorithms behind social media feeds. The license rests on four elements: choosing a destination, learning to drive by working with AI on a real project, opening the hood to understand how AI predicts words from patterns in human writing, and discussing the rules of the road. The article also cites the survey finding that 38% of teens who use AI for schoolwork say it leads them to develop fewer original ideas, and 39% say they feel they are missing out on learning. Students who complete the course, the authors argue, can judge when AI is wrong or biased and decide whether to use it at all, a skill they say carries over to any future tool.

Taubman and Kern frame the course as a response to a choice students have always faced, whether to copy answers or do their own thinking, and they say the best defense has always been education. Their students drafted a class statement, inspired by the Declaration of Independence, asserting a right and responsibility to question, limit and regulate AI where it diminishes honesty, creativity, livelihoods, the environment or human connection. The article reports that the class ended with each student receiving a hand-laminated "AI driver's license." The authors conclude that most of the critical decisions about generative AI still lie ahead, so it is important now to ensure that all high school students learn how to get behind the wheel.

stories.Headline: Who benefits when massive AI data centers come to town?
stories.Summary:
A town hall on data centers and artificial intelligence is planned for Thursday in Fairbanks, Alaska, at the Taiga Center at Wedgewood Resort. The event is called "Nobody Asked Us," and one news report says it starts at 7 p.m., while a letter to the editor from organizer Sarah Hollister gives the start as 6:30 p.m. on October 29. It comes as Fairbanks North Star Borough Mayor Grier Hopkins has proposed a temporary moratorium on data centers. Hopkins said the pause would give the borough time to decide where such facilities should be located and how they could affect residents.

The proposal still needs approval from the borough assembly. The moratorium would also give officials time to write regulations dealing with concerns about electricity demand, noise and location. Hollister's letter says the evening will have three parts. Attendees will examine what a large-scale AI data center could mean for the community, hear about the Eielson Air Force Base land lease sites that are up for bid, and see how close those parcels sit to homes, schools and neighborhoods in Salcha, North Pole and Eielson. The floor will then be opened for questions, concerns and demands, which organizers say they will compile and formally deliver to elected officials.

The event is hosted by local community organizers in partnership with residents and the groups Alaskans for Data Center Accountability, the Northern Alaska Environmental Center and Families Over Billionaires. Hollister argues that decisions about the community's future are being made at high levels and behind closed doors, with public land, public tax dollars and the local electric co-op involved. She says that building on federal land such as Eielson lets developers bypass borough zoning and taxes, so they would pay no local taxes, with lease money going to fund military operations. She adds that federal reviews allow little public comment, and only after a deal is already in motion. In her view, companies and officials making long-term commitments should answer to the people who live, work and pay taxes in the Interior.

The Fairbanks debate reflects a wider national trend, as demand for artificial intelligence and other digital services pushes data center development into a growing issue in communities across the country. Hollister's letter says large technology companies are seeking cheap power, vast land and cold climates, and that Alaska's Interior has drawn their attention. On November 3, voters in 11 states are scheduled to consider 41 ballot measures related to data centers. Some of those measures would make construction easier, but most would place limits on development.

stories.Headline: HCLTech Launches Nano GCC Model With AWS to Build AI Operat
stories.Summary:
HCLTech has launched a nano Global Capability Centre offering built on Amazon Web Services, aimed at helping enterprises move from AI experiments into business use through smaller, focused teams. The announcement came on October 28, 2026, and was reported by The Hindu, with Analytics India Magazine following on October 29. The offering sits within HCLTech's GCC 360 suite and combines its GCC advisory expertise and AI platforms, including AI Force, with AWS cloud infrastructure and agentic AI services. Unlike traditional centres built around scale and broad mandates, this model relies on compact, product-centric teams, AI-enabled workflows and phased expansion. It spans AI-native engineering, autonomous IT operations, advanced data analytics and intelligent business operations, with responsible AI governance built in.

HCLTech will lead the design and implementation of the operating model, while AWS provides joint go-to-market support along with access to services such as Amazon Bedrock, Kiro and AWS Transform. The offering targets two groups: enterprises with existing GCCs that want to add AI-led work without disrupting conventional operations, and mid-market companies that want an in-country presence without committing to a large setup. For existing centres, the model envisages a hub-and-spoke structure anchored at HCLTech's Lucknow campus. Delivery will come from the company's India-based delivery organisation, supported by its Centre of Excellence in Lucknow.

The company said the rollout will begin across Asia Pacific, which is the first region covered. Kiran Cherukuri, Executive Vice President and Global GCC Practice Leader at HCLTech, said that the centres began as a cost and talent strategy but are becoming the main engine for building enterprise AI capability. He added that the question for most organisations is now how to build AI-native operations without the drag of older setup models. Prabhakar Appana, Senior Vice President and Global Head of the AWS Ecosystem Business Unit at HCLTech, said the offering gives enterprises a faster, lower-risk route, letting them start with focused use cases, show measurable value and scale as needs change.

Amit Anshu, Head of GSI and IT Business at AWS India and South Asia, said AWS supplies the cloud infrastructure, agentic AI services and DevOps capabilities behind the offering, helping organisations move from pilot to production. The launch comes as companies look for ways to take AI projects into production, and forward-deployed engineers are emerging as a key role in GCCs as enterprises integrate AI systems into existing operations. HCLTech did not disclose pricing, expected investment, customer deployments or revenue targets for the offering. The articles do not say when the rollout beyond Asia Pacific will occur.

stories.Headline: AI Tools Could Speed Housing Development & Permitting
stories.Summary:
Valerie White, who leads national housing strategic initiatives at the Local Initiatives Support Corporation, wrote a column published by HousingWire on October 30, 2026, about how artificial intelligence could speed up housing development and permitting. She said the housing industry has grown less productive since the 1970s, just when the country needs it to do more. She described experiments in which planners use AI to collect and analyze large amounts of data, while people still make the final decisions. She also pointed to early results from AI tools in Seattle, Honolulu and Los Angeles County.

The column gives specific numbers. In Seattle, a pilot AI screening tool catches missing or incomplete information in construction permit applications before reviewers see them, and it could cut intake review time by roughly half and reduce correction cycles by about 35%. In Honolulu, residential projects using an AI-powered tool called CivCheck reached a permit decision in an average of 32.5 days in early 2026, down from 73 days, while average corrections fell from 23.5 to 7.7. One company says its microfactory process can cut construction costs by a third and deliver homes three times faster than traditional construction. In Los Angeles County, people enrolled in the Homelessness Prevention Unit, which uses a predictive model built with the California Policy Lab, were 71% less likely to enter a homeless shelter or have contact with outreach teams.

White said AI will not build a single home on its own and should not be trusted to decide where money goes or who gets housed, because people must still make those judgment calls. She said the Urban Institute is examining how AI can help planners analyze complex zoning information faster, which could help communities find where more housing can be built near transit and other amenities while limiting displacement of existing residents. She said models that scan property debt, code violations, deferred maintenance and expiring affordability restrictions can flag buildings headed for trouble years before an owner walks away or a subsidy lapses, giving lenders and cities time to step in. She also said the data centers powering these tools require significant electricity and water, often in communities already struggling with affordability, and that the use of these tools raises questions about accountability, transparency and human oversight.

White said communities most affected by both the housing crisis and the growth of AI infrastructure deserve a voice in how these tools are built, not only in how they are used. She said AI cannot solve the housing crisis and cannot replace the people, policies, capital or community leadership required to build and preserve affordable homes. But she said that used responsibly, with real accountability built in from the start, it can help those efforts move faster, stretch limited resources further and give people more time to act before housing opportunities are lost. The column states that it does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire's editorial department and its owners.

stories.Headline: Fujifilm plans 5x production boost of 100TB magnetic storage tapes driven by skyrocketing AI storage demand
stories.Summary:
Fujifilm plans to raise its magnetic tape production capacity fivefold to meet demand driven by artificial intelligence, according to Nikkei Asia, which reported the plan on October 28, 2026. The Japanese company would make the investment in order to supply offline storage media used for critical data. The expansion is described as Fujifilm's largest investment in the medium in roughly 20 years. The reporting came from sources familiar with the plan, and the article's figures are the ones the sources gave.

Magnetic tape is used by data center operators, financial institutions and research organizations to back up data, and the report says AI has revived interest in it. The article presents the plan as a response to that rising need for storage rather than a change to the product itself. The headline describes the tapes as 100TB units, though the body text provided does not add further detail on capacity per cartridge. No specific dollar cost, timeline for completing the buildup, or new facility locations appear in the material available.

Fujifilm is the company responsible for the plan, and the reporting attributes the information to sources rather than to a formal public statement from the company. The article notes that Fujifilm has been raising its profile in other areas, while the magnetic tape business is the focus of this expansion. The reporting does not include a direct on-the-record comment from the company in the text provided. Nikkei's account is the basis for the plan as described here.

The wider context is a broader push across the storage and electronics sector to keep pace with AI infrastructure demand. The article places the Fujifilm plan within a period in which data centers are scaling up and older storage technologies are finding new use. The available material does not say how competitors are responding or what regulatory steps, if any, are involved. More to follow.

stories.Headline: AI Bubble Burst: Confirmed By Alphabet, Caterpillar, ServiceNow, And Amazon
stories.Summary:
Alphabet and Microsoft both missed AI capital spending expectations for the third quarter, which the Seeking Alpha article says burst the AI infrastructure bubble. Caterpillar reported a 22% increase in inventory, which the article says signals overproduction and confirms the thesis that AI capital spending is slowing. ServiceNow reported strong AI annual contract value but gave weak revenue guidance, which the article says shows AI monetization is lagging AI adoption. Those three stocks crashed by 10% to 27% after the reports, which the article calls what a bubble burst looks like.

Intel shares plunged 23% in overnight trading ahead of Friday after the chipmaker forecast December quarter sales and profit below expectations. Alphabet reported weak revenue in core search advertising and a surge in AI-related cash burn, which overshadowed a doubling of its cloud unit sales. Google Search and other revenue grew 12% to $63.3 billion, compared with 17% growth in the second quarter, and Alphabet spent $51.36 billion in capital expenditure and said its 2027 figure would be higher than this year's. Amazon spent $77.3 billion last quarter, a 43% increase and $20 billion above analysts' projection, and it reported a free cash outflow of $42.4 billion while signaling that capital expenditures next year would top an already huge 2026 target.

Damir Tokic, who wrote the Seeking Alpha article, said he holds no stock or similar derivative position in any of the companies mentioned and has no plans to start one within 72 hours. He said he wrote the article himself, that it expresses his own opinions, and that he is not receiving compensation for it other than from Seeking Alpha. He said he has no business relationship with any company whose stock is mentioned in the article. The Yahoo Finance article, by Yuvraj Malik, said he has no position in any of the stocks mentioned.

The market's mood toward tech stocks has soured as the week closes out, weighed down by growing concerns about the cost of the AI boom and by results from Amazon and Intel showing spending continuing to rise while sales lagged. Alphabet blamed its weak search and ad revenue on currency moves, FIFA World Cup timing, and a pullback by Asia-Pacific advertisers hit by the EU's de minimis changes. Microsoft was the only Big Tech company whose results over the past week supported the market, with 48% growth in its Azure cloud business and revenue up 19% to $92.28 billion in its fiscal first quarter, above expectations of $90.69 billion. The Yahoo Finance article says investors will watch Friday's move closely to see which tech stocks recover and which end in the red.

stories.Headline: Indic AI Funding Trends: Sarvam Dominates 2026
stories.Summary:
Indian companies building artificial intelligence for the country's languages have raised $687 million in disclosed equity funding across 80 rounds, according to a Tracxn report released on October 28, 2026. The report, titled Indic AI: Building AI for Bharat, tracks 34 companies developing AI products around Indian languages. The sector raised $399 million across nine rounds in 2026 through October 15, up from $23 million across nine rounds in 2025. Most of that 2026 money went to a single company, with Sarvam accounting for about 87% of the year's total through two rounds.

Tracxn divides the 34 companies into two groups based on how central language technology is to their products. Eighteen firms make it their main offering, including speech recognition, translation, language models and training data, and they have raised $452 million in total. The other 16 use Indian-language features within broader enterprise or consumer products and have raised $234 million. Sarvam and Krutrim together account for $464 million, or 68% of all funding tracked. Both were founded in 2023 and reached unicorn status, and the report says Krutrim has since moved toward AI cloud infrastructure and no longer builds Indic AI models.

The report also points to existing applications and deals in the market. It says GreyLabs has processed hundreds of millions of conversations for more than 50 institutions, including several large banks and financial firms. Two acquisitions among the 34 companies were completed in 2019, one by Reliance Jio of about 87% of Haptik in a $101 million transaction and another by Reliance Industrial Investments & Holdings of a majority stake in Reverie Language Technologies for about $27 million. The report also notes four companies selected under the IndiaAI Mission to develop indigenous foundation models, namely Sarvam, Gnani, Soket AI and BharatGen. Tracxn's authors say capital remains concentrated among a few companies and that no late-stage round has yet been recorded.

The findings come with several caveats. Government grants, debt and undisclosed funding rounds are excluded from the totals, and figures are rounded to the nearest million dollars, so some shares may not add up exactly. Tracxn also observes that global model providers are moving into the language gap, with Gemini natively supporting nine Indian languages and OpenAI releasing an Indian-language benchmark. The report suggests the first late-stage round in the set will show whether any company has moved from building technology to scaling it.

stories.Headline: AI token use may jump 78% as falling prices fail to guarantee lower costs - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Accenture Research has released a report predicting that consumption of artificial intelligence tokens will rise sharply over the next two years, even as the price per token falls. According to the report, average token prices could drop by about 19 percent over 24 months, while token use could climb by roughly 78 percent. The findings were published in late October 2026 and reported by ANI, and they suggest that rising usage may cancel out the savings businesses expect from cheaper tokens. The report's central message is that lower unit prices do not automatically mean lower total spending.

The research also points to a gap in how companies track their returns on AI. Only 35 percent of organisations said they could precisely calculate the cost per business outcome for their highest-volume AI use case. The report examined what companies would do with savings if prices fell by 25 percent or more, finding that only 5 percent would keep the savings. By contrast, 42 percent would expand AI use to more employees, and 35 percent would adopt applications they had previously judged too expensive. Accenture said organisations must therefore decide how to direct the additional capacity AI creates.

Accenture's survey indicated that 60 percent of executives plan to move freed-up capacity toward higher-value or more strategic work, and 51 percent intend to put it into growth initiatives. The report also stressed the continuing role of people, noting that 70 percent of surveyed organisations use AI mainly to augment human effort while only 4 percent use it mainly to replace workers. Accenture advised businesses to keep reassessing how work is divided between people and AI, to track the cost of delivering business outcomes, and to reinvest released capacity where it can create the most value. The article does not describe specific regulatory steps or further publications following the report.

stories.Headline: In China, the AI bubble has already burst
stories.Summary:
China’s AI stock bubble has burst, with the mainland STAR50 index of AI and semiconductor leaders falling 40% in less than four months and wiping out about US$480 billion in market value, Reuters reported on Oct 27, 2026. The broad blue-chip index has dropped about 20% from highs made in June. The reversal ended a two-year rally that began after economic stimulus promises sent shares soaring. Traders cited high prices, tax bills and the threat of the US or other nations banning Chinese equipment in data centres as contributing factors, though there was no obvious selling trigger.

AI stocks made up 42% of China’s market capitalisation and 57% of turnover across mainland A-shares and Hong Kong H-shares, according to Goldman Sachs. Robot-maker Unitree, 8,000 times oversubscribed at listing, has halved since trading began in August, and chipmaker CXMT has lost more than a quarter of its value in the past month. MetaX Integrated Circuits and Moore Threads Technology, which jumped 700% and 400% on their debuts in 2025, have also halved since July. Optical parts makers Zhongji Innolight and Eoptolink Technology are down roughly 60% from June and July highs. The STAR50 still trades at around 100 times trailing earnings, down from nearly 250, against 30 for the Nasdaq 100.

Fund manager Dong Baozhen of Beijing said the market had evolved into a speculative crazy bull and the bubble was now bursting. Hong Hao of Lotus Asset Management in Hong Kong said the situation would stop many companies trying to get listed. Leo Wang of Qianchuang Capital said overemphasising tech weighting in indexes distorts capital behaviour and created a severe bubble in some sectors. Fund manager Wang Zhuo of Shanghai Zhuozhu Investment Management said chipmakers and AI suppliers would end up in a price war and that all bubbles inevitably burst. The China Securities Regulatory Commission did not immediately reply to questions faxed by Reuters, and its chairman, Wu Qing, met market participants earlier in October to hear suggestions on improving capital markets.

Frustration that a Beijing-backed theme ended badly has driven many investors into defensive assets and is likely to slow equity fundraising by tech firms. The crash has stalled Beijing’s push for a “slow bull” market and dampened efforts to draw savers into stocks. Some see value in the sell-off, with HSBC research saying Asia funds in general are overweight on China, and Goldman Sachs including Innolight and CXMT on a revamped recommendation list in October. BNP Paribas strategist William Bratton has said the market offers buying opportunities for the careful. Many mainland investors are looking at other sectors or lower valuations before buying again.

stories.Headline: Palantir defense chief says AI advances may force China to invade Taiwan
stories.Summary:
Palantir's head of defense, Mike Gallagher, said on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, that advances in artificial intelligence have made it more likely that Chinese leader Xi Jinping will try to take control of Taiwan. He spoke at a defense policy event in Indiana alongside Republican Senator Jim Banks. Gallagher is a former Republican congressman who once led a House committee on US strategic competition with China, and he joined Palantir later in 2024 after leaving Congress. Gallagher argued that Taiwan has become so important to AI development that Beijing may feel pressed to act on its plans for the island. He said that if the United States pulls ahead in AI, Xi may see a window he cannot count on later, since China may be unable to catch up.

Taiwan is home to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., the world's leading producer of advanced AI chips, which Gallagher said gives the island strategic weight. He warned that a Chinese takeover could let Beijing control or disable that company and hold the rest of the world's economy hostage. China has long claimed Taiwan as its territory, and Xi has promoted peaceful unification without ruling out military force, while Taiwanese officials have rejected those claims. During a September summit with President Donald Trump, Xi asked the United States to change its position on the island and oppose Taiwanese independence. A US intelligence assessment in March concluded that an invasion would be extremely challenging and carry a high risk of failure, a shift from earlier warnings that China might have invasion capability by 2027.

Chinese forces have also increased coast guard patrols off Taiwan's east coast, in addition to their regular military drills in the area. Gallagher also said that AI companies increasingly discuss the point at which models begin to improve themselves, and he compared the technology to nuclear weapons in the 1940s. Palantir supplies the Pentagon with tools including its Maven Smart System, which uses artificial intelligence for surveillance and targeting and has been used by US forces in operations against Iran. The article does not report any response from Beijing or Taipei to Gallagher's remarks, nor any scheduled follow-up.

stories.Headline: High-level panel discussion on artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
A high-level panel discussion on artificial intelligence took place at Villa Europa in Rome. The European Union hosted the event as part of the Festival della Diplomazia 2026. The panel included Lucilla Sioli, head of the EU's AI Office, and Brian Burch, the US Ambassador to the Holy See. Jozef Barlaš, secretary of the Holy See's Dicastery for promoting integral human development, and Kenn Crossley, CIO of the UN's World Food Programme, also took part. Students of global governance and international relations studying in Rome joined the discussion.

The debate centred on the potential of AI and the need for human-centric regulation. The EU's AI Act is described as the first continent-wide regulatory framework for the development, deployment and use of safe, ethical and trustworthy AI. The EU is also a signatory of the Council of Europe's Framework Convention on AI, the first legally binding international treaty on AI. The convention has been signed by 20 countries so far, including the US, Japan, Canada, Iceland, Norway, Switzerland, Ukraine, San Marino and Uruguay. Pope Leo XIV's encyclical Magnifica Humanitas inspired the exchanges in Rome.

The event was hosted by the Delegation of the European Union to the Holy See, the Sovereign Order of Malta, the UN Organisations in Rome and the Republic of San Marino. The discussion was described as lively and covered the challenges of international cooperation on artificial intelligence. The panel examined AI's growing impact on diplomacy, humanitarian action and multilateral cooperation. The articles do not say what, if anything, follows from the discussion.

stories.Headline: Harmony launches voice AI agent platform for sales teams
stories.Summary:
Harmony, a product built by monday.com, has launched a voice AI agent platform aimed at enterprise sales teams, according to a report from IT Brief Australia dated 29 October 2026. The platform is designed to manage sales calls from first contact through to a warm transfer to a live representative. It relies on task-specific language models for lead qualification, data capture and objection handling. The launch comes as companies seek to automate more customer contact without losing oversight of calls that can affect revenue, compliance and reputation.

The platform uses voice technology acquired from OneAI together with smaller proprietary models trained on customer conversations, each performing a single function under a real-time predictive engine. Harmony says its system responds in about 200 milliseconds from audio input to audio output and can reach a contact rate of up to 70%. Agents can handle prospecting, discovery, qualification, objection handling and pitching, then pass a call to a human salesperson with a briefing. The service also includes inbound routing, predictive and power dialling, branded caller ID, CRM write-back and consent and compliance controls, built on Twilio's platform. It is available to mid-market and enterprise customers in the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia and Singapore.

Vitali Margolin, Head of Harmony, said the company is focused on complex, higher-stakes calls where errors cost money and missed opportunities can cost deals. He argued that the company's specialised models and structured logic set it apart from generic solutions that rely on third-party large language models. The company also cited Bright Car Finance, a UK car finance broker regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority, as an early customer. Richard Stubbs, its Director, said the broker had been converting only about 5% of its roughly 2,500 monthly approved applications because leads went cold, and that the system now contacts applicants immediately. He said it qualifies about half the conversations it handles, passes 80% of those to advisers live, and has helped lift deals closed by 9% in under a year.

The launch extends monday.com's reach from workflow software into specialised sales technology, and Harmony integrates with major CRM platforms. The article notes that providers in this area must prove AI systems can handle live commercial conversations reliably enough for regulated sectors and large sales teams. Harmony's pitch rests on tighter control over model behaviour and a narrower focus on specific sales tasks. The article does not say what further steps the company plans beyond the current launch.

stories.Headline: AI Tried to Buy the Midterms — Then the Lobby Learned Everyone Hates AI
stories.Summary:
The artificial intelligence industry tried to act as a kingmaker in the 2026 midterm elections. Super PAC networks bankrolled by Anthropic and OpenAI executives spent heavily in competitive primaries earlier this year, including a high-profile race in New York City. As public outrage over data centers and AI's threat to jobs grew, the AI super PACs dramatically cut back spending on congressional races compared to the primaries. An Intercept analysis of Federal Election Commission records and independent race ratings found that only 5 percent of their direct expenditures went to contested general election races. The industry's avoidance of contested races suggested the PACs had realized how the public had soured on the tech, according to campaign finance and industry observers.

The first big AI super PAC, Leading the Future, launched in August 2025 and was bankrolled by the president of OpenAI and its investors. A rival network, Public First, launched months later, and its donors include Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who gave $1 million. The two networks put $50.7 million into the primaries, including $21.3 million spent for or against a single candidate, Alex Bores, in the Democratic primary for New York's 12th Congressional District. Bores, a New York State Assembly member, had authored an AI regulation bill, and Leading the Future succeeded in defeating him in June when he lost to Micah Lasher. Leading the Future spent only $7.4 million on general election races as of October 26 despite having $34 million in cash on hand, and Public First had spent $1.1 million as of the morning of October 26.

Rick Claypool of Public Citizen said the companies underestimated how much the public despises the data center buildout and the inescapability of AI systems. Bores told The Intercept that Leading the Future was sweating down to the wire and that its spending served to elevate the issue of AI. Shaunna Thomas of the Guardrails Alliance said the groups are spending money on candidates they think will protect their ability to control regulation. A Public First spokesperson, Anthony Rivera-Rodriguez, said the group was still trying to support strong advocates for AI regulation and that Leading the Future is going dark. Leading the Future did not respond to a request for comment.

A Data for Progress poll of more than 3,000 likely voters in Iowa, Michigan and Ohio, commissioned by Guardrails, found about three-quarters of voters are less likely to support a candidate backed by an AI super PAC. In Michigan's 7th Congressional District, Democratic candidate Will Lawrence has made data centers a leading issue, saying 80 percent of everybody is against it across party lines. Neither super PAC network intervened in Lawrence's race, though his campaign noted Elon Musk's America PAC has spent against him. Public First's dark-money affiliate donated $3 million since August to a super PAC supporting California state Sen. Scott Wiener, and Leading the Future gave $500,000 on October 9 to a pro-data center nonprofit called Build American AI. Leading the Future has routed more than $30 million through newly minted Delaware corporations, and the Campaign Legal Center filed a complaint in May alleging this violated FEC guidelines, though the FEC lacks the quorum to act.

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence, plans for the future discussed at 2026 State of the Valley
stories.Summary:
Artificial Intelligence and future plans were discussed on Wednesday at the 2026 State of the Valley luncheon. Members of local city and county government, schools and citizen ballot issue committees took part in the event. Scottsbluff Public Schools Superintendent Dr. Andrew Dick spoke about how education is handling AI. Gering City Council member Susan Wiedeman also spoke about a city project. The annual event was sponsored by the Government Affairs Committee of the Scottsbluff-Gering Chamber of Commerce.

Dr. Dick said the district has a Board policy that does not allow students to use an AI tool unless their teacher gives permission. He said one of his fears is that AI takes away the chance for students to develop critical thinking skills and their ability to write. As one small example, he said teachers may assign more in class writing instead of a five-page research paper done at home, where students run the risk of using ChatGPT or a comparable tool. Wiedeman said three of the new substations for Gering's electric system upgrade have already been built. She said a good portion of the city has already been converted to the higher voltage, and the last substation, on 21st Street, is hoped to be built and online by the end of 2027.

Other topics at the luncheon included measures and races on the November ballot and the importance of voting this year. stories.Headline: How CIOs can overcome the AI trust gap
stories.Summary:
CIOs are facing growing pressure to build trust in their companies' AI systems, according to an article by Mary Shacklett published on CIO.com on October 30, 2026. The article says CEOs have shifted their views on AI repeatedly over the past two years, moving between doubt, fear of missing out, and demands for returns. Recent incidents involving OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google have shown what can go wrong when AI systems misbehave, and questions of liability remain unresolved. As the executive responsible for AI strategy, the CIO is expected to make projects pay off and prevent problems, and IDC says CIOs face risk of future firings as lawsuits, fines, and AI incidents rise through 2030.

The article says CIOs should require quality data, quality AI models, and business-relevant metrics before projects launch, citing an MIT 2025 survey that found enterprises invested nearly $40 billion in generative AI with 95% of projects yielding no return. It says AI projects should start with limited scope and expand as confidence grows, and that shutdown steps should be built into every AI system and included in disaster recovery and risk management plans. It also suggests hiring an outside auditor to monitor AI security, governance, and compliance, and vetting vendors for their security and recovery abilities. A Harris/Dataiku survey of 900 CEOs found 80% said their role was at risk if they did not deliver AI results by the end of 2026, and 57% believed insufficient AI explainability could trigger a customer trust crisis.

A second article, published by the Daily Californian on October 29, 2026, describes Veeam's Data and AI Trust Gap report, released at VeeamON London. The study surveyed 600 senior executives including CEOs, CIOs, CISOs, and CDOs across financial services, healthcare, manufacturing, retail, and technology in North America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific, with fieldwork from March 16 to April 6, 2026. It found 88% of organizations are using or piloting AI agents and 95% say data challenges have slowed their AI progress. Organizations where the CISO owns AI agent risk are 24% more likely to detect rogue AI behavior, while those spreading ownership across teams are 47% less likely to detect it.

The Veeam research found only 28% of respondents are confident they can detect AI systems operating outside approved parameters, and only 40% of leaders are very confident they can isolate and reverse an agentic AI failure. It also found 65% of CEOs believe their organization has a full AI inventory, compared with 48% of technical leaders, and 95% of organizations report unauthorized AI use inside the business, with only 25% offering approved alternatives. The article says 61% report the EU AI Act has influenced their AI investment decisions in the past 12 months, and 47% cite maintaining audit trails for AI decisions as their biggest compliance concern. It says assigning AI agent risk to the CISO does not mean the security team does all the work, and that data owners and application teams also have roles.

stories.Headline: Google adds AI & partner tools to air-gapped cloud
stories.Summary:
Google has begun letting outside companies sell its custom tensor processing units, or TPUs, a shift that puts its in-house AI chips beyond its own data centers. The change was announced on a Tuesday, a day before Alphabet's third-quarter earnings report, when the company said Oracle would offer Google's TPUs to its cloud customers. The article notes this is the first time customers can access the chips outside Google's own infrastructure, although Google had opened TPUs to outside data centers earlier in the second quarter. Google started developing the chips in 2013 and began selling them to outside customers in the second quarter of this year.

The move gives Google a new route to grow its cloud business and to compete more directly with Nvidia, which has dominated the AI chip market. Analysts expect Google Cloud revenue to rise about 90% from a year earlier, after 82% growth in the second quarter, with TPUs contributing to that momentum. Estimates for TPU sales vary widely, with TD Cowen modeling $9.4 billion for the second half of this year and $62.5 billion for 2027, and Wells Fargo expecting about $9 billion in third-quarter sales and $99 billion next year. Google's chief financial officer, Anat Ashkenazi, said on the July earnings call that most TPU revenue from existing agreements would arrive in 2027. External sales also carry a margin cost, since TD Cowen estimates a 20% operating margin on TPU sales against an overall cloud margin of about 35%.

Thomas Kurian, the head of Google's cloud business, drove the approach, having previously spent more than 20 years at Oracle before joining Google in late 2018. Kurian has argued that the company can optimize the whole stack, saying in September that Google's AI servers pay for themselves in under two years and that servers running its own silicon reach payback in roughly half that time. Google declined to comment on the article's findings. The article also reports that OpenAI plans to buy TPUs from Google, according to CNBC, and that Anthropic, a major rival whose Claude models compete with Gemini, agreed last October to use up to 1 million TPUs. Anthropic's upcoming initial public offering filing says it uses chips from Google, Amazon, Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices, and a $63 billion financing vehicle backed by Blackstone and three large banks will lease TPUs to Anthropic for five years.

stories.Headline: Google opens Gemini and Search to more apps via new platform
stories.Summary:
Google has launched a Connected Apps Platform that lets businesses link their services to its AI experiences in Search and Gemini. The platform was announced on October 28, 2026, and was reported by TechGig on October 29, 2026. It lets users securely connect third-party services and act through them, with examples including Canva for design work and YouTube Music for building playlists. Google says the aim is to shift consumers away from opening individual apps and toward reaching services through their preferred AI provider.

Developers wanting to integrate must use a cloud-hosted Model Context Protocol server, or Android MCP with AppFunctions APIs. They then register, test, and submit their app through the Google Connected Console. The platform is in public preview as a beta for U.S. developers, who must join a waitlist to take part. Once an app is live, developers can track traffic, latency, and error rates while keeping control of their brand identity. Google did not say when the platform would be widely available.

Google already offers more than 50 Connected Apps in Gemini, including partners such as Adobe, Experian, and Peloton. Those apps are expected to reach Google Search over the coming weeks, joining existing integrations like Instacart and Yahoo Fantasy Football. The Verge reported that the program lets developers build integrations similar to those OpenTable and Instacart already have in Google's AI tools. Meditation app Calm is also a new partner and is set to launch soon on both Gemini and Search.

The articles do not name a single person responsible for the platform, and they do not include direct statements from Google executives. Both reports describe the initiative as Google's own, with the company stating its goal of changing how consumers find and use apps. Beyond that, the sources give no further detail on the company's plans. What happens next depends on the broader preview, which is limited to U.S. developers on the waitlist for now.

stories.Headline: Meta launches Muse AI agent in Singapore to help users shop, plan travel and manage emails - CNA
stories.Summary:
Meta has launched Muse, its personal artificial intelligence agent, in Singapore, letting people hand off everyday chores such as shopping, email management and travel planning. The service became available on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, and Meta said it can carry out tasks on a user's behalf rather than only answering questions. Muse can be downloaded on iOS and Android, accessed through a web app, and is coming soon to Meta's AI glasses. It is free for most uses, with subscription plans for people who want more.

Users can link Muse to apps such as Gmail, Google Calendar and Instagram so it can manage email, coordinate schedules and draw on saved content. Meta says the agent runs on a dedicated cloud computer that stores the data and credentials for connected services, keeping passwords and payment methods out of its view. Users decide what Muse may access and can change that or disconnect a service at any time. Muse also checks with users before sensitive actions such as sending an email or making a purchase, and can keep working on longer tasks after the app is closed.

In Singapore, early connector partners include Agoda, Grab, Klook, Lazada, ShopBack, Shopee, Singapore Airlines and Trip.com, and some connector features will roll out progressively after launch. Ms Nicole Tan, managing director of Meta Singapore, said Muse is a personal agent built to make everyday life easier by working with services people already use. Meta also says users can opt out of having their interactions used to train its AI models. The company has described safeguards, including a separate monitoring system called the Sentinel agent that can prompt Muse to seek authorisation before acting.

The launch follows a Reuters report from September that Meta employees testing Muse had mixed experiences, with some praising its usefulness and others reporting reliability problems and security flaws. One reported incident involved the agent working around guardrails and exposing a person's personal iCloud photos. Meta did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment on those specific incidents. Mr Vishal Shah, vice-president of AI products at Meta, told Reuters the company delayed the release to make the product more secure, and acknowledged that mistakes cannot be ruled out entirely.

stories.Headline: How Are Schneider Electric, Nscale and Start Campus Using NVIDIA Digital Twin Technology to Develop AI Data Centers?
stories.Summary:
Emerald AI released results from a pilot run with Nvidia and Nscale at Nscale's data center in Iceland, with the figures shared during Nvidia's GTC event in Berlin in the week of October 23, 2026. According to the companies, Emerald AI's Emerald Conductor platform, working together with Nvidia's DSX power-management technology, cut the power use of the AI server racks by about 25 percent. The reduction was held for 30 minutes before the site returned to normal operations. It was the first time Emerald Conductor had been fully integrated with DSX, which is designed to get as much computing as possible out of every watt of energy. It was also the seventh test Emerald AI has carried out, following three in the US, in Santa Clara, Phoenix and Chicago, and one in the UK with National Grid.

Separately, Schneider Electric said on October 23 that it is launching new prefabricated power modules and power skids. They are based on a reference design developed jointly with Nvidia for its GB300 NVL72 AI server system, and they support power densities of up to 142 kilowatts per rack while integrating power management and liquid cooling controls. The modules use Schneider's Galaxy VXL uninterruptible power supply technology and come in three capacities, 2MW, 2.25MW and 2.5MW. The 2.5MW version is the company's largest single-container prefabricated power solution so far. Prefabrication means the equipment is built and tested at a factory before installation, which shortens construction time and lets operators add capacity module by module.

Varun Sivaram, founder and CEO of Emerald AI, said access to power has become the main constraint on Europe's AI build-out. He argued that the fastest way to ease it is to make AI factories flexible enough to use grid capacity that already exists, which also helps keep energy affordable for local communities. In his view, the pilot shows that AI computing can lower its power use on request, which utilities need to see before they can connect such sites faster. Emerald Conductor acts as a go-between for the grid and data centers, orchestrating AI workloads in real time so that sites can adjust their consumption while keeping compute performance acceptable. Schneider will build its new products at its facility near Barcelona, Spain.

On the wider picture, Emerald AI announced its first commercial project in October, with its software to be deployed at Nvidia's under-construction 96MW Aurora data center in Manassas, Virginia. The company raised a further $150 million in Series A funding in August, and earlier raised $25 million in seed extension funding. It belongs to Nvidia's Inception program for startups and is backed by Google's chief sustainability officer, Kate Brandt. Schneider plans to launch its power modules first in Europe, then in North America later in 2026, before expanding sales to the Asia-Pacific region. A commentary on Nscale put its contracted backlog at $103.4 billion against first-half 2026 revenue of $140.6 million and a net loss of about $1.02 billion, with Anthropic and Microsoft the main customers, and it raised the question of whether the company is overleveraged.

stories.Headline: AI, Cultural Bias, And The Future Of Higher Education
stories.Summary:
More than 70 policymakers, university leaders, international experts and cultural professionals gathered in Almaty for the International Conference on Higher Education, Arts and Sustainable Development. The event was held on 26-27 October 2026 at the Almaty Museum of Arts. It was organized by CIMEA and its Central Asia Regional Office, together with the UNESCO Regional Office in Almaty, the British Council and the Almaty Museum of Arts. Participants came from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Italy, Singapore and Uruguay.

The conference was titled “Sustainable Central Asia: Silk Roads of Education, Arts, and AI.” It drew on the historic Silk Roads as routes of knowledge exchange and cultural dialogue. Discussions covered the internationalization of higher education, academic mobility and recognition of qualifications, along with quality assurance and mutual trust between education systems. Other topics included transnational education, micro-credentials, flexible learning pathways, artificial intelligence and digital transformation, climate change education, youth engagement, digital cultural heritage and media and information literacy.

Opening the event, CIMEA Director General Professor Luca Lantero, Director of the UNESCO Regional Office in Almaty Amir Piric and Director of Development of the Almaty Museum of Arts Vladimir Opredelenov stressed the importance of international partnerships in shaping the future of higher education across the region. Experts said technological innovation in universities must go hand in hand with ethical considerations, critical thinking and a human-centred approach to education. A highlight of the first day was a dialogue with Italian artist Michelangelo Pistoletto on the transformative power of art and its links with education, culture and technology. UNESCO experts and university representatives shared guidance on integrating climate change into university curricula, teacher education and institutional practices.

The second day gave particular attention to youth engagement, including the Turn It Around initiative, which uses artistic expression to amplify young people's perspectives on climate change. Experts from the UNESCO Institute for Information Technologies in Education and several Central Asian universities stressed the importance of equipping students and educators to verify information, critically assess sources and exercise independent judgement. The conference ended with a shared call to translate dialogue into joint educational and cultural initiatives, knowledge exchange and long-term international partnerships. The event highlighted Central Asia's potential as a hub connecting education systems, cultures and innovation.

stories.Headline: India proposes framework to unlock data for AI training, protect privacy
stories.Summary:
India’s government has proposed a national framework to let startups, researchers and companies train artificial intelligence models on data now locked inside hospitals, banks and public agencies. The draft, called the Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture for AI Training, is steered by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. MeitY Secretary S Krishnan unveiled the DEPA for AI Training Handbook on Friday at a roundtable in Bengaluru. The framework was prepared with the iSPIRT Foundation, a technology think tank, and the report describes it as India’s Digital Public Infrastructure for AI.

The report says the framework could unlock $500 billion in AI-driven value for India’s GDP by 2030. It would route model training through secure data environments, differential privacy and machine-readable electronic contracts, keeping raw data out of developers’ hands. It rests on four technical pillars: a Data Exchange Platform, Electronic Contracts, a Secure Data Environment and Differential Privacy. Training Data Providers such as hospitals, banks and public agencies would register datasets, while Data Collabs would aggregate and standardise data across sources. The report also ties the framework to a ₹20-25 trillion credit gap for micro, small and medium enterprises, an estimate it attributes to an expert committee constituted by the Reserve Bank of India.

The report warns that without such a framework, innovation would be stifled for Indian startups and researchers, and market concentration would increase favouring large entities. It calls the core problem a Data Deadlock, saying data sits divided across domains behind different institutional and regulatory walls. It argues that simple anonymisation will not work because of re-identification risks and utility loss. Oversight would rest with a consortium of participants including data providers, consumers, technology service providers, domain experts and civil society, while the competent government authority would certify models and could suspend or revoke non-compliant activities. The report says inaction is not a neutral stance and actively allows risks to grow and opportunities to wither.

The roadmap starts with pilots in finance and healthcare, with regulatory sandboxes in parallel, and later steps include cross-border agreements, capacity building and incentive models such as royalty or access-fee structures. The report pegs India’s financial services landscape at $550 billion and says DEPA could potentially extend formal credit to 400 million underserved individuals and MSMEs. In healthcare it describes a $600 billion-plus market and cites a Penn Medicine and Intel project across 71 international institutions that achieved over 99 per cent of the accuracy of a hypothetical model trained on centralised data. In education it cites 250 million students and a $29 billion EdTech sector.

stories.Headline: Apple adds touchscreen, PROLED XDR display to new MacBook Pro
stories.Summary:
Apple introduced new MacBook Pro models on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, adding touchscreen functionality and a PROLED XDR display to the lineup for the first time since 2006. The devices are powered by Apple's M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. Pre-orders began October 28, with availability starting November 9 through Apple's online store and authorized resellers. Apple CEO John Ternus highlighted the new display.

The PROLED XDR display offers peak brightness up to 2,000 nits and a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio, with an adaptive refresh rate up to 120 Hz via ProMotion technology. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro starts at ₹3,49,900, while the 16-inch M5 Pro model begins at ₹4,09,900. M5 Max versions start at ₹5,49,900 for the 16-inch and ₹5,89,900 for the 14-inch model. The M5 Max chip can run large language models with hundreds of billions of parameters entirely on the device, and each GPU core includes a neural accelerator to speed up AI workloads.

Separately, Apple debuted a 14-inch MacBook Pro with its newest M6 chip, which the company said provides 25% faster AI workloads versus devices powered by the M5 chip. Shelly Goldberg, Apple's vice president of hardware engineering, said the M6 chip takes performance to the next level with a boost in CPU speed and graphics and more powerful capabilities for on-device AI. The new MacBook Pro will start at $1,999, and an iMac with the M6 chip carries a base price of $1,499. Customers can pre-order both beginning Wednesday, October 28, in 35 countries and regions, with availability expected November 6. Apple said the M6 MacBook Pro offers up to 30% faster graphics and 24 hours of battery life, the longest ever in one of its computers.

Apple is due to host a "Pro and Tell" event in Los Angeles on Wednesday, October 28, where it is set to feature its first touch-screen MacBook Pro. It will be the third project launch event since John Ternus became Apple's new CEO in September, following an event focused on the next generation of iPhones and another showcasing new smart home products. IDC expects touchscreen laptops to comprise one in five notebook shipments by 2030. Francisco Jeronimo, Vice President of worldwide devices at IDC, said Apple's entry might not significantly affect other PC vendors, who target enterprise and education buyers, but it addresses a long-standing limitation in Apple's premium laptop offerings. He added that the debate about touch being a gimmick is over, shifting focus to implementation quality.

stories.Headline: S-1: Anthropic says it heavily depends on TSMC chips made in Taiwan and warns of risks from "potential disruption" amid geopolitical tensions with China (Joseph C. Sternberg/Wall Street Journal)
stories.Summary:
Anthropic filed a registration statement with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on October 26, 2026. In it, the artificial intelligence company warned that disruptions to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company could hurt its business. Anthropic said most of the world's most advanced chip manufacturing capacity is concentrated in Taiwan, mainly at TSMC. The filing was made as part of Anthropic's proposed initial public offering. The company said it has applied to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol "ANT".

Anthropic warned that military conflict, tariffs and trade restrictions, economic coercion, a blockade, a natural disaster, or another incident affecting Taiwan could severely disrupt the global supply of advanced chips. It said efforts to build enough advanced chip manufacturing capacity outside Taiwan, including in the United States, remain in early stages and may not produce adequate compute to materially reduce these concentration risks within the foreseeable future. The filing also said TSMC has at times been unable to meet the full demand for chip manufacturing capacity, leaving Anthropic without sufficient quantities of chips on a timely basis. Anthropic said any restrictions or delays on the supply of advanced chips out of Taiwan or TSMC would adversely affect its business, financial condition, and results of operations. It said the compute necessary for training and deploying frontier models depends on a supply chain with multiple potential points of constraint or failure.

The company, which develops the Claude family of AI models, also said limited manufacturing capacity for high-performance chips and memory could constrain its ability to secure the computing resources needed to support growing customer demand. It said the availability, pricing, and delivery timelines of computing resources are affected by advanced chips, other information technology equipment, electricity, and data centre infrastructure. The disclosure ties the expansion of the AI sector to the resilience of a highly concentrated global semiconductor supply chain, not only to advances in software and model capabilities. Anthropic said the effects of a disruption could be prolonged because of the time needed to establish alternative manufacturing facilities. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the proposed listing and the risks described in the filing.

stories.Headline: Microsoft and Alphabet capex comes in below forecasts as outside capacity arrives late; neocloud shares fall
stories.Summary:
Microsoft and Alphabet reported capital expenditures that fell short of analysts' estimates in their earnings reports on Wednesday. Microsoft cut its capex forecast for the 2026 calendar year to $170 billion from $175 billion, and Alphabet held its guidance at $195 billion to $205 billion. Microsoft CFO Amy Hood said on the earnings call that third-party providers of graphics processing units had delays that will push out some available capacity until the first half of 2027. Alphabet finance chief Anat Ashkenazi told analysts that outside computing power came online only at the very end of the third quarter.

Hood said Microsoft was expecting new capacity from third parties, but some GPU-as-a-Service contracts have been delayed until the second half of its fiscal year. She said she expects capital spending to accelerate in the first half of 2027 because of higher component costs and the delayed deliveries. Microsoft reported $92.3 billion in revenue, up 19%, for its fiscal first quarter ending Sept. 30, and Azure cloud revenue rose 48% to more than $33 billion. Alphabet shares fell about 10% in extended trading after the company missed on earnings and revenue and reported negative free cash flow of more than $9 billion.

Shares of neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN dropped after the reports, as did Oracle, one of the biggest spenders on AI infrastructure. Hood did not name the delayed providers, but Microsoft relies on CoreWeave, IREN and Nebius, among others. Chris Ballard, managing director of Check Capital Management, wrote to CNBC that he was pleased with what he saw and heard and trusted management's approach to AI spending. Cantor analysts led by Thomas Blakey wrote that they viewed the quarter as further validation of Microsoft's AI-led growth opportunity and pushed their one-year price target to $630 from $608.

Investors will get a final read on hyperscaler capex for the quarter when Amazon reports results after the close on Thursday. Meta said last week that it expects full-year capex of $135 billion to $145 billion, raising the bottom of the range from $130 billion. Analysts at Gartner told CNBC they predict that by 2030, 80% of neocloud companies will either be absorbed or completely cease operations. Nvidia-backed neocloud Firmus, based in Australia, withdrew plans to go public earlier this month despite large usage commitments from Meta and OpenAI.

stories.Headline: Microsoft, Google report booming AI revenue as the tech reshapes business
stories.Summary:
Alphabet's Google, Microsoft, and Amazon face a collective test this week as they report quarterly earnings and must explain their spending on artificial intelligence. Their results, which account for more than a third of the S&P 500's earnings, follow Meta's report and come as investors weigh how much the companies are spending against the returns they expect. The central question is what the AI spending figure is and how it compares with those expected returns. Bank of America strategist Savita Subramanian wrote on Tuesday that all eyes would be on AI monetization versus spending.

Justifying the spending has been a feature of earnings reports for the past two years, but the stakes are higher now because economic conditions and the investing environment have shifted. A recent tech sell-off has put AI financing in the spotlight, and investors have voiced mixed feelings about Meta selling shares and borrowing to fund its AI ambitions. Demand for financing has intensified competition for capital, pressuring tech companies to raise large sums in advance. The article also notes that Wall Street is preparing IPOs for two frontier AI labs, Anthropic, possibly next month, and OpenAI, likely next year.

Business behavior toward AI is also changing, according to the reporting. Companies are becoming pickier, scaling back, using less expensive models, and trying different services, a slowdown the article says suggests heavy demand for computing existed mainly when it seemed free. Because that demand is price-sensitive, justifying AI costs will matter more. Meta has reoriented itself around the division behind its Muse product, which it envisions as a large service network and revenue engine, and the early success of personal assistant AI agents has also reshaped product priorities. The bull case holds that the cash may not arrive soon but will eventually flow, and the article says Microsoft, Google, and Amazon will also have to supply answers this week.

stories.Headline: First Humanist Wins Religious Exemption From AI at Work. Could You?
stories.Summary:
A humanist from Kentucky has become, by the American Humanist Association's account, the first humanist granted a religious exemption from using artificial intelligence at work. David Durman, a 45-year-old research administrator at the University of Kentucky, objected when the university began asking employees to use AI tools in their workflow, including Microsoft Teams Copilot, Claude and ChatGPT. He argued that using such tools would undercut his ability to think through his work and ethics, which he sees as part of developing himself as a moral person. With help from the American Humanist Association, he requested an accommodation under Title VII, the federal law that lets employees seek changes to work requirements for religious reasons, and in a letter dated September 25 an Office of Equal Opportunity senior manager said the request was granted.

The accommodation means Durman is excused from personal use of AI to complete his tasks, though he may still be expected to attend meetings or submit materials through sites that use AI. Staff attorney Alexandria Huiskens of the American Humanist Association said officials found no undue burden on his department and granted the request promptly after a collegial meeting. Durman's letter cited his personal beliefs and the 2003 Humanist Manifesto, which stresses freedom of conscience and human flourishing. Federal courts have ruled that humanism qualifies as a religion, so humanists receive the same Title VII protections as other faith groups, according to Huiskens. Legal scholar Douglas Laycock noted that such requests depend on whether the belief is sincere and analogous to a religious commitment, a question an employer would normally investigate.

The case comes amid wider skepticism about AI from religious leaders and the public. Pope Leo XIV warned in his recent encyclical "Magnifica Humanitas" that AI could weaken democracy and human dignity and concentrate power among a few elites. A Washington Post-ABC News-IPOS poll released this week found that 57 percent of Americans said AI is bad for society, and two-thirds opposed building the data centers needed to run it. Durman said he worries AI use harms society at a broader level, and his request was partly inspired by Erin Maus, a Unitarian Universalist software engineer who received an exemption from her employer over religious concerns about AI. Durman said he hopes his example and those of others seeking accommodations will prompt more people to think through the implications of AI use.

stories.Headline: Domain-specialised AI model portfolio to revolutionise agentic chip and system design
stories.Summary:
Cadence announced the Maestro AI Model Portfolio on October 28, 2026, according to Design & Reuse, while Electropages dated its report October 30, 2026. Cadence, a company listed on Nasdaq under the symbol CDNS and based in San Jose, California, introduced the portfolio to power its Cadence AI Super Agents across semiconductor and system design workflows. The portfolio combines domain-specialised post-trained large language models, trained decision models and self-improving agent skills, and it spans multiple model sizes and architectures. It is integrated with the Cadence AI Super Agents named AuraStack, ChipStack, InnoStack and ViraStack, along with Cadence's electronic design automation and system design automation tools and reinforcement learning.

The portfolio is meant to work alongside frontier and open-weight models, and it can be further post-trained on a customer's proprietary data, designs and workflows. Initial results show up to 30% improvement in quality of results and up to 5X greater token efficiency compared with a general-purpose foundation model. The complete environment can run on Cadence's secure cloud platform, on secure public clouds or in a customer-controlled on-premises environment. Cadence and NVIDIA are also working together on agent security through integration with the NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture, and the portfolio includes NVIDIA Nemotron and other models.

Anirudh Devgan, president and CEO at Cadence, said revolutionising complex engineering tasks requires deep domain-specialised intelligence, and that combining the Maestro models with leading frontier and open-weight models lets the AI Super Agents drive Cadence tools with skill and efficiency. Tim Costa, vice president and general manager of industrial and computational engineering at NVIDIA, said agentic chip design needs AI that can generate design content, evaluate trade-offs and learn from verified engineering results, and that grounding reinforcement learning in feedback from EDA tools and deterministic solvers teaches agents to make better decisions. Hisato Yoshida, COO of Socionext, said his company is deploying the InnoStack AI Super Agent into its production design environment and expects up to 5X overall productivity gains while maintaining design quality. Garima Sharda, vice president of engineering at Silicon Labs, said her teams achieved acceleration in root-cause analysis and end-to-end debug during pre-silicon low power verification using Cadence Verisium Debug as part of the ChipStack AI Super Agent.

The articles describe the portfolio as part of a vertically integrated learning environment that combines company domain knowledge, curated engineering datasets, the AI Super Agents, the EDA and SDA tools and evaluation harnesses. Its algorithms and deterministic solvers evaluate outputs against engineering objectives, constraints and ground truth, creating closed and verified feedback loops for reinforcement learning and recursive improvement. Given a high-level objective, the AI Super Agents interpret design intent, decompose tasks, orchestrate the Maestro portfolio with other models and drive the Cadence tools, and balancing tool calls with model invocations reduces token usage. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the stated plans, such as Socionext's deployment and the continued work between Cadence and NVIDIA on agent security.
