stories.Headline: Achieving client trust with AI: The importance of governance in wealth management - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Puneet Asthana, Executive Director and CTO of Shriram Group's capital market businesses, wrote an article published by ETCIO on October 29, 2026 about using AI in wealth management. He described how clients want an app that seems to know them, with portfolios that reflect how they behave when markets drop. He said the pitch decks rarely mention the price of entry, which is holding sensitive things clients have told very few people. He argued that guardrails with explainability are the key drivers that make clients willing to share in the first place.

Asthana said AI needs to see three kinds of signals: how a client behaves under volatility, what he buys, ignores and redeems early, and whether his declared risk appetite matches what he does when things turn ugly. He called this the most sensitive data a wealth firm holds, noting that a PAN tells you about an account while a pattern of panic-selling tells you about a person. He set out principles including not training AI models on client behaviour, getting "no training" in writing, and preferring India-hosted enterprise deployments inside your own tenancy. He also said firms should mask names, PANs, account numbers and contact details with tokens, and let consent set the boundary under the DPDP Act.

He said the regulated entity answers for its AI, as SEBI has made clear, and that SEBI's cybersecurity framework, access logs, hard walls between group entities and a human checking AI output sit around all this. He acknowledged the approach slows firms down early on, but said speed without governance is sophisticated risk. He said a leaked behavioural profile would bring a regulator to the door and the client would leave, which for a wealth firm is the whole business. He was surprised at how little personalisation is given up, since relationship managers want something that pulls the right context at the right moment rather than a model that remembers a client forever.

His advice to peers chasing this is to sort out the data foundation and the guardrails before listing use cases. He said personalisation built on that can afford to be ambitious, while built on anything else it is a liability waiting for a date. He noted the industry is still learning where the edges are and that everyone will get some calls wrong. The article carries a disclaimer that the views are solely the author's and that ETCIO does not necessarily subscribe to them.

Articles.Title: Achieving client trust with AI: The importance of governance in wealth management - ET CIO

stories.Headline: Nearly 60% of firms yet to move AI beyond pilots as deployment remains key challenge - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
A report by Citi Institute found that nearly 60 percent of organisations surveyed are still in the exploration or pilot stages of artificial intelligence adoption. Only around 40 percent have moved to production or scaling across their operations. The report was published in a story dated October 29, 2026. It said the next phase of AI adoption depends on companies moving beyond trials to wider implementation.

The survey found a clear regional gap. North America is ahead, with 77 percent of surveyed organisations already using AI in production or scaling it. Asia Pacific is more focused on exploring applications, running pilot programmes and building capabilities, while Europe sits in an intermediate position. Business model transformation was the leading objective for AI investment, cited by 34 percent of respondents, followed by capability building at 32 percent and improving specific business performance indicators at 25 percent.

Among companies in the production and scaling stages, 60 percent reported transformational value creation of more than 15 percent through cost reduction, employee productivity or revenue growth. The report said AI's biggest opportunity lies in redesigning business models rather than only automating existing tasks. It said scaling would depend less on access to models alone and more on proprietary data, expertise and integration into core operations. It also noted that companies moving toward production tend to adopt shorter investment horizons, treating AI as an operational business capability rather than a long-term experiment.

Articles.Title: Nearly 60% of firms yet to move AI beyond pilots as deployment remains key challenge - ET CIO

stories.Headline: Which human skills become more valuable as AI becomes better at doing the work? - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Kshama Singh, HR Head at Powerweave, wrote an article published by ETCIO on Oct 29, 2026, about which human skills gain value as AI takes over repetitive and mundane tasks. She argued that critical thinking, creativity, communication, empathy and adaptability are becoming more important to organisations. These skills help people make sound judgments, collaborate and handle different situations, she wrote. She said human skills will play an increasingly significant role alongside AI as technology advances.

The article cites the World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025, which draws on more than 1,000 leading employers representing over 14 million workers across 22 industry clusters and 55 economies. Analytical thinking is the most sought-after core skill, with seven out of 10 companies calling it essential, followed by resilience, flexibility and agility, then leadership and social influence, with creative thinking fourth and motivation and self-awareness fifth. The report projects that 39% of key skills will change by 2030, down from 44% in 2023, and that 170 million new jobs will be created globally over the next five years, equal to 14% of today's employment, with a net increase of 78 million jobs. It also projects that AI and big data skills will grow in importance faster than any others, while creative thinking, resilience, flexibility and agility, and curiosity and lifelong learning also rise.

Singh said employers are hiring for curiosity, judgement and collaboration rather than just technical credentials, and are training people in communication, critical thinking and working effectively with AI tools. She said managers at Powerweave are becoming a source of clarity, encouragement and empathy, helping people question an AI output rather than simply accept it. She said the development challenge is broader than teaching people to use AI, and is about building the judgement and confidence to use it well. She credited a growing focus on continuous learning, upskilling and reskilling for helping companies anticipate change better.

Singh wrote that work is not simply disappearing but changing, and that people who combine technical fluency with curiosity, judgement, communication and adaptability are likely to be better placed to navigate the shift. She said AI literacy will become part of being effective at work, including knowing what AI can do, how to use it well and where its limitations lie. She said performance is being viewed differently, with the quality of decisions, the questions people ask and the ownership they take mattering more than volume. She concluded that as AI gets better at doing the work, human judgement does not become less valuable and in many situations becomes the thing that matters most.

Articles.Title: Which human skills become more valuable as AI becomes better at doing the work? - ET CIO

stories.Headline: The AI Slowdown Narrative Doesn’t Reflect Enterprise Realit
stories.Summary:
Industry leaders say the debate about slowing frontier AI development does not match what is happening inside enterprises, which are still adopting the technology across business processes. They argue the challenge is no longer only model performance, because organisations must also deal with unreliable data, integration with existing systems, governance, implementation costs and accountability for outcomes. Several of them spoke in an article published on 29 October 2026 by analyticsindiamag.com. The piece was updated the same day.

Ram Kumar Nimmakayala, a product leader for AI, machine learning and data at Western Governors University in the US, said nine out of ten AI pilots fail to reach production, rarely because of the model itself. He said the hard problems are poor data quality, resistance to changing workflows and a lack of clear ownership. Rakesh Pal, an insurance industry leader working on AI adoption in India's financial services sector, said many organisations need to step back and work on readiness first. Guru Ananthanarayanan, managing director for India at Cognite, described a slowdown as a rest before a sprint, giving the industry time to put governance and responsible AI frameworks in place, especially for frontier large language models.

Dr Prashant Ramappa, who leads data science, AI, generative AI and machine learning at AT&T, rejected the slowdown narrative and said what is visible is exhaustion at the model-creation layer, with team burnout and heavy capital spending from repeated training cycles. He said model developers need to slow down to make systems safe, but competition keeps them from easing off. Dr Rajan Gupta of Deutsche Telekom Digital Labs called the gap between fast-advancing AI and the pace at which enterprises can absorb it the enterprise autonomy gap. He said an agent that answers a customer query is simple, while one authorised to approve refunds or change financial records is a different engineering challenge, and the real slowdown is in the ability to trust, govern and operationalise such actions at scale.

Jyotishko Biswas, an AI leader at HP Finance in India, said continuous reevaluation as new models arrive slows implementation and leaves execution teams unclear. Gupta said his team switches models only for cost savings, lower latency, better response quality or when support for the existing model ends. The article says the focus is shifting from AI-assisted workflows to systems that execute business tasks independently, which requires confidence in reliability, security and accountability. It adds that the question for enterprises is increasingly not how fast they can adopt the latest model but whether they can use it reliably, responsibly and at a sustainable cost.

Articles.Title: The AI Slowdown Narrative Doesn’t Reflect Enterprise Realit - analyticsindiamag.com

stories.Headline: ‘You’re Not Doing This AI Stuff,’ Databricks CEO Tells Snowflake
stories.Summary:
Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi took a public jab at rival Snowflake over its AI strategy on X, after Snowflake CEO Sridhar Ramaswamy questioned Databricks' revenue growth. Ghodsi wrote that the two companies are complementary and should not fight, then said that since Snowflake is not doing this AI stuff, it should consider getting its AI tokens through Databricks. He pitched Databricks' platform as a way for Snowflake to access open-source and frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and xAI, and promoted Unity Gateway, which offers model routing, budget management and access controls. He said most customers used the platform to cut token spend by about 30% in recent months while token counts went up, and ended by asking for a quick proof of concept. Ramaswamy replied that the offer was generous but that he had been asking about revenue, not contributing to it.

The exchange began when Ramaswamy called on Databricks to disclose more details about its financial performance, quoting a post by venture capitalist Ben Horowitz titled Databricks and the Future of the Firm and writing, release all the numbers. He questioned whether Databricks' reported 80% year-on-year revenue growth would fall to 65% after excluding pass-through inference revenue. He also asked how much growth came from AI-native customers and how much reflected the shift from one-time software licences to service-based revenue. He sought further details on free cash flow, remaining performance obligations, current remaining performance obligations, GAAP and non-GAAP operating margins, and share dilution.

Databricks announced in August that its annualised revenue run-rate had crossed $7 billion, with revenue growing more than 80% year-on-year in the second quarter. It also raised $5 billion in a funding round at a $190 billion valuation and reported positive adjusted cash flow over the preceding 12 months. The company said its Lakehouse data warehousing business had crossed a $1.5 billion revenue run-rate, while its Lakebase database product had exceeded $100 million. Databricks has been expanding its AI offerings as enterprises look to deploy AI models and agents using their corporate data, and its Unity AI Gateway provides tools to manage access to models and control AI spending. Snowflake offers AI capabilities through its Cortex platform, which lets customers work with AI models and build applications using their data.

Articles.Title: ‘You’re Not Doing This AI Stuff,’ Databricks CEO Tells Snowflake - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: India’s Enterprises are Scaling AI. Is the Infrastructure Ready?
stories.Summary:
Indian enterprises are investing in artificial intelligence, but moving AI agents from pilots into production is testing their existing digital infrastructure. Many organisations still rely on legacy applications, fragmented data and architectures that were not built for software that acts across multiple systems. An agent processing a customer order may need to pull details from a CRM platform, check inventory in an ERP system and start the next workflow step. If those applications cannot exchange information reliably, the process can fail even when the model works as intended.

A Dell Technologies study conducted with Vanson Bourne found that 67% of Indian organisations believe their current data centre environments are not ready to support AI workloads at production scale. Vishal Kappanna, Engineering Director at Tesco Technology, said the biggest hurdle in moving an agent from pilot to production is rarely the model itself, but integrating with fragmented data, legacy applications, security controls and long-standing business processes. Vijay Yellapragada, Consulting AI and Data and US Commercial Leader at EY GDS, said a pilot shows an agent can perform a task, while production requires proving the enterprise can trust it to do so repeatedly, securely and at scale. Premalakshmi PR, Managing Director and Area VP, India and SAARC at NetApp, said the biggest challenge is often the data behind the model, spread across on-premises, cloud and edge locations.

Venkat Sitaram, Senior Director and Country Head, Infrastructure Solutions Group, India, at Dell Technologies, said agentic AI is changing demands on enterprise infrastructure, which must now accommodate software that interprets information, makes decisions and initiates actions. Dell pointed to customer deployments: Lakshmikumaran & Sridharan Attorneys runs an in-house AI assistant on-premises using the Dell AI Factory, Zoho is developing privacy-first, multimodal enterprise and agentic AI capabilities on the platform, and Omega Healthcare has modernised its infrastructure with Dell Private Cloud. The article says most enterprises are not replacing legacy systems but wrapping and modernising them through orchestration platforms, APIs and governance layers. It says the deciding factor will be whether existing digital infrastructure can support agents as they move from isolated tasks to connected business workflows at scale.

Articles.Title: India’s Enterprises are Scaling AI. Is the Infrastructure Ready? - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: Gnani AI Launches Prisma v3.0 Speech Recognition Model for 10 Languages
stories.Summary:
Bengaluru-based Gnani AI launched Prisma v3.0, an automatic speech recognition model, on 29 October 2026. The model is designed to transcribe multilingual conversations, including speech that switches between Indian languages and English within a single sentence. It supports Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Gujarati, Punjabi, Kannada, Telugu, Tamil, Malayalam and English. According to the company, it recorded a macro Word Error Rate of 16.93 on the Vistaar benchmark.

The company compared that figure with 19.98 for ElevenLabs Scribe v2, 20.51 for Microsoft Azure Speech-to-Text and 26.57 for Deepgram Nova 3. Prisma v3.0 offers four transcription modes, named Verbatim, Transcribe, Code-mix and Transliterate, which let users keep fillers and repetitions, produce cleaner text, retain original scripts or write speech in English letters. It also supports custom vocabulary prompting, with up to 200 terms per request, and Gnani reported that recall of supplied terms rose from 70.9% to 90.3% without additional training or fine-tuning. The company described that result as an upper bound from an evaluation using public read speech with the relevant terms supplied.

Gnani reported 98% accuracy for language identification on audio clips longer than three seconds across the Vistaar and Svarah datasets. It also said false text generated from noise-only audio fell from 13.4% to 4.2% compared with Prisma 2.5. In its announcement, the company said it built the model because a correct transcript still was not a usable one, pointing to the challenges of making speech recognition useful for real-world conversations. The model outperforms Prisma 2.5 and targets transcription errors involving mixed-language speech, spoken numbers, brand names and short responses that can affect enterprise voice applications.

Prisma v3.0 accepts 8 kHz telephony audio and 16 kHz audio from applications and voice-over-internet-protocol systems. Gnani said it can be deployed through cloud, hybrid and on-premises infrastructure, including air-gapped environments. In its language-level comparison, the company said the model recorded lower Word Error Rate than Microsoft Azure Speech-to-Text across all nine supported Indian languages. The article notes that the aggregate Vistaar results reflect a separate comparison across the benchmark's datasets.

Articles.Title: Gnani AI Launches Prisma v3.0 Speech Recognition Model for 10 Languages - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: Maharashtra Government Adopts Sarvam AI Solutions
stories.Summary:
Sarvam AI has rolled out its Indus Cowork platform to 2,500 Maharashtra government officials, after Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis launched it on October 28. The Maharashtra government approved the deployment of Sarvam's sovereign AI solutions in August. The rollout comes under a two-year agreement valued at ₹11.26 crore. The state is among India's first to commit to sovereign AI across its administration.

The platform helps officials draft documents, analyse reports, summarise files and search government records. It supports 22 languages, including Marathi, and lets officials draft official notes and replies, research policies, translate and summarise lengthy documents, analyse data and convert scanned records into searchable text. The package also includes GR Expert for searching Government Resolutions across departments and tracking changes to them, Email Summariser for condensing official correspondence, and RFP Bid Evaluator for comparing and assessing tender bids. Beyond Indus Cowork, the agreement covers Samvaad, a voice and WhatsApp-based system for citizen outreach, and integrates Sarvam's Saaras speech recognition and Bulbul text-to-speech models with the state's MahaAI platform.

Sarvam said its solutions would run on secure, audited infrastructure located entirely within India, keeping government data in the country. The company also said the state could inspect the systems hosting the deployment. The agreement places AI tools within government workflows involving official correspondence, policy documents and departmental records. The two-year outlay of ₹11.26 crore covers the deployment of Sarvam's sovereign AI solutions.

Articles.Title: Maharashtra Government Adopts Sarvam AI Solutions - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: AI changes how accountants work, not what they do
stories.Summary:
The article reports on how artificial intelligence is changing accounting work, based on interviews ahead of the 2026 AICPA National Tax Conference. The conference first spotlighted generative AI in November 2023, when tax professionals were still trying to understand how the technology might reshape tax practice. OpenAI introduced ChatGPT about a month after the 2022 conference. Since then AI has steadily gained visibility at the event: two sessions at the 2024 conference included AI in their titles, the 2025 conference featured an AI keynote and another AI-focused session, and in 2026 AI is listed among the conference's six hot topics and appears in the titles of four sessions. This year AI is the focus of sessions on ethics, workflow, firm operations, and the changing role of practitioners.

David Lifson, a CPA and senior advisor at Crowe, said in a 2023 keynote that he hoped AI would make people smarter rather than replaceable, and three years later he said he is more convinced than ever that AI cannot replace humans. He described it as an evolutionary tool without judgment and a data accelerator. Brian Davis, a CPA who is CEO of One Stop CPA and founder of OneForm for Accountants, leads a session titled "What in the AI Is Happening With Tax Firms" with two other CPAs, examining how firms adopt AI tools and where practitioners find value. Davis said AI is bigger than earlier advances such as cloud computing or e-filing because it is in every area of the business, but he also said it is sometimes overhyped and not the flip-on switch people make it seem.

Both men view AI as the latest step in a progression of technologies that changed how accountants work, with spreadsheets replacing columnar pads and electronic research replacing shelves of tax books. Lifson, who is 76 and has spent five decades in the profession, said technology has historically changed the nature of the work rather than reducing its amount, because as firms became more efficient, client expectations rose, the tax code grew more complex, and more choices required professional judgment. Davis said he once counted 250 clients meaning 250 tax returns, but now counts relationships and can have fewer than 50 relationships while doing more work than those 250 returns, and he said AI accelerated a five-year road map into a single tax season. He said there is still a difference between someone with two years of experience and someone with 20.

Lifson said the 2023 panel did not fully appreciate the need for safeguards as AI systems became more powerful and autonomous, and he said anyone reviewing AI's first-stage work must be trained, informed, and skillful enough to find its mistakes. Davis warned that overreliance on AI can create false confidence, and he said nobody knows where the technology is going or whether it will wipe out an industry or make the world a better place. Lifson said he worries about global risk for banks, governments, and other entities because of reliance on computers to process transactions and store data as paper books and records disappear, though he distinguished that risk from the use of AI in human life. His takeaway, he said, is that AI makes people better.

Articles.Title: AI changes how accountants work, not what they do - Journal of Accountancy

stories.Headline: Hybrid Bonding Is Costly. Is There a Cheaper Bumpless Option?
stories.Summary:
TrendForce published an article on October 30, 2026, asking whether a cheaper bumpless option exists as hybrid bonding remains costly. The article follows an earlier piece on why hybrid bonding has become the key to getting past the scaling limit of micro-bumps. It notes that TSMC's SoIC-X is expected to lift demand for hybrid bonders as its adoption in AI chips grows. The road from micro-bump to hybrid bonding is not a single step, and the industry is still seeking intermediate or complementary options.

As bump pitch shrinks, bonding has progressed from flip-chip, suited to bump pitches of roughly 50 µm, to micro-bump plus thermo-compression bonding. Fluxless TCB now supports a bump pitch as small as about 8 µm, but the micro-bump still faces a physical scaling limit. Bumpless bonding means no conventional solder balls, with metal on the chip surface such as Cu pads or under-bump metal making direct contact. This allows smaller interconnects and a bond pitch that can reach around 5 µm. Hybrid bonding is currently the only commercialized bumpless technology, bonding dielectric layers and Cu pads directly through steps such as plasma activation and pre-bonding.

SK hynix's roadmap, published in August 2026, positions bumpless TCB as an interim step between fluxless TCB and hybrid bonding. The article says it looks at the bumpless options beyond hybrid bonding, how they work, how they differ, and how equipment suppliers are developing their strategies. It states that behind the paywall it explores what drives the cost of hybrid bonding and how bumpless flip-chip, bumpless TCB and hybrid bonding compare. It also covers when memory makers could move to bumpless bonding and how die bonder suppliers are pursuing multiple tracks at once. The article does not say what happens next beyond these listed topics.

Articles.Title: Hybrid Bonding Is Costly. Is There a Cheaper Bumpless Option? - TrendForce

stories.Headline: SEMICON Europa 2026 puts advanced packaging and AI in focus ...
stories.Summary:
SEMICON Europa 2026 will take place in Munich, Germany, from November 10 to 13, 2026, according to an article by Asma Adhimi published on eeNews Europe on October 29, 2026. The event will be held at Messe München alongside electronica and will bring together semiconductor industry leaders. It is organized by SEMI Europe, whose president is Laith Altimime. The gathering is meant to explore advanced packaging, AI-driven manufacturing and cross-border collaboration.

The event will focus on technologies and investment strategies aimed at improving Europe's competitiveness and the resilience of its semiconductor supply chain. The Advanced Packaging Conference will examine heterogeneous integration, chiplets and next-generation packaging, with topics including wafer- and panel-level packaging, hybrid bonding, silicon photonics, co-packaged optics and thermal management. AI-powered inspection, advanced metrology and testing will also feature, along with Europe's packaging ecosystem and pilot-line activities. The Fab Management Forum is scheduled for November 11 and will cover AI-driven factory automation, progress toward autonomous fabs, and silicon carbide, wide-bandgap semiconductors, photonics and advanced foundry services.

Altimime said that as Europe navigates a complex geopolitical and technological landscape, advanced packaging is becoming a strategic pillar of semiconductor supply chain resilience. The program will also address moving advanced packaging innovations from research into high-volume manufacturing. The Voices from the Industry program will broaden the discussion to semiconductor security, supply chains and regional cooperation. The co-located imec Technology Forum will address emerging chiplet architectures, sustainable manufacturing and policy frameworks supporting Europe's AI ecosystem.

Other sessions will cover secure-by-design computing through the CHERI Alliance, agentic AI for semiconductor supply chain management, and advanced packaging industrialization. CEA-Leti will showcase innovations in 3D integration, silicon photonics and energy-efficient AI hardware. Representatives from the Baltic Sea region will discuss opportunities for a more resilient European semiconductor corridor. The program will also highlight transatlantic collaboration opportunities, including Arizona's expanding semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem.

Articles.Title: SEMICON Europa 2026 puts advanced packaging and AI in focus ... - eeNews Europe

stories.Headline: Glass Substrates Open the Window to Advancing AI Chip Packaging
stories.Summary:
Glass substrates are being developed for advanced packaging of AI and high-performance computing chips, Lam Research said in a blog post published on October 29, 2026. The company said glass has long served as a temporary round carrier in packaging, and the industry is now working on large rectangular panels and permanent uses such as glass-core package substrates. Lam described glass as gaining momentum because of its mechanical, electrical and chemical properties. The post said glass substrates support more complex, high-density chip assemblies.

Lam said glass can be tuned so its coefficient of thermal expansion closely matches silicon and is significantly lower than that of organic substrates, which helps prevent warpage during thermal cycling. It said the flat surface allows fine line and space patterning down to two microns, and that glass offers superior isolation for wiring along with low dielectric loss and high resistivity. The post said glass is used as a temporary carrier for AI accelerators and is being developed as a core substrate for future generations, and that it suits 5G RF modules operating above 28 GHz and photonic integrated circuits. Lam said glass carriers are established in production, while permanent glass interposers and glass-core IC substrates remain at earlier stages of development and adoption.

Lam said glass is brittle, which creates challenges in handling, singulation and defect management, and that forming features inside glass requires care to avoid chipping or cracking. It said depositing metallic films on glass requires advanced plating processes, with adhesion promoters often used before electroless seed deposition and specialized electroplating needed to fill through-glass vias. The post said handling panels larger than 500 mm demands vacuum or edge-grip tools, and thermal processing must be carefully ramped to avoid stress fractures. Lam said it is investing in research, process expertise and panel-processing hardware, including its Kallisto panel electroplating system and its Phoenix panel processing system.

Lam said the industry must address manufacturability and standardization challenges before wide adoption, because panel sizes, via specifications and material stacks vary across suppliers. The company said it collaborates with substrate makers, outsourced semiconductor assembly and test providers, equipment manufacturers and material suppliers to co-optimize electroplating solutions. The post said adoption is still evolving, with technical, manufacturing and ecosystem hurdles to overcome. It said the potential benefits include higher performance, greater integration, new applications and more efficient panel processing.

Articles.Title: Glass Substrates Open the Window to Advancing AI Chip Packaging - Lam Research Newsroom

stories.Headline: SK Hynix Creates Americas Chief Post, Taps President Ahn Hyun to Spearhead US Big Tech HBM Push
stories.Summary:
SK Hynix carried out a president-level reshuffle effective November 1 and created a new president-level organization called the Americas Chief, based in the United States. President Ahn Hyun, who had led development of AI memory including HBM and SOCAMM, was named to head the new unit. The company announced the regular personnel appointment on October 30. Ahn will build a response system for US big tech customers.

Cha Sun-yong, head of the Future Technology Research Institute, was named to lead development, the post left vacant by Ahn's move. He will also keep his role at the institute, strengthening the link between advanced technology research and product development. Yoon Poong-young, who headed the Global Growth Task Force, moves to lead the Corporate Center. CEO Kwak Noh-jung was retained, after SK Hynix posted record results for six consecutive quarters.

The company described Ahn as the right person, combining technical expertise and leadership with business, strategic and global capabilities. It said he will work to strengthen technical leadership and R&D capabilities. The company expects Cha to lead next-generation memory technology development based on his expertise in advanced semiconductor technology. Yoon will lead global business expansion and the hunt for new growth engines.

The market views the reshuffle as weighted toward mid- to long-term customer relationships and the technology roadmap rather than short-term results. HBM is an essential component in AI accelerators, making joint development between suppliers and customers from the design stage increasingly important. With AI memory demand continuing, the depth of cooperation with US big tech has emerged as a variable that will determine leadership in the next HBM generation transition. Through the reshuffle, SK Hynix plans to strengthen US customer response, enhance the link between research and product development, and accelerate global business expansion.

Articles.Title: SK Hynix Creates Americas Chief Post, Taps President Ahn Hyun to Spearhead US Big Tech HBM Push - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: Hanmi Semiconductor lifts Q3 profit 34% and eyes record revenue on HBM demand
stories.Summary:
Hanmi Semiconductor reported higher third-quarter profit on Thursday, October 30, 2026, even as its revenue and operating profit fell from the previous quarter. On a consolidated basis, the company posted revenue of 181.0 billion won and operating profit of 90.8 billion won for the July to September period. Compared with a year earlier, revenue rose 8.9% and operating profit increased 33.9%, lifting the operating margin to 50.2% from 40.8%. Against the second quarter, however, revenue dropped 27.9% from 251.2 billion won and operating profit fell 30.3% from 130.3 billion won. Cumulative revenue for the first three quarters slipped 2.1% to 483.1 billion won, while cumulative operating profit rose 2.6% to 229.6 billion won.

The company attributed the quarterly decline to a weaker exchange rate, which reduced the won value of its results, and to the deferral of revenue recognition for some equipment into the fourth quarter. It expects the deferred equipment revenue to be recognized in the final quarter, alongside higher equipment supply to overseas customers, which it says should produce its highest quarterly revenue on record. Hanmi expects to set a new annual revenue record this year, after records in 2024 and 2025, and anticipates further growth next year. It also said shareholder returns should expand, with a official noting that dividends are expected to reach a record level this year following a dividend of 800 won per share for last year.

The forecasts rest on rising demand for high-bandwidth memory and advanced artificial intelligence packaging from global chipmakers. The company's main product is a thermocompression bonder used in HBM production, which uses heat and pressure to stack and bond multiple DRAM chips vertically, and demand for precise bonding grows as HBM stacks gain layers. Hanmi plans to expand supply of next-generation HBM bonders as well as new thermocompression and flip-chip bonders for large-area AI semiconductor packaging. It is also pursuing overseas customers, with overseas revenue averaging more than 72% of total revenue over the past 15 years.

This month it set up a local subsidiary, HANMI USA, in San Jose, California, after earlier subsidiaries in Taiwan, China and Singapore. A representative said the U.S. unit will support local technical service and new customers in the American advanced packaging market. The articles do not give further detail on the timing of the fourth-quarter equipment recognition or on the size of the dividend expected this year. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Hanmi Semiconductor lifts Q3 profit 34% and eyes record revenue on HBM demand - Chosunbiz

stories.Headline: TSMC Expands AP7, AP8 as CoWoS Capacity Remains Tight
stories.Summary:
TSMC and 精材 (3374) are linked to a potential purchase of two 友達 (2409) factories for more than NT$20 billion, according to a report published on October 29, 2026. The plants, L7A and L5C, are in Taiwan's Central Taiwan Science Park and sit beside TSMC's Fab 15. L5C makes laptop panels, while L7A began operating in 2006 and primarily produces television panels along with some monitor panels. Both factories remain in operation, and the transaction has not been confirmed.

If the reported price is reached, it would exceed the NT$17.1 billion sale of an Innolux factory. The final price, scope and division of buyer roles have not been disclosed. The report comes as CoWoS capacity remains tight and TSMC expands its AP7 and AP8 advanced-packaging facilities. TSMC owns about 41% of 精材 and is its largest customer, accounting for more than 70% of 精材's revenue. 精材's P2 plant has about 23,000 square meters of clean-room space and is already at capacity.

The two companies are also working on a 12-inch integrated voltage regulator process using backside copper for high-performance computing chips. Validation and pilot production could be completed as early as late 2026, with mass production projected to begin in the second half of 2027. If a sale proceeds, 友達 plans to requalify products at other factories to maintain supply. The transfer and closing are expected around the end of 2027.

Articles.Title: TSMC Expands AP7, AP8 as CoWoS Capacity Remains Tight - www.tokenpost.com

stories.Headline: Chinese-Made HBM Spot Prices Top Imports by 5%-10% as Mature-Generation Quotes Near $110 Red Line
stories.Summary:
In the fourth quarter of 2026, China's AI compute supply chain showed a structural split in memory, according to BigGo Finance. Contract prices for single-stack HBM3E and HBM4, the international frontier generations, climbed above $200 to $300. Procurement prices for mature-generation HBM2 and HBM2E used in mainstream Chinese accelerator cards rose from $30 to $40 to $95 to $120. Spot quotes for Chinese-made HBM ran about 5% to 10% above comparable imports from Samsung and SK Hynix, approaching the downstream tolerance limit of $110 per unit.

The article attributes the price inversion to three overlapping factors. Chinese HBM production lines are still in the yield-ramp phase, with a blended yield of about 25% and a next-stage target of 40% to 50%, and early equipment depreciation and trial-production outlays are large. Core buyers such as Huawei's Ascend, Cambricon and Hygon Information Technology are on export-control entity lists, so incremental demand flows back to China's limited spot supply and domestic lines. Channel research expects China's total demand for high-compute chips in 2027 to reach 3.5 million to 4 million units, with Huawei's Ascend series alone at no fewer than 2.4 million on a conservative view.

Huawei is responding with a tiered memory architecture. The Ascend 950DT carries self-developed HiZQ 2.0 memory with 144GB capacity and 4.0TB/s bandwidth, about 60% to 65% of 950-series shipments. The Ascend 950PR carries low-cost HiBL 1.0 with 128GB capacity and 1.6TB/s bandwidth, bringing the end-unit card price down to roughly 50,000 yuan, about $7,500, and together they account for about 35% to 40% of shipments. The tiered approach is expected to extend to the Ascend 960 series in 2027, with samples in the first quarter and volume shipments in the third quarter on a full-year plan of about 400,000 to 500,000 cards.

The article says capacity expansions at CXMT and YMTC are seen as key to easing the shortage. CXMT's total DRAM capacity is about 320,000 to 330,000 wafers per month and is expected to expand to about 420,000 in 2027, with HBM3 shipments targeted at about 50,000 wafers for the year. YMTC's total capacity is expected to reach 300,000 wafers per month once Phase III is fully loaded in 2027. The supply-demand gap in Chinese high-bandwidth memory is expected to ease gradually in the second half of 2027.

Articles.Title: Chinese-Made HBM Spot Prices Top Imports by 5%-10% as Mature-Generation Quotes Near $110 Red Line - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: Samsung's AI Boom Delivers Bad News for Its Phones
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics reported a record third-quarter profit on October 29, 2026, as the AI memory boom lifted its semiconductor business, but its stock still fell. Operating profit surged to 107.4 trillion won, up from 12.2 trillion won a year earlier. Semiconductor operating profit jumped roughly 15-fold to 106.5 trillion won, meaning the chip division generated virtually all of the group's quarterly operating profit. The driver was AI, and Samsung said its high-bandwidth memory supply is already sold out for 2027, with major customers asking for more.

Samsung expects AI infrastructure spending to reach a historic level next year and said demand growth should significantly outpace industry supply. It also expects the broader memory market to remain tight through 2028, even as it accelerates spending. Chip capital expenditures are expected to rise 62% to 76.8 trillion won in 2026, with another sharp increase planned next year as the company adds capacity. Samsung said it would finalize its next capital-return policy in January, despite expectations for a fresh buyback or dividend announcement, and it previously said 2026 shareholder returns would total between 90 trillion and 110 trillion won.

Investors wanted more, and Samsung shares fell as much as 6.2% after the company offered a more conservative shortage outlook than SK Hynix. SK Hynix recently said DRAM and HBM capacity was effectively sold out through 2029 and shortages could persist into 2030. Samsung is expanding long-term supply agreements that could eventually cover 60% to 70% of production capacity by 2030. The articles say the key things to watch are HBM pricing, long-term contracts, capex, foundry losses, and Samsung's January shareholder-return decision.

Articles.Title: Samsung's AI Boom Delivers Bad News for Its Phones - TradingView

stories.Headline: AI Debt Wrecks Earnings Season for Hyperscalers
stories.Summary:
Alphabet, Google's parent company, reported third-quarter results after the market closed on October 28, 2026, and its shares fell 12.64% the next day. Nearly $500 billion in market value vanished in a single day, the second-largest such loss in New York market history after Nvidia's $593 billion drop on January 27 last year. Revenue was $127.58 billion, up 25% from a year earlier but about $600 million short of the $128.22 billion LSEG estimate. Earnings per share of $2.12 fell well below Wall Street's $3.02 estimate, and excluding valuation losses on stakes in SpaceX and Anthropic, EPS was only $2.67.

Alphabet's third-quarter capital expenditure rose to $51.36 billion, and free cash flow was negative $9.065 billion, after negative free cash flow in the second quarter for the first time since its 2004 listing. Google Cloud revenue rose 103% to $30.71 billion, and Google Services revenue rose 11% to $96.3 billion, but search revenue of about $63 billion fell short of the $65 billion estimate. Microsoft, whose fiscal 2027 first-quarter results covered July through September, reported revenue of $92.279 billion, up 19%, net profit of $36.63 billion, up 32%, and EPS of $4.89, all above LSEG estimates. Microsoft issued at least $25 billion in dollar-denominated bonds, its first bond issuance in nine years since 2017, in 10 tranches with maturities from two to 40 years, drawing more than $115 billion in orders.

Amazon reported third-quarter revenue of $201.94 billion, up 12% but below the $202.31 billion estimate, and EPS of $1.89 missed the $1.96 expectation. Its trailing 12-month free cash flow was negative $42.4 billion, widening nearly sixfold from $7.6 billion in the second quarter, after a $94.8 billion yearly surge in property and equipment purchases, and it kept its capital expenditure forecast at $220 billion. Intel's third-quarter revenue rose 21% to $16.51 billion and EPS of 52 cents beat the 41-cent estimate, but its client computing division revenue fell 5% to $8.1 billion. Intel guided fourth-quarter revenue to $15 billion to $16 billion, below the $17.1 billion LSEG estimate, and its shares traded more than 23% lower in after-hours trading.

Alphabet Chief Executive Sundar Pichai said an across-the-board approach to AI was driving the entire business. Amazon Chief Executive Andy Jassy said he expected AWS to grow more than 40% next year and in 2028. Meta shares had already tumbled 6.98% the day after its third-quarter results on October 21, with capital expenditure of $34.91 billion, negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion, and non-cancellable AI-related contracts totaling $825 billion, above the $700 billion reported in July. Market participants have been unusually sensitive to AI-related debt since October 14, when corporate bonds from CoreWeave and other neocloud companies came under concern over distress, and Bloomberg projected the PC market would contract 12% this year and another 10% next year.

Articles.Title: AI Debt Wrecks Earnings Season for Hyperscalers - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: HD Hyundai Heavy Develops AI Ship Coating Inspection System
stories.Summary:
HD Hyundai Heavy Industries developed an artificial intelligence-based inspection system for ship coating quality, the first of its kind in South Korea's shipbuilding industry, and is pushing to make it a global standard. The company announced on the 29th that it had signed a memorandum of understanding on advancing AI technology with four classification societies, Lloyd's Register, the American Bureau of Shipping, DNV and the Korean Register. The signing took place at its human resources development center in Ulsan's Dong District on Sept. 29. HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering and HD Hyundai Samho also joined the agreement. The system is called AI CIP, or AI Coating InsPector, and it combines vision AI and deep learning to automatically identify and analyze coating defects on ships.

HD Hyundai Heavy Industries and the AX Center of HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering have jointly developed the system since 2024, training the AI on coating quality data gathered from shipyards. Coating inspections on newly built ships had relied on workers' eyes and experience, so results varied with the inspector's level of skill. The company said it recently completed technical reviews with major classification societies, laying the groundwork to shift inspections from subjective judgment to an objective, data-based framework. Under the agreement, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries and HD Hyundai Samho will expand use of the system at their yards and upgrade their data collection and management systems. HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering will improve the program's performance and verify its compatibility with different coatings and systems.

The four classification societies will cooperate on technical reviews and on establishing standard inspection procedures to ensure the reliability of inspection results. An official at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries said introducing the AI coating inspection system had secured consistency in inspections and made quantitative quality analysis possible through accumulated data, and that the company would work with classification societies to raise confidence in the technology and broaden the scope of AI-based quality management. HD Hyundai Heavy Industries said it will continue technical cooperation with major classification societies to improve transparency in quality control procedures and build trust with shipowners. The company framed the agreement as a step toward wider AI-based quality management in its yards. The article does not say what further steps or timelines follow beyond that continued cooperation.

Articles.Title: HD Hyundai Heavy Develops AI Ship Coating Inspection System - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: AI Hacking Spreads, but 97% of Korean Firms Report Security Staff Shortages
stories.Summary:
At the 31st Seoul Economic Daily Financial Strategy Forum, held at the Westin Josun Seoul in Jung-gu, Seoul, on the 29th, speakers addressed South Korea's cybersecurity weaknesses as AI-driven hacking attacks spread. Lee Gun-young, head of EY Hanyoung's Financial AI Center, said most financial institutions complain of a shortage of AI security personnel. He said the network separation environment has left insufficient systems for financial security staff to grow or be trained. According to EY Analysis, a Cisco survey of 8,000 security executives in 30 countries found that 97% of participating South Korean companies said they lacked security personnel. Lee said domestic cybersecurity is highly vulnerable compared with major countries, calling it the result of structural limits across organization, governance, resources and systems.

Shin Jin-chang, vice chairman of the Financial Services Commission, delivered the keynote address and also pointed to the need for stronger security frameworks. He said a review of security management systems at 555 domestic financial companies found that 25% were vulnerable, and most of them were small and mid-sized financial firms. He added that some large financial firms also have weak points, so the shortcomings need to be addressed. The FSC signaled it would continue easing regulations so the industry can actively use AI. The second round of selections for easing network separation rules, provisionally postponed after recent hacking incidents in the financial sector, will resume once a supplementary review is completed.

Shin said the FSC takes seriously the criticism that the Information Security Management System is ineffective, and it will re-examine whether the certification framework and standards are appropriate. He said whether banks are allocating an appropriate share of their budgets to security is also under review. He said setting investment amounts in absolute terms could be an easy solution that does not account for side effects, and that the matter would be examined. Lee said it is important not simply to lock the door but to manage the flow so that incidents do not occur.

Articles.Title: AI Hacking Spreads, but 97% of Korean Firms Report Security Staff Shortages - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Samsung Nears 40% HBM Share, Doubles Long-Term Supply Deals
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics said on October 29, 2026, that it is pursuing a medium- to long-term growth strategy centered on next-generation high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, after becoming the first global technology company to post quarterly operating profit above 100 trillion won in the third quarter. The company is focusing on three pillars: reclaiming the top spot in the HBM market now held by SK hynix, locking in future demand through long-term agreements and infrastructure investment, and narrowing losses at its foundry business. Samsung's HBM market share rose to the high 30% range in the third quarter, up from around 20% in the first quarter and 33% in the second quarter, according to industry accounts. The gain brought Samsung close to 40%, within striking distance of SK hynix at about 50%.

Kim Jae-joon, executive vice president of the memory business at Samsung's Device Solutions division, said on a third-quarter earnings conference call that the goal of securing an HBM market share on par with the company's DRAM share in the second half appeared to have already been achieved in the third quarter. He said HBM4 revenue tripled from the previous quarter and its share of total HBM revenue expanded to around 60%. He also said Samsung has completed long-term agreements with 10 large customers and is in negotiations with another 10 major customers, with a goal of raising the share of memory volume supplied under such agreements to 60% of total capacity by 2030. The number of long-term agreement customers doubled in a single quarter from the five Samsung disclosed in late July, and the total could rise to 20 by the end of this year or early next year.

Capital expenditure this year came in higher than initially expected at 84.4 trillion won, up 60% from last year, after Samsung decided early this year to spend 110 trillion won on capital expenditure and research and development combined. Investment accelerated at new fabs in Yongin, Gwangju in Jeolla Province and Taylor, Texas, and the company decided to spend more than 10 trillion won above the original plan. Kang Seok-chae, executive vice president of Samsung's foundry business, said demand far exceeds capacity for advanced processes at 8 nanometers and below, with utilization expected to top 100% in the second half. He said Samsung plans to more than double the number of 2-nanometer order wins from last year, and the foundry division is estimated to have posted an operating loss of 1 trillion to 2 trillion won in the third quarter, while some brokerages expect a return to quarterly profit as early as the second half of next year.

Eugene Investment & Securities projects the average selling price of HBM will more than double to $3.48 per gigabit next year from $1.65 this year, while commodity DRAM is expected to reach only $2.34 next year from $1.71 this year. Demand for HBM4 is surging as it is used in the latest AI chips, including Nvidia's Vera Rubin. Beyond the fourth quarter, HBM4E will enter mass production in the first half of next year following HBM4, with volumes set to increase significantly through a ramp-up in the second half. Samsung is pursuing extensions beyond the existing maximum five-year terms with long-term agreement customers, and in foundry it will break ground on a second plant in Taylor this year and is already discussing orders ahead of building out its 1.4-nanometer process, targeted for 2029.

Articles.Title: Samsung Nears 40% HBM Share, Doubles Long-Term Supply Deals - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Firms Face 200 AI Data Violations a Month, Security Frameworks Must Be Redesigned
stories.Summary:
Lee Gun-young, head of the Financial AI Center at EY Hanyoung, gave a keynote speech at the 31st Seoul Economic Daily Financial Strategy Forum on Nov. 29 at the Westin Josun Hotel in Jung-gu, Seoul. He said global companies record more than 200 generative AI data policy violations a month on average. Citing the 2026 Cloud and Threat Report from security firm Netskope, he said violations at Netskope client companies averaged 223 per organization each month, double the figure from a year earlier. Source code made up 42% of exposed data, followed by regulated data such as personal and financial information at 32% and intellectual property at 16%.

Lee said AI adoption at financial institutions has moved beyond the pilot stage. In the 2026 survey on AI use in financial services by the Institute of International Finance and EY, 98% of global financial institutions said they had applied AI to actual operations, and the share deploying agentic AI rose to 70% this year from 23% a year earlier. He said AI use is expanding faster than control systems are being put in place, with risks around control and visibility and around decision-making. He also said security management at Korean companies is falling short, citing Cisco's 2025 Cybersecurity Readiness Index, released in May last year, in which 83% of Korean companies said they were not confident in detecting unapproved AI tools and more than 66% said they struggled to respond to threats even while operating 10 or more security solutions.

Lee said cybersecurity management frameworks must be redesigned to cover the entire process of AI use. Companies should clarify the purpose and permitted scope of AI use, the boundaries for data and model use and the structure of accountability, and build security orchestration that integrates detection and response across multiple security systems. He urged firms to go beyond using AI safely and to create business value and reinvest it, citing Singapore's DBS Bank, which generated more than 1 billion Singapore dollars in economic value from AI last year. He said work should be redesigned so AI handles market analysis and proposes adjustments while people focus on verification and final judgment, and that productivity standards should shift from output to outcome. He also called for strategic reinvestment through partnerships with or acquisitions of outside AI companies, pointing to Ode, an AI services company set up through a partnership involving U.S. private equity firm Blackstone and AI company Anthropic.

Articles.Title: Firms Face 200 AI Data Violations a Month, Security Frameworks Must Be Redesigned - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Bessent Dismisses AI Financing Fears Despite Credit Market Warning Signs
stories.Summary:
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent dismissed concerns about AI financing in a CNBC interview on Oct. 28, saying double-digit yields on some AI-related debt were not problematic at all. He said neocloud companies, which rent out AI computing infrastructure, are only a small part of the wider AI ecosystem. He argued that trouble at individual operators does not necessarily signal a broader market crisis. He also said another Federal Reserve rate hike would not necessarily be a policy mistake.

Credit market data nonetheless showed strain. According to Bloomberg, at least 18 speculative-grade bonds and leveraged loans tied to data centers carried double-digit yields. JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs changed the terms of a $5 billion loan for Volta Infrastructure, an AI infrastructure company, and the yield exceeded 11%. Morgan Stanley said yields on top-rated data center bonds approached 7%, up from less than 5% at the start of the year. Citadel Securities warned the financial burden could spread to the major technology firms backing these companies, and the cost of credit default swap protection on Oracle hit a record high last week.

Bessent stressed that financing and dealmaking were still continuing and that capital for AI investment had not dried up. He pointed to companies raising money in equity markets, including a reported $25 billion Meta financing transaction that drew demand more than five times the amount sought. Asked whether another Fed rate hike would be a mistake, he replied, not necessarily, hours after the central bank held its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4.00%. Traders widely expect another increase in December, after last month's hike, the first in three years. Bessent also reaffirmed confidence in Fed Chair Kevin Warsh.

On Oct. 25, xAI CEO Elon Musk warned that companies without enough revenue beyond AI data centers had effectively been shut out of financing markets. He predicted that more than 200 neocloud operators could face widespread failures or consolidation, and CoreWeave has become a focal point of market concerns. Bessent said markets were already applying considerable tightening pressure on their own, with the 10-year Treasury yield above 5%. He described Operation Economic Outcast, the U.S. campaign to isolate Iran economically, as successful and said Iran's economy could contract by as much as 25% over one year. He said he had not yet seen third-quarter GDP figures due Oct. 29 but expected strong growth, while economists forecast 3.2%, up from 2.2% in the second quarter.

Articles.Title: Bessent Dismisses AI Financing Fears Despite Credit Market Warning Signs - Businesskorea

stories.Headline: [Opening Market] KOSPI Opens Above 6,000 on Semiconductor Rally
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, Oct. 29, the KOSPI opened at 6017.22, up 0.08%, after closing with a steep surge in the 6% range the previous day. Foreign investors drove early gains with net purchases in the 200 billion won range, about $149.36 million. Retail investors also bought in the 200 billion won range, while institutional investors sold in the 500 billion won range. The KOSDAQ opened down 0.45% and widened its losses, trading around the 760 mark.

SK hynix had forecast a shareholder return policy reaching 100 trillion won, about $74.68 billion, along with its highest-ever performance. SK hynix rose more than 5% at one point and passed 1.55 million won, and SK Square rose more than 5%. Samsung Electronics gained 2.07% and exceeded 245,000 won ahead of its third-quarter results and shareholder return details later that day. The won-dollar exchange rate opened at 1,339.10 won, down 4.40 won or 0.33% from the previous day, and stood at 1,339.90 won as of 10:00 a.m.

Foreign investors were described as driving the index through net buying tied to large-cap stocks. Institutional selling was interpreted as profit taking and risk management after recent surges and short-term price burdens. In the KOSDAQ, retail investors bought in the 100 billion won range while foreign and institutional investors sold in the 70 billion won and 10 billion won ranges. Editor Park Jung-hwan wrote the article.

Experts said the market settled safely at the 6,000 mark on SK hynix-led semiconductor shareholder return momentum and performance expectations. They said KOSDAQ weakness and institutional profit taking partly limited the upside. They said the key to a sustained rally is whether strength spreads beyond semiconductors and whether foreign supply continues. They added that the exchange rate stabilizing in the 1,330 won range is expected to help additional foreign inflows.

Articles.Title: [Opening Market] KOSPI Opens Above 6,000 on Semiconductor Rally - Businesskorea

stories.Headline: Can AI save global health or will it deepen inequities?
stories.Summary:
Governments, philanthropies and technology companies are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence as a way to address clinician shortages and expand access to care in low-resource settings, according to a tip sheet published by the Association of Health Care Journalists on October 29, 2026 and written by Lara Salahi. The article says AI is being promoted as a scalable solution for expanding access to care, and that this comes as billions of dollars in global health funding are disappearing. It also says studies show AI research is overwhelmingly concentrated in countries with stronger health systems and fewer people living with certain diseases. That raises concerns that the next generation of AI tools could reinforce rather than reduce global health inequities.

The article describes two central problems. The first is what researchers call health data poverty, meaning AI systems are only as good as the data used to train them, so algorithms trained mostly on patients from high-income countries may perform less accurately in underrepresented populations, including many communities in low- and middle-income countries and racial and ethnic minority populations elsewhere. The second is who generates the evidence, since AI development requires data, research infrastructure, funding, technical expertise and regulatory pathways, and research suggests these resources remain concentrated in wealthier countries. That could lead to earlier validation, deployment and commercial adoption in places where the clinical need may actually be lower. The article says this does not mean AI will inevitably worsen disparities, and it points to India and China as examples of how sustained national investment in digital infrastructure and AI research can help shift innovation toward countries outside the traditional high-income research centers.

The article says reporters covering these developments should be cautious about framing AI as a simple technological fix, and it lists questions to consider about implementation, representation and accountability. These include who was included in the datasets used to develop and validate a tool, whether the technology has been independently evaluated in the populations where it is intended to be used, who owns the data collected through global health AI partnerships, whether research is led by investigators in the countries most affected by the disease or primarily by institutions in high-income countries, and whether the technology addresses a clearly identified health need or is being promoted as a substitute for investments in the workforce, public health infrastructure or health systems. The article says all of these questions get to whether AI is being developed and deployed in ways that genuinely expand access to care, or whether it risks leaving behind the very populations it promises to serve. It also lists additional resources from the World Health Organization, Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and Harvard University, and links to a related post saying that so-called black box medical AI can deepen health disparities.

Articles.Title: Can AI save global health or will it deepen inequities?

stories.Headline: Network modeling of science teachers’ perceptions of artificial intelligence integration in science curriculum development
stories.Summary:
A study published in Scientific Reports on October 29, 2026, examined how Saudi science teachers view the use of artificial intelligence in building science curricula. The research was led by U.M. Ibrahem and used a validated questionnaire completed by 691 Saudi science teachers. The authors applied psychological network modeling to map how teachers' views of benefits, challenges and attitudes connect to one another. The work was published in volume 15, issue 20, and carries the citation DOI 10.3390/su152014766.

The study used network estimation with regularization and centrality analyses to identify key themes in teachers' perceptions. Curriculum content generation and innovative pedagogical tools came out as the most central benefits, while data processing challenges and algorithmic bias stood out as the main structural barriers. Teachers' attitudes showed ambivalence, with resistance to automating administrative functions alongside guarded optimism about interactive and adaptive learning applications. The authors said the findings point to a need to address technical constraints, ethical considerations and the changing professional identities of educators.

The authors framed the study around the Technology Acceptance Model and Social Cognitive Theory, which they said informed their interpretation rather than their formal measurement model. They argued that teachers are the main implementers of educational technology, so their acceptance and engagement directly affect how AI enters classroom practice and curriculum planning. They also tied the research to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 emphasis on digital transformation and educational innovation. They said the results could offer actionable insights for policymakers, curriculum developers and professional development providers.

The article described a gap in the literature, noting that earlier studies often used linear or isolated frameworks that fail to capture the interconnected nature of teacher perceptions. It said few studies have focused on science, where curriculum development requires specialized pedagogical and technological considerations. The authors said the study contributes a systemic understanding that can inform tailored AI tools and support frameworks. They concluded that this could advance transformative innovation in science education.

Articles.Title: Network modeling of science teachers’ perceptions of artificial intelligence integration in science curriculum development

stories.Headline: UNR conference examines the role of AI in cybersecurity
stories.Summary:
The University of Nevada hosted a conference on Thursday about the role of artificial intelligence in cybersecurity, according to KOLO. Experts who attended the event in Reno described the topic as a double-edged sword. The conference brought together people from many sectors, from students to industry leaders. It also introduced high school students to cybersecurity.

The UNR cybersecurity director, Shamik Sengupta, said the conference focused on AI cyber versus cyber-AI. That means discussing the security of AI itself, including how to make it safe, its risks, and how to use it properly, he said. It also means weighing those issues against how AI can benefit and grow cybersecurity. Sengupta said the question is no longer whether AI is used, but how. He said conversations about implementing AI in cybersecurity while also protecting it are critical for smart growth.

Jack Donelson, a UNR senior and team leader of the Nevada Cyber Range Security Operations Center, said the best way to go about it is a balanced approach. He said that means acknowledging people's fears about AI, especially how it is used in corporate environments with data and security, while also acknowledging its benefits in software patching, vulnerability finding, and other uses. Heather Case-Hall, an award-winning cybersecurity leader and author, said that as AI keeps advancing, it will help improve security, but attackers are also advancing their capabilities. She said defenders need to move at the same speed, and that is the difficult balance. Leaders at the conference acknowledged public fears and said these conversations are critical to establish strict, protective, and ethical standards.

Researchers found that implementing proper safeguards and infrastructure makes businesses and cybersecurity more efficient overall. Case-Hall said AI has become a powerful tool in society, so talking about its complexity is needed to keep it safe. All the leaders interviewed said they were excited to have these conversations and expand their knowledge. Experts said the focus is on finding a balance between allowing AI to support humanity and implementing ethical and protective standards.

Articles.Title: UNR conference examines the role of AI in cybersecurity

stories.Headline: Some voters turn to AI in making election decisions
stories.Summary:
Some voters are turning to AI chatbots for information on candidates and to help decide who to vote for in the election on the Nov. 3 ballot, Fox 8 reported on Oct. 29, 2026. Aron Culotta, a Tulane University computer science professor and AI expert, said using a chatbot means the bot goes to the web to collect and summarize information for you, which differs from using a search engine yourself. He said AI is not foolproof, and that chatbots can seem more authoritative than a website that turns out not to be. Fox 8 interviewed citizens, and Kyleigh Kaminski said she thinks AI is wrong the majority of the time and is not somewhere to get the truth about politics. Another person said AI is as trustworthy as anybody you ask and that it gets a lot of stuff wrong.

In 2024 the Associated Press reported on chatbots giving inaccurate and misleading responses about elections, and two years later there is more reporting on the topic. Culotta said some errors come from faulty information on the web and some from chatbots making things up or getting things incorrect, which he called a pervasive problem. He advised people to push back and ask a chatbot to show its sources, comparing it to a really book-smart 12-year-old who graduated from Harvard. He said some voters may turn to AI because they see it as a time saver, since there is a lot to vote on and voters do not have time for in-depth research on every issue. He said there is a lot of value in these systems summarizing sometimes very complex issues, and that voters want to be engaged and know what they are voting for.

Culotta is the Tulane computer science professor and AI expert quoted on the risks and on how voters should use chatbots. He said the problems with factual information around elections that people have faced historically are still here today. He said the challenge is that a chatbot can seem more authoritative than a website that you realize is not that authoritative once you visit it. He said voters want to know what they are voting for and that it can be hard to parse that out in the normal ways. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the Nov. 3 election date and the continued reporting on the topic.

Articles.Title: Some voters turn to AI in making election decisions
