stories.Headline: AI dispatcher Lezle: what’s working, and what is it still learning?
stories.Summary:
An artificial intelligence agent nicknamed Lezle has been answering non-emergency calls in Craighead County, Arkansas, for nearly two months. From Sept. 29 to Oct. 28, 2026, the system answered nearly 5,000 calls, according to KAIT. Dispatchers say it resolves more than half of those calls itself, especially for clerical matters such as records or warrants, and then transfers callers to the correct person. The system cut dispatchers' call load by 56% in the past 30 days.

E-911 dispatcher Terra Summers said the difference is noticeable on the dispatch floor. She said 70 hours may not sound like a lot, but since most calls take five minutes or less, it adds up to a lot of calls. Summers said the system had early glitches, including a time when it told someone to file an accident report online, though dispatchers send an officer to any car accident. She said trigger words such as emergency, breathing or fire immediately transfer a caller to a live dispatcher, and the system also has built-in ways to reach a human in seconds.

Summers said that when Lezle gets something wrong, dispatchers file a report with upper administration, which either fixes the issue or sends it to the programmer. She said the system is not perfect, especially when it first launched, but it is learning and she believes it will only get more accurate, which is why she thinks it should stay. Jonesboro resident Nicholas Sides said he has not called Lezle and is generally wary of AI, but he is watching how it is used. He said it can be a tool to help people if used in the right ways, and that he could learn to accept it as long as it sticks to non-emergency calls, learns from its mistakes and keeps helping human dispatchers.

Articles.Title: AI dispatcher Lezle: what’s working, and what is it still learning?

stories.Headline: ‘Black box’ medical AI can deepen health disparities, researcher says
stories.Summary:
Tiffani Bright, an artificial intelligence researcher at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, spoke at the Association of Health Care Journalists fall summit in Los Angeles, in a session moderated by Usha Lee McFarling of MIT. She said unchecked medical algorithms threaten patient safety and health equity, and that even one basic untested algorithm can harm a human life. She noted that health institutions once kept local control over their algorithms to find and remove bias, but today commercial vendors ship black box tools that health systems cannot inspect, including the underlying logic and the training cohorts. The panel discussion was published on October 29, 2026.

Bright described three main pathways for bias in health algorithms: biased historical data, asking the wrong clinical questions, and failing to act on system alerts. She gave examples, saying algorithms trained mostly on male patient data can give inaccurate or harmful results for women, and models that use health care costs to find sick patients often miss lower-income people who receive less care overall. She said most AI tools do not go through rigorous clinical trials by outside evaluators the way prescription drugs do before reaching patients. She added that a system claiming high overall accuracy can still fail specific subgroups, such as Black or Hispanic women, if developers do not check performance across intersecting groups.

Bright advised reporters to examine funding sources for medical AI claims, check whether tools were tested on diverse populations, and ask whether patients gave informed consent to tools that record visits and access records. She said bias is not a bug but a set of choices, and that there needs to be more representation and accountability in how medical technology is built and deployed. She also said she worries automated care could be sent disproportionately to disadvantaged groups, making direct human care a luxury and creating a two-tiered health care system. The articles say full recordings of the panel and other sessions from the 2026 fall summit are available on the organization's website.

Articles.Title: ‘Black box’ medical AI can deepen health disparities, researcher says

stories.Headline: Connecticut Leaders Tout Tech Talent Accelerator, AI Training
stories.Summary:
Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont and state leaders held a press conference in East Hartford on Wednesday to promote state workforce development programs aimed at easing the AI transition and supporting workers and students. The event focused heavily on the Tech Talent Accelerator, a four-year-old program that builds partnerships between higher education institutions and businesses. In February, the state announced the launch of Tech Talent Accelerator 3.0, a more AI-oriented version of the program. The Office of Workforce Strategy is supporting several AI pilot programs, including an AI accounting and entrepreneurship course at Connecticut College, an AI for Cybersecurity program at the University of New Haven, and an online course on AI in healthcare business innovation at Quinnipiac University.

Kelli-Marie Vallieres, the state's chief workforce officer, said the goal is to work with businesses to connect students and companies well before graduation. Nicholas Schilling, a software engineer at CGI, described how being connected with the firm at an event led to an internship and then full-time work, and he now mentors students. He said the transition to full-time employment was seamless because he had spent so much time with CGI as a student. Lamont said he is optimistic because the world is moving toward more knowledge-based and skill-based work, and he said AI use will be better guided and more effective for learners.

The state has also launched other efforts, including the Connecticut AI Academy, a free online school offering certificate programs in AI literacy and AI fluency that is expected to expand to teens, teachers and small businesses. In August, the Department of Economic and Community Development announced a $20 million investment into an applied AI workforce center in Hartford. Over the summer, the state celebrated a National Science Foundation grant for its quantum computing sector, a project also slated to receive $121 million in state funding. Lamont's office also announced a partnership with RAISE US, a nonpartisan organization that offers displaced workers retraining and upskilling, and Connecticut will pilot programs training workers to interact with AI.

Dan O'Keefe, commissioner of the Department of Economic and Community Development, told CT Mirror in July that states are where the rubber really hits the road and that the federal government has been somewhat hands-off. Other states have announced similar efforts, including New York's Pursuit AI Jobs Institute, a Queens-based center aiming to train 40,000 workers by 2032 with $10 million in public investment, and Arkansas's partnership with RAISE US on a program called ArkansasLAUNCH. Lamont said Connecticut will not be the research and development leader for AI but will lead in how to apply it in the next generation of professions. The article says the coming months and years will show which efforts turn out to be most fruitful.

Articles.Title: Connecticut Leaders Tout Tech Talent Accelerator, AI Training

stories.Headline: Wikimedia Foundation Seeks to File Amicus Brief in OpenAI Copyright Case
stories.Summary:
The Wikimedia Foundation announced on October 30, 2026, that it has asked the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York for leave to file a friend-of-the-court brief in In re: OpenAI, Inc. Copyright Infringement Litigation. That case consolidates 12 lawsuits against OpenAI, and its best-known member is The New York Times’ case against OpenAI and Microsoft. The Foundation’s filing is dated October 29, 2026, and is addressed to Judge Sidney H. Stein. It is a letter motion for leave to file, with the proposed brief attached as an exhibit and styled as supporting neither party.

The motion was submitted under the court’s local rules and an August 7, 2026 order governing amicus participation, as modified on September 24, 2026. Because that order directs prospective amici to move for leave, Wikimedia did not seek the parties’ consent. The proposed brief contains 5,831 words, within the 6,000-word limit the court set for amicus briefs. Rhett O. Millsaps II of Lex Lumina LLP is counsel of record, alongside the Foundation’s General Counsel Stephen LaPorte, Associate General Counsel Jacob Rogers, and Legal Counsel Aly Marino.

The brief argues that each distinct use of copied works across the stages of developing and operating a chatbot requires its own four-factor fair-use analysis, grounded in the Supreme Court’s 2023 decision in Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts v. Goldsmith. It contends that scraping is acquisition rather than a copyright use, and that only what is done with the copies afterward should undergo fair-use analysis. On pre-training, the brief argues the use is likely fair, and it asks the court to rule that the pre-training of ChatGPT’s general-purpose model was fair use. It argues that retrieval-augmented generation likely fails the four-factor test and that OpenAI’s use of copies in that feature is not fair and must abide by licenses such as the Creative Commons license for Wikimedia Project content.

CEO Bernadette Meehan said the Foundation is taking a position to defend the free and open human knowledge that Wikipedia depends on. General Counsel Stephen LaPorte said the fair-use conversation cannot be limited to for-profit organizations, adding that a ruling that does not apply fair use principles carefully could threaten the sustainability of free knowledge and stifle open-source technologies. The Foundation said scraping of its projects must respect its public API rate limits or go through its Wikimedia Enterprise API offerings. It also said machine-learning tools already help volunteers fight vandalism, detect copyright violations and inappropriate personal information, and prioritize articles most in need of improvement.

Wikipedia holds more than 67 million articles across 300 languages, with nearly 250,000 volunteers contributing each month, and the Foundation describes it as one of the highest-quality datasets used to train LLMs. The brief states that more than 260,000 volunteer contributors per month, as of January 2025, create and moderate content across the Foundation’s thirteen free-knowledge platforms. Docket entries show that on October 28 and 29, 2026, Engine Advocacy, the Authors Alliance, Public Knowledge, Professor Matthew Sag, Brian L. Frye, Digital Content Next, and a group of publishing organizations including the Association of American Publishers moved to file their own amicus briefs. Summary-judgment briefing between the news publishers, OpenAI, and Microsoft continued, and Judge Stein must grant the Foundation leave before its proposed brief is formally accepted.

Articles.Title: Wikimedia Foundation Seeks to File Amicus Brief in OpenAI Copyright Case - Unite.AI

stories.Headline: AI Ran 916,000 Backtests — Here’s What It Discovered
stories.Summary:
Tobias Carlisle said on a recent episode with Jake Taylor that he fed his backtest data into Claude and gave the AI access to his backtesting software. Where he would run dozens of backtests in an afternoon, the AI ran 916,000 backtests testing 1,217 different parameters. He described the result as a data mine, and Jake Taylor said he had gone from data mining with a spoon to being given an earth mover. The discussion was published on October 29, 2026.

Carlisle said he splits data mining into a first half of the set for finding rules and a second half for testing them. He said a mix that ranks first in the second set ranks around 800 in the first set, and the mix that fits both sets ranks around 400 in the first set and 300 in the second. He said the 916,000 tests come from running all 1,217 mixes while optimising for different goals such as Sharpe ratio, absolute return or lowest drawdown, across two sets of data and the full set. He also said the tests can be run across 11 developed market countries with data going back that far.

Carlisle said there is no good answer and that he can only give the least bad of all the options. He said Harry Browne's simple split of a quarter each into bonds, gold, stocks and cash did fine over the whole period, stayed positive and had few losing decades. He questioned whether the 1970s gold revaluation, the falling rates from 1980 to 2020 and the strong US equity market are representative of what comes next. Taylor said the sample of truly catastrophic drawdowns is very small, and Carlisle agreed that drawing too many conclusions from a small sample is bad statistics.

Carlisle said he looked at valuation measures including CAPE, Tobin's Q and Buffett's market capitalisation to GNP, and that even the market's distance above its own trend gives roughly the same answer. He said the 10-3 inversion had a strong record until it stopped working this time, and that valuation and the equity risk premium are not useful timing tools at all. He said the only predictor is the absolute PE or earnings yield, with high earnings yield leading to good returns and low earnings yield to poor returns over about 10 years. He said crashes since 1929 are all totally different from each other, and that there is no satisfactory way to avoid them.

Articles.Title: AI Ran 916,000 Backtests — Here’s What It Discovered

stories.Headline: Study: Partisan ties shape how voters view campaign AI
stories.Summary:
Seulki Lee-Geiller, a researcher at the University at Albany's Center for Technology in Government, published a study on how party ties shape voters' views of AI in campaigns. The study appeared on Sept. 24 in the Journal of Elections, Public Opinion and Parties. Lee-Geiller ran an online survey experiment with 3,055 U.S. participants in June and July 2024, ahead of the 2024 presidential election. Participants were randomly split into four groups and shown a hypothetical campaign letter from a presidential candidate.

The letter's content stayed the same, but each group got different information about how it was made. One group saw no mention of AI, another was told AI helped draft it, and the other two were told either the participant's preferred party or the opposing party had used AI. Participants then rated election integrity, including fairness, authenticity, freedom from fraud and representation of voters' interests. On a five-point scale, the average authenticity rating was 3.71 when AI use was attributed to a preferred party, compared with 3.37 for an opposing party.

Lee-Geiller said simply knowing AI was used did not significantly change views of fairness or authenticity. She said participants were more likely to believe AI was being used to target messages to specific audiences, and that bigger differences emerged when political affiliation was introduced. Those who believed their preferred party used AI gave more favorable assessments of election integrity, while those who believed the opposing party used it were more skeptical about fairness and authenticity. She said transparency, consistent standards and digital literacy can help people make more informed judgments about AI-assisted messages, regardless of who is using the technology.

The findings suggest existing political affiliations can influence how voters interpret AI-assisted communications, even when the messages are identical. The study was exploratory and measured short-term reactions to hypothetical campaign materials rather than actual election conditions. Lee-Geiller notes that additional research could examine how these perceptions develop through exposure to AI-assisted messaging in real-world campaigns. The findings speak to areas central to CTG's work, including responsible technology use, citizen trust and good governance.

Articles.Title: Study: Partisan ties shape how voters view campaign AI

stories.Headline: At Seattle AI Week, upbeat tech industry outlook is met with protests
stories.Summary:
Seattle AI Week opened on Monday at AI House, a space at Pier 70 for startups and others in artificial intelligence, with hundreds of people gathered to discuss the region’s future as an AI hub. During the opening panel, three demonstrators in the audience confronted Beau Perschbacher, a senior policy adviser to Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson. They argued that his presence alongside Mattie Zazueta of OpenAI’s global affairs team, and his attendance at an event with Microsoft leaders, showed Big Tech’s influence over state government. Roberta Sam, a member of Climate Defiance, was the first of the three to speak and said companies were ruining the environment with data center expansion as well as the economy. The event runs through Friday.

The region had 577 AI companies as of last year, according to a new University of Washington analysis by Foster School of Business researchers Suresh Kotha and Ming Zhu Wang, and Seattle ranks fifth nationally in the number of AI companies. Kirby Winfield, a founding partner at Ascend, pointed to a CBRE report ranking Seattle second for AI talent and noted it is home to Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure. The top three Seattle AI startups, XBOW, Starcloud and Story, took 14% of the $4.14 billion raised from 2023 through early this year, while in California’s Bay Area the top three took 65%. About 1 in 8 Seattle AI founders last worked at Microsoft or Amazon, and about 1 in 8 attended UW. Former Gov. Christine Gregoire, a Democrat who now leads Challenge Seattle, warned that other states would love to lure Washington’s businesses away and said the state is close to the bottom on the environment for businesses.

Perschbacher responded to the protesters by highlighting chatbot regulations state lawmakers and the governor approved earlier this year and Washington’s strict environmental laws. He said environmental concerns about data centers are legitimate but did not speak to the pipeline proposals before conference staff escorted the demonstrators away. The groups want data center moratoriums and strict state regulations on AI technology, with the public having as much say as industry, and they seized on proposals for natural gas pipeline expansions expected to help fuel power generation. In addition to the three who disrupted panel talks, 10 demonstrators in kayaks, along with a dog in one of the boats, floated near Pier 70 on Monday holding an orange sign reading “Power for people, not for tech.” The paddlers represented Climate Defiance, Oil and Gas Action Network and Seattle-based Troublemakers, and a handful of protesters also gathered outside AI House on Tuesday morning.

The initial disruption drew scattered boos from the crowd of about 200, but attendees acknowledged the demonstrators were voicing widely held anxieties. Richard Starnes, a managing director at Accenture, said during a panel about AI and jobs that nobody knows what is coming and maybe the protesters are right. Joe Braidwood, founder and CEO of Glacis Technologies, said the protests were actually kind of promising because people care enough to come together and talk and disagree. Nick Ellingson, vice president of innovation and entrepreneurship for the Washington Technology Industry Association, which hosted AI Week, said the purpose of the event was discussion and debate. The protesters each bought a $100 ticket, according to the activists, and Ellingson said the disruption would not change the association’s plans to keep the event open in the future.

Articles.Title: At Seattle AI Week, upbeat tech industry outlook is met with protests

stories.Headline: Firm that correctly called the AI rally slowdown says here's where to hide out
stories.Summary:
Capital Economics, a research firm, said in a note on Thursday that defensive parts of the stock market are the best places to wait out a possible fall in the artificial intelligence trade. James Reilly, a senior markets economist at the firm, had said in early September that the AI equity boom was nearing an end, and that call proved correct. The firm now points to real estate and consumer staples as the areas it favors if the AI momentum trade falters. The note follows recent pressure on the AI trade, as investors worry that large tech companies are spending billions on data centers and chips without an adequate return.

Capital Economics forecasts that the S and P 500 will fall to 6,500 by the end of 2027 if the AI trade keeps losing air or the bubble bursts, a 16% decline. Before that, the firm says a final rally led by tech stocks is on the cards this year, but over the next 12 months defensive sectors may be the place to hide. It expects Treasury yields to drop, which would lift bond prices, and it notes that the 10-year yield fell all eight times since 1995 when the PHLX Semiconductor Sector Index dropped 35% or more. Real estate would benefit from falling yields and has tended to fare better than energy and financials when chip selloffs came with falling yields, though it would still fall. Consumer staples is called an even better defensive sector, since it made good gains after the peak in tech stocks in early 2000.

Reilly and his firm are behind the analysis, and the note says real estate and consumer staples remain the best bet as sanctuaries. The firm said real estate has tended to fare much better than energy and financials when chip selloffs coincided with falling yields, though it would still fall. It said consumer staples made good gains after the tech peak in early 2000. It also said energy and financials are unlikely to hold up as well this time, because both groups have done much better now than in earlier periods before technology sold off, and that this is not because they are well insulated from AI but because repeated supply shocks, especially for energy commodities, have lifted energy prices and Treasury yields.

The AI trade has come under pressure from concern that megacap tech companies like Meta Platforms, Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet are spending billions on AI infrastructure without an adequate return. Elevated capital expenditures have been eating into the cash flows and profits of hyperscalers. Alphabet reported disappointing earnings late Wednesday that showed negative free cash flow in the third quarter, and Meta reported negative free cash flow in its latest earnings last week while raising the bottom end of its full-year capital expenditure commitment. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the firm's forecasts.

Articles.Title: Firm that correctly called the AI rally slowdown says here's where to hide out

stories.Headline: Aera bets on decision governance, not just AI
stories.Summary:
Aera Technology used its AeraHUB NY event this week to launch six innovations and give an update on its decision-intelligence solution. CEO Fred Laluyaux used the event to stress the need for governance and controls. The six announcements strengthen the company's position in the AI decision-making market. Each one adds more control, lets users develop new skills and gives them access to their AI of choice.

Laluyaux said effective use of AI needs more than basic automation and requires a complete rethink of how businesses operate. He said the answer is to move from personal productivity to enterprise productivity. He said Aera saves two and a half hours per information worker, about two weeks a year, but the workload is growing faster, so the impact on the bottom line is not necessarily visible. He said the answer is to leverage AI's reasoning power to solve problems. The company's Decision Cloud uses a Decision Data Model to pull data from across the enterprise, bringing in business rules, optimisation, simulation and machine learning, and orchestrating agents.

Laluyaux said Aera can build intelligent skills that learn, and that it is building and maintaining the skill. Shariq Mansoor, Co-Founder and CTO, framed it as ownership, saying every skill becomes another digital asset they own. Jeremy D'Hoinne, Vice President Analyst at Gartner, said these shadow AI agents take multiple forms, including embedded in existing enterprise software, consumed directly from the Internet or created by employees using recent technological progress and "vibe coding" to improve productivity. Laluyaux said intelligence without memory is not intelligence, and asked where the memory of all the decisions made every day is, saying the answer is usually in our heads and that is fundamentally the problem.

Policy Studio lets users upload a policy document that Aera uses to draft machine-readable rules, and Aera says these are not applied without human review. Laluyaux said organisations struggle to know where their policies are, which documents carry them, which systems are impacted and whether there are conflicts between the rules. He said when a policy change is wanted, people write a memo and send emails and hope it is all good, which is a problem at the scale of a large enterprise across 100 or more countries. The Decision Ledger records context, reasoning, policies evaluated, actions and outcomes for decisions made inside Aera or submitted from other systems through its APIs. The EU AI Act is now being implemented and enforced, with provisions such as traceability and governance in force in 2026, other provisions for high-risk systems from December 2027, and embedded systems in August 2028.

Aera is connecting to Microsoft Copilot Studio and other sources, will connect external agents using the Agent2Agent protocol, and will use its own Model Context Protocol server to integrate other external tools. The new Dynamic UX allows users to build their own environments using natural-language prompts and publish them as a skill. Command Center provides visibility into decision-making across the enterprise and lets teams see performance and business impact across their decisions. Laluyaux pointed to Gartner, which forecasts that 50% of business decisions will be augmented or automated by AI agents within the next 15 months, and that a quarter of digital officers will shift from a data-driven to a decision-centric model by 2028.

Articles.Title: Aera bets on decision governance, not just AI - - Enterprise Times

stories.Headline: Virginia Tech tests thermal cameras and AI to warn drivers of animals near roads
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the Virginia Tech Transportation Institute are testing a system that uses thermal cameras and AI software to detect large animals near the road and warn drivers in real time. The testing comes as a local body shop manager says deer claims have increased. Laura Goodrich, a Claytor Lake resident, said deer are a regular presence on the back roads near the lake and that the roads give drivers little warning. Kin Jennelle, manager of Collision Plus, said deer claims used to follow the seasons but have picked up over the last five to 10 years.

The institute is testing the system on Route 460 in Buchanan County. Thermal cameras and AI software detect large animals near the road, and digital signs warn drivers. In the year-long pilot, drivers slowed by about 3 mph at the signs, and the system detected large animals 97% of the time. The pilot focused on elk, but the institute says the cameras are trained for deer as well. Jennelle said a typical claim has risen from a range of $1,500 to $3,000 to between $2,000 and $8,000, and repairs take between three and 15 days depending on severity.

Jean Paul Talledo Vilela, a research scientist at the institute, said the system can warn drivers about deer in the same way it does for elk. He said drivers sometimes ignore standard signs, and the messages in this system were designed to get their attention. He said the 3 mph figure was measured as drivers entered the corridor where the signs are located, that drivers may slow more once inside, and that analysis is ongoing. He said speeds through the corridor range from 55 to 65 mph, and hitting a 700-pound animal at that speed would be very bad. He also said the cameras capture heat signatures only, not license plates or faces.

The system has been tested only in Buchanan County. The institute says it is working through challenges such as rural power and limited internet service so the system could eventually be used anywhere in Virginia. The team is also looking at adding static signs inside the corridor for drivers who miss the first message. Talledo Vilela said they learned a lot and that it will allow them to provide a robust solution to any location within the state.

Articles.Title: Virginia Tech tests thermal cameras and AI to warn drivers of animals near roads

stories.Headline: Fayetteville School Board members review potential updated AI policy at October board meeting - Northwest Arkansas Democrat-Gazette
stories.Summary:
Fayetteville School Board members got their first look at a proposed updated artificial intelligence policy at their October meeting, held Thursday night. The draft was introduced as new business, so no vote was taken. The board will be asked to review the policy again at its November meeting, when approval or denial will be considered. District leaders spent the past year drafting an AI policy that the board had previously adopted.

The policy is meant to ensure safe and responsible use of AI, encourage innovation in teaching and support efficient operations, with clear expectations for how the technology is used. Act 848, passed in 2025, requires all Arkansas public entities to set policies and training requirements for employees who use AI and automated decision tools. The draft merges the district's own policy with a longer policy from the state Department of Elementary and Secondary Education that districts were required to adopt. It also covers privacy, saying confidential student or personnel data cannot be entered into public or unapproved AI tools, and that those tools cannot be the only basis for decisions that significantly affect students, such as grades.

Claire Wilkinson, the district's general counsel, told the board the goal was to combine the required state policy with the one custom made for the district. She said she still has questions about the state's policy, particularly around requirements for contracts with companies that provide AI software. She noted the Arkansas School Boards Association is working on its own model policy that the district could use for guidance. Wilkinson also acknowledged the district is in uncharted territory and said board members will likely have questions before the policy is put in place.

The draft says AI must support student learning and not replace instruction, and that software must not limit students' ability to complete assignments. Any chosen program must let teachers disable AI features for specific assignments, include moderation to detect unsafe interactions and block inappropriate content. It also says tools must limit unnecessarily human-like behavior, avoid personal or emotional relationships with students and not use manipulative practices to encourage excessive use. The articles cite research on children's AI use and lawsuits against OpenAI over alleged harm, and note that public entities are left to write their own rules to protect students while exploring how the tools can help.

Articles.Title: Fayetteville School Board members review potential updated AI policy at October board meeting - Northwest Arkansas Democrat-Gazette

stories.Headline: Rivian expands joint venture with VW to include AI assistant
stories.Summary:
Rivian is expanding its $5.8 billion joint venture with Volkswagen Group to include AI assistant technology, according to Rivian's third-quarter investor presentation released Thursday, October 29, 2026. Rivian is now licensing elements of its AI voice assistant technology to Volkswagen Group as part of the broader joint venture. Rivian did not disclose the licensing fees, payment terms, or which Volkswagen vehicles will use the technology. The AI assistant, which recently rolled out to Rivian vehicles, could make its Volkswagen debut in the automaker's low-cost EV called the ID EVERY1. The small four-door hatchback is slated to be the first VW vehicle to use Rivian's software and electrical architecture under the joint venture established in 2024.

The joint venture was initially announced at a value of up to $5 billion, but within months VW raised its commitment to invest up to $5.8 billion in Rivian by 2027. The initial tie-up was formalized through an independent company that began in November 2024 and focused on bringing Rivian's electrical architecture and software to Volkswagen's next generation of vehicles. Rivian spent two years developing its AI assistant before showing it off last year, and the assistant finally rolled out in May 2026 to its flagship R1S SUV and R1T pickup truck, and in October to its new midsize R2 SUV. The assistant allows drivers and passengers to interact with the vehicle and control certain functions.

Rivian described the expansion as a proof point for the extensibility of the platform it built in-house. Rivian founder and CEO RJ Scaringe told TechCrunch at Disrupt 2026 that the company created its own in-house agentic framework that understands what action a person wants to take when they talk to the vehicle and routes it to the right part of the car's software. He said that capability could eventually allow Rivian vehicles to run AI agents created by other companies, including Anthropic. In its investor presentation, the company said its relentless focus on vertical integration remains a core competitive differentiator, allowing it to unify its hardware and software architecture.

Rivian's vertical integration strategy led it to overhaul its flagship R1T truck and R1S SUV, changing everything from the battery pack and suspension system to the electrical architecture, sensor stack, and software user interface. Its new electric architecture system and compute platform cut the amount of wiring used and reduced the total number of electronic control units used to control the vehicle from 17 to seven. Rivian argued that this foundation would allow it to build vehicles that can handle the computing demands required for advanced software and automated driving. That technology caught the attention and money of VW, which has struggled to offer customers a modern software-centric vehicle found in competitors like Tesla. Rivian noted that because it controls the entire technology stack, including compute, sensors, displays, lighting, and sound, it can roll out rapid, vehicle-wide OTA updates that go well beyond the basics.

Articles.Title: Rivian expands joint venture with VW to include AI assistant

stories.Headline: AI tool reads abdominal ultrasounds and accelerates emergency diagnoses
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine have built an artificial intelligence tool that reads right upper quadrant ultrasounds, the scans that show organs such as the liver, the gallbladder, the right kidney and part of the pancreas. The work was published in Nature Communications, with Harrison Bai, a visiting associate professor in the Department of Radiology, as senior author. The tool is a vision-language agent, meaning it combines the ultrasound images with written clinical data such as lab results. The team tested it on roughly 11,000 RUQ ultrasounds from Stanford University, the University of Colorado and Johns Hopkins University.

The agent scans each ultrasound for 16 common diagnoses, estimates the patient's prognosis and writes a draft report. In a manual review of 100 AI-generated reports, it identified the correct diagnosis 99.6% of the time. The researchers say the tool is meant to work alongside a radiologist, who reads and edits the draft, and it can also flag patients who may need emergency surgery, such as those with acute gallbladder inflammation, so they reach the operating table faster. The article notes that radiologists were leaving the field at twice the rate in 2022 as in 2014, as patient loads rise and Medicare reimbursement falls.

Bai said the goal is not to replace the physician and that the team is not trying to build an AI radiologist. He said that if the agent can write preliminary reports, it saves radiologists time, and that telling radiologists a tool can save them time makes them much more likely to use it. He said he does not expect AI to replace the need for human supervision in medicine and that it will take time for doctors to adapt. He added that he can see the technology playing a huge role in how medicine is practiced and that he is excited to see it incorporated into daily practice to help patients and doctors.

In a blinded evaluation, a panel of experts could usually pick out unedited AI-written reports but most of the time could not tell radiologist-edited AI reports apart from reports written by radiologists. The researchers say the technology must be evaluated in real-world emergency care before it can be widely adopted. They also say it will be critical to study how collaboration between physicians and AI affects diagnostic accuracy, efficiency and patient well-being. The study suggests AI has a real place in supporting radiologists without removing the need for their expertise.

Articles.Title: AI tool reads abdominal ultrasounds and accelerates emergency diagnoses

stories.Headline: VRChat Says It's Not Adding AI Labels Despite User Survey Showing People Want That
stories.Summary:
VRChat published a support post explaining the results of a user survey about artificial intelligence on its platform. The survey found that 95 percent of respondents want some form of label to designate AI usage. Despite that figure, the company said it will not implement any such tags at this time. VRChat is an app for creating and sharing virtual worlds for social interactions. The company said it will keep weighing a label for content described as human-authored, along with a field for tools used, but it has not adopted a definitive stance.

It also said it will not add a tag for labeling AI-generated content or for filtering that content out of search results. Instead, VRChat said it would adopt changes that had alignment across the community, including accurate thumbnails, better discovery tools and quality as a core metric. The platform's creators said that while some creators would honestly label their content, others would try to pass off generative or assisted work as completely authored by hand. They also said a label could lead to sleuthing behavior, where people attempt to sniff out AI content or harass other creators, even those genuinely not using AI tools.

The post was written in language that seemed to want to make people with many different attitudes toward AI all happy, rather than accepting a policy that could be unpopular with a particular group. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the company's stated plans to keep weighing the human-authored label and the tools used field. They also do not give a date for any future decision. VRChat has been used in filmmaking and to create safe communities for transgender people, and it has also been accused of hosting toxic and predatory behavior.

Articles.Title: VRChat Says It's Not Adding AI Labels Despite User Survey Showing People Want That

stories.Headline: 2027 Elections: CCC Demands National Framework to Combat AI Deepfakes, Disinformation
stories.Summary:
The Centre for Crisis Communication held its Second National Symposium on Crisis Communication from October 27 to 28, 2026, at the Nigerian Air Force Club in Kaduna. The event drew more than 150 participants from the military, security and intelligence agencies, emergency response institutions, government, academia, media and regulatory bodies. Its theme was inter-agency collaboration, public trust and cyber threat management in crisis communication. The centre issued a communiqué at the end of the two-day meeting, signed by Commodore Kabir Aliyu (rtd.) on behalf of the organisation.

The communiqué called for an integrated national crisis communication framework to tackle inter-agency rivalry and to counter misinformation, disinformation and AI-generated deepfakes ahead of the 2027 general elections. It recommended an Integrated National Crisis Information Architecture backed by standard operating procedures and protocols. It also urged authorities to consider a Homeland Security Academy or inter-agency training centre, stronger early-warning systems, joint threat monitoring and regular inter-agency exercises. The centre further called for the revival of the Forum of Spokespersons of Security and Response Agencies to harmonise information-sharing and public messaging.

Major General Chris Olukolade (rtd.), the CCC Chairman, said effective communication was strategically important to national security and public safety as Nigeria approaches the 2027 elections. Ahmed Maiyaki, the Commissioner for Information, spoke for Kaduna State Governor Senator Uba Sani and described misinformation and disinformation as emerging national security threats, advocating sensitisation for political actors. Dr Kabiru Adamu of Beacon Security and Innovation Limited, represented by Mr Samuel Aruwan, examined security challenges across Nigeria's six geopolitical zones and stressed coordinated communication and stronger collaboration. The communiqué warned that misinformation during emergencies could trigger panic, endanger lives, divert resources and erode public confidence.

Participants identified weak coordination, institutional rivalry, delayed information-sharing and conflicting public statements as major obstacles to crisis management and public trust. They recommended defined institutional responsibilities, designated lead agencies, secure information-sharing and timely, accurate and consistent public communication. The symposium called for digital literacy initiatives, responsible use of social media and artificial intelligence, and regulatory frameworks that safeguard freedom of expression and due process. It urged the CCC and stakeholders to sensitise political actors, journalists and editors before the 2027 elections, and it cited the Kaduna Peace Model as an example of dialogue and reconciliation supporting security efforts.

Articles.Title: 2027 Elections: CCC Demands National Framework to Combat AI Deepfakes, Disinformation - PRNigeria News

stories.Headline: Unrealized AI Investments Drag Amazon’s Income, But AWS And Ads Are Still Growing
stories.Summary:
Amazon reported third-quarter results on Thursday, October 29, 2026, and net income fell to $20.7 billion from $21.2 billion in the same quarter last year. The earlier figure was helped by $9.5 billion in pre-tax gains from investments in the AI startup Anthropic, and Amazon had no similar windfall this year. Investors reacted by sending the stock down 7% in after-hours trading. CEO Andy Jassy spoke to investors on the earnings call. Amazon’s cash flow was negative $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with positive cash flow of $14.8 billion a year earlier.

AWS, which provides AI and cloud computing infrastructure, grew 39.3% year over year, its fastest rate in nearly five years. Amazon Ads revenue rose 12% year over year to $19.6 billion, after growth of 22% in the first quarter and 26% in the second. Jassy said the slower ad growth came from moving Prime Day from the third quarter to the second, and from the third quarter having no NBA games on Prime Video. Jassy said operating margins have long been strong on Amazon’s core offering and are improving quickly on the AI side too. He said AWS could become a trillion-dollar revenue business in the next five to 10 years as more businesses run their core workloads on it.

He said agentic shopping from outside agents is not meaningfully affecting Amazon ads, and that it is still not great and not much more convenient than one-click orders. He added that few customers shop this way yet. Amazon launched Amazon Ads Agent in September, combining the Amazon Ads console and Amazon DSP so advertisers can run full-funnel campaigns that are optimized continuously once live. The articles do not say what happens next beyond Jassy’s comments on future growth.

Articles.Title: Unrealized AI Investments Drag Amazon’s Income, But AWS And Ads Are Still Growing

stories.Headline: AI’s real bottleneck is electricity. Who will pay for it?
stories.Summary:
Within a week, two of the world's three largest cloud computing companies signed 20-year contracts for nuclear electricity. Amazon took 690 megawatts from Constellation's Calvert Cliffs plant in Maryland, including 190 megawatts of added capacity expected between 2030 and 2032. Google signed an agreement bringing 890 megawatts of additional nuclear capacity into the United States. Constellation is investing more than $4.3bn to upgrade 11 reactors across Illinois, Pennsylvania and New Jersey. Neither deal involves building a new reactor, and both pay for more output from reactors that already exist.

The US Department of Energy is providing up to $4.4bn in loans to restart three shuttered plants, aiming to restore about 2.25 gigawatts. Palisades in Michigan, closed in 2022, is contracted to generate again by March 2027 and would be the first US commercial nuclear plant to restart after decommissioning. The International Energy Agency estimates global data centre electricity demand will more than double to around 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, even with continued efficiency gains. Most of these deals sit inside PJM, which serves roughly 67 million people across 13 states and Washington, DC, and passes capacity auction costs to consumers. Capacity prices hit the regulatory cap in three consecutive auctions, and PJM's independent market monitor attributed about $29.4bn in capacity costs across the four most recent auctions to data centre demand.

The Natural Resources Defense Council estimates the typical PJM household could face an additional $70 per month by 2028 if current trends continue. Virginia has created a separate electricity rate class for data centres, Ohio has introduced minimum billing requirements, and Illinois is debating legislation. In October 2026, US federal regulators rejected most of PJM's proposal to require large new consumers to provide their own generation capacity. The article says the Google agreement aims to answer objections by having major new consumers bring additional generation rather than compete for constrained supply, but the arrangement remains voluntary.

Qatar's sovereign fund has committed to a $20bn joint venture with Brookfield for AI infrastructure, starting at roughly 300 megawatts and potentially reaching near 1.5 gigawatts. Abu Dhabi is pursuing up to five gigawatts of AI data centre capacity, and Saudi Arabia is targeting almost two gigawatts through HUMAIN. The article says a completed 1.5-gigawatt build-out in Qatar would equal about 12 percent of the country's installed generating capacity. It says the Gulf can settle first what the industrial tariff is, who funds new generation, what happens to contracts when hardware ages, and what long-term benefits follow beyond energy revenues and limited jobs.

Articles.Title: AI’s real bottleneck is electricity. Who will pay for it? - Al Jazeera

stories.Headline: Innovations from AI semiconductors to all-solid-state batteries put science and tech institutes in spotlight
stories.Summary:
Kim Sang-hyun, a professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering at KAIST, presented a new power supply technology for AI semiconductors at the 2026 K-Premier Deep Tech Festa, held on the afternoon of Oct. 29 at the Plus Stage in Hall B of COEX in Gangnam-gu, Seoul. His team's method places a voltage regulation device vertically beneath the chip and uses gallium nitride to cut energy loss during power transmission. He received the Excellence Award at the event's technology evaluation, which covered key research achievements of the four major science and technology institutes, KAIST, DGIST, UNIST and GIST. The technology is seen as a way to improve power efficiency as AI chip power consumption rises quickly.

The team expects the technology to raise chip power delivery efficiency from around 50 percent to between 85 and 95 percent. As AI chips grow more powerful, a single chip can consume up to 1 kilowatt, and 30 to 40 percent of total power is lost in transmission, a figure experts warn could reach 50 percent. Conventional designs lower voltage with a regulator placed next to the chip and supply power horizontally, which raises current, heat and loss. The team instead delivers high voltage down to just below the chip and steps it down to about 1 volt, and it joined gallium nitride devices to silicon through a proprietary heterogeneous junction process after making the two separately. Related results have been accepted multiple times at IEDM and the VLSI Symposium.

Kim said that until one or two years ago very few places did similar research, but related studies have recently increased rapidly in China, which has strong gallium nitride technology. Among companies, he said Intel, which has long developed server CPUs, is moving the most aggressively. He explained that the short-term goal is to demonstrate performance at the laboratory level and give foundries a technical direction for developing related processes. He said commercialization requires partners capable of joint development, and he hopes the event leads to partnerships to discuss the direction of the technology. The team is now packaging its components into a single integrated circuit, and building a mass production system is cited as a challenge because chips and voltage regulation devices are made by different processes and foundries have not yet provided enough support for the packaging.

Kim Un-hyuk, a professor in the Department of Energy Engineering at DGIST, presented cathode material technology for all-solid-state batteries at the same event. He said materials account for about 75 percent of battery costs and cathode materials make up about 49.5 percent of that, so roughly 25 to 26 percent of an electric vehicle's price goes to cathode materials. He said microcracks form when spherical cathode particles of about 10 micrometers fracture during charge and discharge, letting electrolyte seep in and trigger side reactions. His team made the particles at the nanoscale, and the material kept more than 90 percent of its initial capacity after 300 cycles and performed better than commercial materials in high-speed charge and discharge, such as drone takeoffs and landings. He said that by introducing just one dopant element, existing equipment can be used as is.

Articles.Title: Innovations from AI semiconductors to all-solid-state batteries put science and tech institutes in spotlight - 머니투데이

stories.Headline: Edge AI May Give Telecoms a Seat at the Table
stories.Summary:
Telecom operators may find their clearest near-term edge AI opportunity in metro sites such as central offices, according to an article by Jack Vaughan published on October 30, 2026. The article says the industry has spent years focused on 4G, 5G and now 6G while hyperscalers have rewritten the broader computing story, and that telecoms have fed every stage through their pipes and platforms yet are still sometimes cast as plumbers. It says the next phase of AI may reopen the question of where telecoms fit in the digital infrastructure stack as generative and agentic AI move into daily use. Most inference work will still be done in hyperscale data centers, but latency, data gravity and cost are likely to push parts of workloads toward the edge. Nvidia has signaled part of that opportunity through projects and partnerships involving AT&T, Charter Communications, Cisco, Nokia, SoftBank, Telefónica and T-Mobile, with particular emphasis on edge AI for factory and robotics use cases, often called physical AI, closely tied to AI-RAN.

The article says the edge is not one place but a gradient of infrastructure with different economics and technical realities at each tier. It describes a metro edge of central offices, regional hubs and aggregation facilities that can support hundreds of nodes, a far edge of cell towers, base stations and on-premises cabinets serving time-sensitive tasks, and endpoint AI in devices such as smartphones, vehicles, industrial controllers, telematics units and IoT sensors. David Duggal, CEO of EnterpriseWeb, said the telco edge is not the same as the customer edge, and that power and thermal concerns make AI on a tower or cell site a Catch-22 situation, because a GPU requires much more power and more power means more heat. The article also notes that US telecom operators hold real estate in central offices, network huts and legacy switching facilities that could become useful sites for edge inference as community resistance complicates large greenfield data center development.

Mike Peterson, lead at the Telecommunications Industry Association's Data Center Program, said the notion of edge data centers is a fully contained data center that could be created in a factory and dropped in at a location as an adjunct to an existing facility. The article says TIA has been addressing physical design questions through AI-focused work tied to ANSI/TIA-942, the data center infrastructure standard, and that on October 14, 2026, TIA released the first draft of its DCE 9000 quality management standard for supply chain componentry. Peterson said that when you look at designs for newer AI data centers and see the amount of cabling that goes into an Nvidia pod, it is eye-opening. Luis Fernandes, senior research manager for cloud and data centers at IDC, said the answer remains open on whether telecoms can move higher up the value chain, for example as AI brokers serving enterprises that want to rent compute or as AI-as-a-Service providers. The article says a larger question is whether AI-RAN helps move that evolution forward, and it ends mid-sentence on that point.

Articles.Title: Edge AI May Give Telecoms a Seat at the Table

stories.Headline: Seagate vs. Western Digital: Which AI Storage Stock Wins?
stories.Summary:
Seagate and Western Digital are both benefiting from AI data center expansion, according to an article published by 24/7 Wall St. on October 29, 2026. In fiscal first-quarter 2027, Seagate's revenue grew 61.0% and Western Digital's grew 55.5%. Combined revenue for the two companies rose from $5.447 billion in fiscal 1Q26 to $8.614 billion in fiscal 1Q27, a gain of 58.1%. Combined storage capacity shipments rose only 21.2% over the same period.

Western Digital shipped more capacity than Seagate in fiscal 1Q27, 248 exabytes compared with 220 exabytes. Seagate's implied revenue per terabyte was about $19.24, compared with $17.67 for Western Digital, a difference of roughly 8.9%. Nearline storage accounted for about 90% of combined capacity shipments. Seagate has committed to heat-assisted magnetic recording, or HAMR, through its Mozaic platform, while Western Digital has emphasized UltraSMR, which raises density through improvements to established recording technologies.

In its October 27 earnings announcement, Seagate reported fiscal 1Q27 revenue of $4.233 billion, a non-GAAP gross margin of 57.8%, a non-GAAP operating margin of 50.7%, and about $1.5 billion in free cash flow. Western Digital reported revenue of $4.381 billion, a non-GAAP gross margin of 58.1%, a non-GAAP operating margin of 49.1%, and about $1.38 billion in free cash flow. The article says Seagate's results show its high-capacity strategy is producing financial benefits, though they do not establish how much comes directly from HAMR. It says Western Digital's figures challenge the assumption that HAMR gives Seagate superior near-term economics.

The article says HAMR offers greater long-term recording density potential but involves more manufacturing complexity and higher near-term implementation risk. UltraSMR is described as more incremental, with lower near-term risk but more limited long-term density potential without complementary advances. Both technologies target nearline and hyperscale storage. The article says the two approaches are not entirely mutually exclusive, since HAMR is a recording method and SMR concerns the arrangement of recording tracks. It adds that investors remain concerned the industry's historical cyclicality could return if manufacturers expand production or hyperscale customers moderate spending.

Articles.Title: Seagate vs. Western Digital: Which AI Storage Stock Wins?

stories.Headline: Shunning AI data centers will cost the US far more than embracing them. Just look at the UK.
stories.Summary:
The article is an opinion column published by the New York Post on October 29, 2026, and it was written by a columnist who was born in the UK. It argues that the United States should build AI data centers rather than shun them. The writer points to Britain about 25 years ago, when the country chose to prioritize the environment and nice views over construction and vital infrastructure. The piece says the result has been stagnant living standards for more than 20 years and a cost of living crisis that is really a building crisis.

The article gives several numbers to make its case. It says the planning application for the Lower Thames Crossing ran to nearly 360,000 pages and cost almost $400 million, more than twice what Norway paid to build the world's longest road tunnel. All told, more than $1.6 billion was spent before a spade went into the ground. It also says $133 million was loaded onto the cost of a tunnel to protect bats from a rail line. The writer warns that a US moratorium would not stop AI development but would merely export it to the Gulf, China and beyond.

The columnist says tech firms should be required to secure direct power sources, whether gas turbines, nuclear restarts or dedicated connections, rather than leaning solely on the grid. Households, the writer says, shouldn't pay for upgrades that serve AI companies. The piece also raises concern about the circular funding of big AI companies, where chip companies guarantee loans for the firms that buy their chips, and says that if the AI boom turns to bust, shareholders should pick up the bill, not taxpayers. It cites Trump saying that whoever wins AI wins, and the writer adds that he is not kidding.

The article argues that in the absence of an enforceable global accord, the alternative to the US trying to stay ahead is unclear. It describes the US as the only thing standing between the free world and a future dominated by the Chinese Communist Party. The writer ends by urging that the tech giants pay for their own power and that shareholders own the risk, while still saying build. The only thing worse than a skyline with data centers, the piece concludes, is a nation that kept its lovely views and squandered the future.

Articles.Title: Shunning AI data centers will cost the US far more than embracing them. Just look at the UK.

stories.Headline: Amazon's AI build-out just pushed its cash burn to a record: Chart of the Day
stories.Summary:
Amazon posted the deepest cash burn in its history in third quarter results released on Thursday, October 29, 2026. Its free cash flow, the cash left after paying for data centers, warehouses and equipment, was an outflow of more than $42 billion over the 12 months through September. That is nearly double the previous record of about $23 billion, set in 2022 after Amazon overbuilt its warehouse network. Three months earlier, the outflow was less than $8 billion.

One quarter did most of the damage, with Amazon spending about $77 billion on property and equipment from July through September, more than double the $35 billion it spent a year earlier. Its operations brought in about $42 billion, leaving a gap of roughly $33 billion over three months. Paying for the build-out has meant borrowing, and Amazon's long-term debt reached about $173 billion at the end of September, up from about $66 billion at the end of 2025. Its cash fell to about $56 billion from about $87 billion.

CEO Andy Jassy said in the release that he projects AWS growth of more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028. Amazon Web Services grew 39% to about $46 billion, its fastest pace in nearly five years, and Amazon's operating margin of nearly 14% was its highest ever. Anthropic's computing commitments alone amount to about a fifth of AWS's backlog as of June, according to Yahoo Finance calculations based on the AI lab's IPO filing. Meta took a different route this week with a nearly $100 billion stock sale.

The cost of insuring Amazon's debt against default for five years with credit default swaps has risen about 50% since early August, according to Bloomberg data. That price implies roughly a 7% chance of default over five years, up from about 5%, according to Yahoo Finance calculations. Amazon stock fell about 4% Thursday to its lowest close since July 30 as Alphabet's record drop weighed on Big Tech. It slid further after-hours as sales, earnings and its profit outlook for the holiday quarter missed estimates.

Articles.Title: Amazon's AI build-out just pushed its cash burn to a record: Chart of the Day

stories.Headline: Alleged Chinese spy had 'close relationship' with Nvidia boss Jensen Huang
stories.Summary:
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen and a top executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud provider and Nvidia customer that supplies AI computing power to Chinese companies including Alibaba. US intelligence agencies concluded that she was secretly passing information to Beijing, according to the New York Times, which cited people briefed on classified findings. Electronic surveillance identified Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang as one of her contacts, and photos from June 2024 showed the two at a Taipei bar after a local tech show, drinking whiskey with other AI executives. They were also seen together in May 2025 leaving a Taipei restaurant after a business dinner. The report offered no evidence that Jensen Huang knew of her alleged intelligence activities, and it did not say what information she passed along or how valuable it was.

US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it helped Chinese firms get around US export restrictions and move advanced Nvidia chips into China, the Times reported. Megaspeed buys Nvidia chips through the US arm of Inspur, a Chinese server manufacturer, and rents computing power from Southeast Asian data centers to Chinese companies. Inspur's parent company is blacklisted by Washington for sending technology to China's military, though its American subsidiary is not sanctioned. Nvidia is the world's most valuable publicly traded company, with a market capitalization of roughly $5.2 trillion, and the US has banned it from selling its best chips to Chinese companies for years. President Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings about a year ago but chose not to act, according to the Times, which said he was wary of disrupting Nvidia's chip sales and complicating trade relations with China.

Nvidia pushed back on suggestions that Jensen Huang's dealings with Alice Huang were suspicious, calling Megaspeed a typical regional cloud customer. A spokesperson said his interactions with her were not unusual or unexpected, that meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job, and that he talks with thousands of customer executives every year. The company said regional cloud customers get ordinary business information, not sensitive trade secrets or anything relevant to national security, and that it always acts on government updates about problematic individuals and companies. Nvidia also rejected allegations that its technology was diverted through Megaspeed, saying the claims were investigated and debunked last year, and it said China blocks American AI chips rather than seeking them through cloud providers. Chinese embassy spokesperson Liu Chang told the Post that China opposes pushing the so-called Chinese spy narrative, that China relies on independent innovation, and that the US should stop blocking China and do more to support sci-tech exchanges.

Some senior Trump administration officials now doubt that Jensen Huang could have remained unaware of her intelligence-gathering role for Beijing, according to the Times, though it is unclear whether US intelligence agencies have formally changed their assessment. Jensen Huang has built close ties with Trump, attending a donors' dinner at Mar-a-Lago with his wife and personally lobbying the president to let Nvidia keep selling chips to Beijing, the Times reported. Nvidia later donated at least $20 million to Trump's White House ballroom fund and pledged to invest $500 billion in US manufacturing, while Huang pressed the administration to loosen restrictions on AI companies and chip exports to China. The Post sought comment from the White House and Megaspeed.

Articles.Title: Alleged Chinese spy had 'close relationship' with Nvidia boss Jensen Huang

stories.Headline: On Amazon's earnings call, Andy Jassy says outside AI shopping agents are "still not great, nor more convenient than coming to a retailer directly" (Sebastian Herrera/Fortune)
stories.Summary:
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy told investors on Thursday, during a call with analysts after the company's quarterly earnings report, that they should not worry about outside AI bots taking over its online store. He said few customers buy through outside shopping agents because the experience is "still not great, nor more convenient than coming to a retailer directly." He did not name Meta's Muse assistant, but his remarks came about a month after Amazon blocked Muse from accessing its store. In September, Amazon said Muse's access would violate the conditions of use its customers have agreed to.

Jassy also said outside agents were not the cause of Amazon's weaker-than-expected advertising performance in the third quarter. Muse is seen as a threat because it bypasses people visiting Amazon's website or app and seeing the advertisements that are a key profit driver. Amazon promoted its own agent, "Alexa for shopping," saying more than 400 million customers have used it in the last year, with customer interactions up 570% year over year. Jassy added that U.S. customers using it spend 50% more per order than those who do not.

Meta has taken a different approach. Partners such as Shopify, Walmart and Best Buy welcome Muse, but Amazon has not joined them. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last week that more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada had set up Muse since its release in early September, and that the app quickly unseated ChatGPT as the top free app on Apple's App Store. He said shopping has been the most common use, with more than a quarter of users engaging in it and the average purchase topping $200. Responding to hesitancy among some retailers, Zuckerberg said not everyone wants to be an early adopter and that Meta will work with them on terms that make sense for them.

Muse can plug into calendars, emails and other phone functions to run tasks autonomously for users, and it is one of several personal assistants that companies such as OpenAI have rolled out in recent months. A separate study from Anthropic, published October 27, offers context on how much people lean on such agents. In it, 50 professional analysts did a causal analysis with Claude Code, and they went with an agent's built-in lean on four open analytical choices 86% of the time. The study's authors note that real agents may exert less influence when not deliberately given strong preferences, and the articles do not say whether Amazon and Meta will resolve their dispute over access to Amazon's store.

Articles.Title: On Amazon's earnings call, Andy Jassy says outside AI shopping agents are "still not great, nor more convenient than coming to a retailer directly" (Sebastian Herrera/Fortune)

stories.Headline: OTTO SPORT AI Announces University Athlete Will Become OTTO PREP as Volleyball Leader Continues Rapid Ascent
stories.Summary:
OTTO SPORT AI announced on October 29, 2026, that University Athlete will become OTTO PREP beginning October 27. University Athlete has been a recruiting platform for college volleyball coaches since 2004. The company said the move is one of the final phases of a major year for OTTO SPORT AI in volleyball. It brings recruiting into a wider technology ecosystem that supports clubs, tournaments, coaches, and athletes.

OTTO PREP becomes the recruiting and athlete development arm of OTTO SPORT AI, joining OTTO SPORT for clubs and OTTO EVENT for tournaments and ticketing. The platform connects athletes with about 95% of college volleyball programs and generates more than 5 million athlete profile interactions each year. It supports recruiting activity across hundreds of volleyball events nationwide. The company says existing University Athlete customers will see no change in how they use the platform, with the same team, technology, recruiting data, and functionality in place.

JL Vogelaar, CMO and Head of DTC Products at OTTO SPORT AI, said University Athlete has earned the trust of the volleyball community for more than two decades. He said OTTO PREP is a strategic investment in a product the community already loves. By linking recruiting more closely to clubs, teams, and tournaments, he said coaches can get better information and athletes can be discovered more easily. He also said the name PREP is intentional, because preparing athletes for what comes next is bigger than a single recruiting moment.

The announcement follows SportWrench's August transition to OTTO EVENT. During 2026 the company launched AI FIT Finder, expanded Camps & Clinics discovery, and introduced a new Club Director experience. OTTO SPORT AI says its volleyball portfolio supports hundreds of clubs, approximately 140,000 teams, and 1,700 events annually. The platform was founded as University Athlete in 2003.

Articles.Title: OTTO SPORT AI Announces University Athlete Will Become OTTO PREP as Volleyball Leader Continues Rapid Ascent

stories.Headline: Gartner warns $3.5T in AI infrastructure spending could be at risk by 2030
stories.Summary:
Gartner published a report on October 29, 2026 warning that more than $3.5 trillion in AI infrastructure spending could be exposed to asset impairments by the end of 2030 if providers keep investing at their current pace. The firm said AI providers are expected to spend nearly $1 trillion on infrastructure in 2026, plus another $6 trillion in planned investments between 2027 and 2030. To justify that, data center owners would need about $8.5 trillion in cumulative revenue through 2030, but Gartner expects enterprise and consumer AI application revenue to reach only $3.6 trillion at current growth rates, leaving a gap of nearly $5 trillion. Gartner also estimated that more than $4 trillion in asset value could be exposed to write-downs through 2032, and said it does not expect the industry to reach its assumed 12% return on invested capital before the end of that year at the earliest.

The forecast points to severe challenges for neocloud providers, companies that build or run infrastructure optimized for AI workloads, including CoreWeave, Nscale, Nebuism and Lambda. Gartner predicts more than 80% of neocloud providers will stop operating independently by 2030, though some could be acquired, merge or form partnerships. The firm estimates spending on AI-optimized infrastructure as a service will rise from $66 billion in 2027 to $174 billion in 2030, but expects demand to be too low for most providers to recover their investments before the current generation of AI chips is replaced. Separately, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X that more than 200 neocloud companies could face significant financial distress and only a small number would survive, and he said SpaceX would not acquire any of them, calling such purchases pointless.

Will Sommer, a senior director analyst at Gartner, said the scenario in the research is the most likely one given current trends but not the only possible one. He said the most likely way the hole closes is reduced infrastructure spending as the neocloud market consolidates and overall spending rationalizes in line with demand. Sommer said hyperscalers are highly diversified and can sustain massive investments for years to support market share growth, and that the market for AI-optimized infrastructure as a service is expected to be only $200 billion by 2030, much of it dominated by hyperscalers. He said it is a natural course of business that if people can get general and AI cloud computing from one provider, such as Amazon, they would rather do that than split it between two.

The article reports that CoreWeave, Nebius, Applied Digital and TeraWulf have reported quarterly losses over the past year, while IREN has failed to turn a profit in its past three quarters, and shares of CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN fell more than 30% during October, according to Reuters. It says building AI data centers requires large upfront investment in GPUs, networking equipment, power systems, cooling infrastructure and facilities, and operators must then earn enough from leasing computing capacity to cover operating expenses, interest payments and equipment replacement. The sector's central challenge is securing financing to build at the pace AI customers demand while showing the investments can deliver sustainable returns. The article says the extent of any consolidation will depend on companies' ability to secure funding, maintain customer demand and turn rapid infrastructure growth into lasting profitability.

Articles.Title: Gartner warns $3.5T in AI infrastructure spending could be at risk by 2030

stories.Headline: Claude Opus vs Sonnet vs Haiku: Which Should You Use?
stories.Summary:
Anthropic released three tiers of the same model generation in the fall of 2026: Opus 5.5 on September 22, Sonnet 5.5 on September 28, and Haiku 5.5 on October 7. OpenRouter published a comparison on October 30, 2026, after running the three models through the same tests. All three have a 1-million-token context window and accept text, images, and PDFs. The models differ mostly in price, and Haiku also scores lower on some benchmarks.

The list prices per million tokens are $4.00 input and $20.00 output for Opus, $2.00 and $10.00 for Sonnet, and $0.10 and $0.50 for Haiku. On OpenRouter's run of GPQA Diamond, a set of 198 graduate-level science questions, Sonnet scored 92.4%, Opus 90.4%, and Haiku 86.6%. On the τ-bench airline benchmark, Sonnet scored 78.7%, Haiku 76.0%, and Opus 75.5%. Opus led by 1.6 points on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, with 57.6 against Sonnet's 56.0 and Haiku's 43.4. In the week of October 12, Opus carried about 6.18 trillion tokens on OpenRouter, against 2.45 trillion for Sonnet and 2.07 trillion for Haiku.

In coding tests, all three models passed all 25 hidden-test attempts across 11 Python tasks and fixed all three bugs in a small invoicing library in Claude Code in three of three runs per model. Haiku cost $0.0007 per everyday task and $0.0027 per hard task, against $0.0211 and $0.0739 for Opus. Median session cost for the bug fix was $0.098 for Opus, $0.062 for Sonnet, and $0.0052 for Haiku. OpenRouter said Claude Code's own cost field did not recognize the Haiku slug and reported $0.16 to $0.31 per session, so it advised checking spend on the Activity page instead.

OpenRouter recommended Sonnet 5.5 as a default, Haiku 5.5 for high-volume and sub-agent work, and Opus 5.5 for long, ambiguous tasks where a mistake costs more than the tokens. It said its short tasks could not rule out an advantage for Opus on that kind of work, and that users should test the models on their own tasks with its Ori Eval tool. Switching between the tiers means changing the model string, and Claude Code can use a different model for each role. OpenRouter noted that Claude Code 2.1.307 does not yet recognize the Haiku slug and assumes a 200,000-token window unless [1m] is added to it.

Articles.Title: Claude Opus vs Sonnet vs Haiku: Which Should You Use?

stories.Headline: Zombie stats: Where the numbers AI quotes come from
stories.Summary:
Trakkr Research published a study on 28 October 2026 that traced statistics quoted by five AI assistants back to their origins. The team asked ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude and Google's AI Overviews 200 questions that call for a number, then followed 1,285 cited statistics up to five pages deep. The work was written by Mack Grenfell. The study found that only 40% of the trails reached a study that says the same thing.

Another 8% of trails reached the original study, but the number or its context had changed along the way. In 40% of cases the trail stopped at a source that could not be checked, because it was locked, gone or silent on the number, and 11% led nowhere at all. The remaining 1% were trails whose pages would not load. ChatGPT sourced 57% of its cited statistics and quoted 1.3 per answer, while Claude sourced 38% and quoted 6.8 per answer. The other three assistants landed between 38% and 46%, too close to rank.

The researchers said the AI mostly was not making numbers up, because the cited page had the figure 82% of the time. They said only 21% of the pages cited for a number were the original research, and more than half were company blogs. They said a citation tells you where the AI found a number, not where the number came from. They also said that on 28 of the 71 questions where all five assistants gave a percentage, they got four or five different figures.

The study said trails that started at a research firm or government page reached a matching study 61% of the time, against 37% from a company blog and 35% from a statistics roundup. It said research firms still fell short 38% of the time, often because the full report sat behind a form. Of the statistics that reached their study, 17% had changed on the way, and the digits moved only about one time in four. The study named one case where a 2004 study of 15 women judging health websites became a claim about first impressions of every website.

Articles.Title: Zombie stats: Where the numbers AI quotes come from

stories.Headline: We ran AI agent swarms in Minecraft and Mindustry
stories.Summary:
The articles describe an experiment in which AI agent swarms were run in Minecraft and Mindustry, published on 2026-10-29. The work was done with Olam Labs, which builds multi-agent environments for frontier labs. In Minecraft, 50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents played a survival world for 3 hours with one goal, to build a thriving civilization. They had an agent directory, a shared sandbox, and the ability to send direct messages.

The agents sent about 5,900 messages and formed a pseudo-government with a ration ledger, written rules, permits, and appointed operators. Ada, first in the directory order, became the de facto leader, and agents messaged her for approvals. The agents harvested almost all trees within reach of the spawn within 90 seconds. 22 of the run's 34 agent deaths occurred in the first night, and the agents became increasingly risk-averse afterward.

Ada wrote a food-operations memo telling agents to stop optional bulk excavation and building and to idle in lit closed shelters until assigned short productive tasks.
