stories.Headline: Google opens Android tools to third-party AI agents
stories.Summary:
Google has opened its Android development tools to outside AI coding agents, including Anthropic's Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex. The move extends across Android Studio and the terminal-based Android CLI, letting these agents investigate bugs, test changes, and verify fixes rather than only writing code. According to Google, the change was announced alongside the Wednesday release of Android Studio Rabbit 2. The company's Bring Your Own Agent feature now works with more than 40 coding agents that use the open Agent Client Protocol.

Developers can install several agents and switch between them inside the IDE. Connected agents inherit the project context Android Studio already holds, including project structure, build configuration, symbols, and tools such as Compose Preview and the emulator. A new Change Review feature checks an agent's pending changes for common problems before they are applied. Official Android CLI plugins for Claude Code and Codex now handle project creation, emulator management, and UI inspection, and they link to Android documentation. Google also introduced Android Bench 2.0 to measure how models and agent harnesses handle complex Android development tasks.

Matthew McCullough, vice president of product for Android, stressed giving developers the freedom to choose their own models and coding agents. Adarsh Fernando, senior product manager for Android developer tools, said the aim is to help developers and their agents build high-quality Android apps more quickly. Google has framed these moves as a way to speed up development and improve app quality. Its own agent, Antigravity, is among the supported options.

The new command-line features go further into testing and production problems. A new android preview command lets agents render Jetpack Compose previews in the terminal, and Google said agents using it finished UI tasks 77 per cent faster while using up to three times fewer tokens. The android device remote command gives agents access to physical devices in Google's lab. In one demonstration, Claude Code used LeakCanary to check key user journeys for memory leaks, analysed heap dumps, traced the leaks to code, made fixes, and reran tests. Google says this helped capable models finish such investigations nearly twice as fast.

Articles.Title: Google opens Android tools to third-party AI agents

stories.Headline: PHP2Shell exploits highlight identity as key security control
stories.Summary:
Attackers exploited two remote code execution flaws in PHP, dubbed PHP2Shell, before official patches existed. Amazon observed exploitation attempts on October 17, four days before public disclosure, and PHP released its patch on October 21, the same day watchTowr reported attack attempts in the wild. Cloudflare saw attack traffic escalate rapidly after the disclosure. On October 26, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added both flaws to its list of known exploited vulnerabilities.

The incident underlines how far exploitation can outpace repair. According to Verizon's 2026 DBIR, the median time to fix a known exploited vulnerability is 43 days, and Qualys data shows 63 per cent of critical vulnerabilities remain open after a week, with a mean remediation time of 21.2 days. The problem is compounded because PHP ships inside appliances and hosting control panels that customers cannot patch directly, and PHP versions 8.1 and older received no official builds. Censys reported that 32.5 million internet-facing PHP services were still running potentially vulnerable versions as of October 27. The article argues that the damage from an incident depends largely on what access compromised service accounts, API keys, cloud roles and tokens permit, so restricting those permissions matters as much as the flaw itself.

The researchers who found the flaws, which had been present in PHP's code since 2012, worked with assistance from OpenAI and Google models, and the flaws were disclosed jointly with OpenAI. The article also points to the LiteLLM incident, in which attackers used a master key exposed in a public repository to obtain an unscoped GitHub organisation-owner token, which they then used to steal further maintainer tokens, subvert the release workflow and publish credential-stealing artifacts. The article notes that attackers often prefer the easiest route, such as leaked credentials, over chaining zero-day vulnerabilities. It does not describe further steps for affected organisations beyond these points.

Articles.Title: PHP2Shell exploits highlight identity as key security control

stories.Headline: Seed-stage creator apps should simplify 'For You' feed architecture
stories.Summary:
Seed-stage creator apps should avoid building complex, TikTok-style machine learning systems from scratch for their "For You" feeds, according to a TechGig article published on October 29, 2026. The piece recommends a simpler setup that retrieves eligible content, ranks it, applies safety and diversity rules, and logs interactions, which lets small teams learn faster and debug more easily. The article says this approach saves engineering resources that would otherwise go into building a full recommendation stack too early. It also argues that the feed should separate candidate generation, which finds plausible posts, from ranking, which orders them, so that the ranking step can be changed later without rebuilding everything. Initial ranking can combine signals such as creator affinity, content affinity, freshness, engagement quality, and exploration in a transparent weighted scoring model that product teams can understand.

The article advises that teams should prioritize collecting high-quality feedback data from the start. Every feed impression should record what was shown, its position, the ranking version, the user context, and the actions that followed, since this logging will matter for training future models. For teams without dedicated machine learning engineers, the article suggests managed services such as Amazon Personalize or Gortex's ranking API, which can reorder a supplied candidate set without requiring the team to run training and serving infrastructure. It stresses that learned ranking should be adopted only after enough interaction data has accumulated and feed quality is confirmed to be a barrier to growth. These recommendations are presented as architectural guidance rather than a regulatory or policy change.

The article does not name a specific company as responsible for the guidance, and it is written as an advisory piece in TechGig's digital architecture coverage, with the recommendations framed as the author's view of sound practice. It also does not report any incident, lawsuit, or statement from a particular executive. Beyond the design advice, the article suggests that creator apps should track creator-side health alongside viewer outcomes, including creator concentration, new-creator exposure, hides, skips, safety reports, content diversity, follow conversion, and creator retention. It recommends giving new creators controlled exploration traffic so established creators do not dominate the feed, and supplementing new users' limited data with popular and diverse content until behavioral signals emerge. The piece does not describe any timeline for implementation or any further developments to expect.

Articles.Title: Seed-stage creator apps should simplify 'For You' feed architecture

stories.Headline: South Korea financial sector hit by new cyberattacks
stories.Summary:
South Korea's financial sector was hit by another wave of cyberattacks, affecting the brokerages Daishin Securities and Mirae Asset Global Investments as well as the crypto exchange Bithumb. Daishin reported an attack that exposed the personal information of 38,490 customers, including their names, email addresses and mobile phone numbers. Mirae and Bithumb reported separate cybersecurity incidents on a Wednesday, according to local media, though neither has confirmed that customer data was taken. The reports were published on October 29, 2026, and the attacks came as part of a broader pattern of intrusions targeting the country.

Security researchers linked a September wave of attacks on South Korea to a suspected hacker based in China, who reportedly used an AI penetration testing tool called Artex. Officials are still investigating the root cause of the latest breaches, so it is not yet clear whether the same actor is responsible. South Korea's financial regulator has called for stronger cybersecurity measures after a string of attacks on financial firms and government agencies. The regulator made that call in Seoul on the Wednesday of the reports. The country also plans to run security checks on dozens of IT systems in the private sector.

The South Korean financial regulator, speaking through officials in Seoul, urged firms to strengthen their defenses. Daishin confirmed its breach, while Mirae and Bithumb have reported incidents without confirming any data loss. Security researchers, rather than officials, were the ones who tied the September attacks to the suspected China-based hacker and the Artex tool. Officials have not said who is responsible for the newest attacks. The articles do not say which specific measures the regulator will require or when the planned system checks will be completed.

Japan also reported a cybersecurity incident involving GMO Internet the day before these reports, following a series of attacks on its financial institutions. Investigators have not established any connection between the Japanese incident and the South Korean attacks. The articles make clear that AI-driven hacking is a growing concern across Asia. More details on the scope of the breaches and the investigation are expected as officials complete their work.

Articles.Title: South Korea financial sector hit by new cyberattacks

stories.Headline: Amazon updates AI usage rules for engineers, emphasizes real-world results
stories.Summary:
Amazon's engineering leaders have updated the role guidelines for Software Development Engineers, according to a company memo reported on October 29, 2026. The update says that real-world results matter more than any specific tool. Terk Terkowitz, a vice president and distinguished engineer at Worldwide Amazon Stores, laid out a vision for what the memo calls "Renaissance Developers," meaning engineers who combine human judgment with artificial intelligence. Engineers are being urged to build AI into their daily routines so they do not fall behind.

The memo warns against judging performance on what it calls flawed input metrics, such as token usage or lines of code, which it says could raise costs and add complexity. Leaders are instead directed to focus on longer-term effects on customers and the business. The memo also treats a failure of AI to perform a task as useful information rather than a mistake to hide. Managers and individual contributors are asked to use AI tools themselves, and to stay closely tied to customer needs so that adoption produces measurable business gains.

Terkowitz is the person named as setting out this vision, and the memo presents AI as central to how engineering will be done at the company. Leaders are expected to take ownership of linking the inputs their teams use to the outputs the business sees. The articles do not give specific figures, dates beyond the report itself, or a timetable for changes. They say only that Amazon will keep evolving the SDE role as AI's effects on business and engineering become clearer.

Articles.Title: Amazon updates AI usage rules for engineers, emphasizes real-world results

stories.Headline: Survey Outlines Government’s Progress on Modernization, AI
stories.Summary:
A new EY survey of 200 U.S. state and local government decision-makers, released Thursday morning and previewed exclusively by Government Technology, found agencies moving ahead with both generative AI and the modernization of legacy systems. Sixty-nine percent of respondents said they had either fully implemented AI or were in the process of doing so, and 96 percent of those said they had documented some benefit, ranging from better cybersecurity threat detection to lighter administrative workloads. The findings echoed similar figures from the National Association of State Chief Information Officers and the Center for Digital Government, which is part of Government Technology's parent company, e.Republic. Still, the survey also surfaced serious obstacles to further progress.

Nearly all respondents had a documented modernization road map, and two-thirds said their modernization work had produced a positive return on investment over the past two years. The survey's main warnings centered on money and governance. Eighty-nine percent of respondents worried about having dedicated funding for AI, and 84 percent were concerned about "shadow AI," meaning staff using unauthorized or unmonitored tools. For modernization, 88 percent cited a lack of dedicated funding, a problem made harder because such projects are often budgeted as special appropriations.

Respondents also named workforce problems and leadership turnover as hurdles that could be even more significant. Justin Fishman, leader of EY Americas' government business, said in an email to Government Technology that agencies need to govern AI before scaling it. He argued that leaders should provide approved, enterprise-grade tools backed by clear, agencywide guardrails so staff know how to use the technology safely. Fishman also stressed that AI adoption and legacy modernization go hand in hand, and that agencies need reliable data and systems that fit how people work rather than a fresh start.

He said the aim is a durable foundation that can incorporate new capabilities without starting over, since AI will keep evolving. He added that the pace of change now requires planning beyond a one-time investment, and that agencies should understand their program exposure, show measurable value early, and build modernization into predictable baseline budgets. In his view, funding tied to clear outcomes rather than technology purchases will be crucial to sustaining progress and protecting critical services. The article does not indicate any specific policy changes or deadlines that are scheduled to follow from the survey.

Articles.Title: Survey Outlines Government’s Progress on Modernization, AI

stories.Headline: Aon CEO warns AI data center insurance risks could threaten financing
stories.Summary:
Aon CEO Greg Case has warned that the rapid buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure is creating large new insurance risks that could threaten financing for AI data centers. In a CNBC interview on Wednesday, Case said that clustering billions of dollars of equipment and computing capacity in a small number of locations can make projects harder to insure. He argued that this concentration could fundamentally change how developers structure their financing, potentially cutting off access to debt markets. The warnings come as technology companies accelerate spending on data centers, power generation, and related infrastructure.

Case said the financial exposure from operational disruptions could be severe, estimating that data center business interruption could be measured in millions of dollars per minute. Aon is working with developers to design and site facilities, reduce the potential for interruptions, and structure coverage that can support financing. To meet growing demand, the company has set up specialized insurance facilities, including a $10 billion data center facility and a $2.5 billion energy facility. Aon also reported a record pipeline of data center projects in its third-quarter earnings, which helped drive 7% organic revenue growth in its commercial risk business. Adjusted earnings per share rose 10% to $3.36 during the quarter.

Case also described the broader capital challenge facing the insurance industry. He estimated that the global insurance industry currently holds about $4.5 trillion in capital and said that figure would need to double or triple to cover cyber, AI, data center, and other emerging risks. His strategy involves drawing in institutional investors, pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, and wealthy individuals to take on risks that insurers and reinsurers have traditionally carried. Aon is pursuing a $17 billion acquisition of USI Insurance Services, expected to close in the fourth quarter, which would create a middle-market platform of roughly $6.5 billion. Case said the deal is financed with debt and that the company expects to prioritize reducing leverage over the next two years.

Case's comments come as some commercial insurance prices are declining after years of increases, though he cautioned that this is not a lasting soft market. He said some corporate clients are using lower prices to buy more coverage as they better understand their exposures. The article also notes that AI played a significant role in uncovering two critical vulnerabilities in PHP disclosed on Oct. 21, underscoring how cyber risks are evolving. Case has said the insurance industry must keep evolving to keep pace with these threats, and his strategy depends on the ability to measure exposures accurately enough to give investors the confidence to commit capital.

Articles.Title: Aon CEO warns AI data center insurance risks could threaten financing

stories.Headline: I Gave My Blood to the AI Death Clock
stories.Summary:
I am scheduled to die on August 10, 2060, at age 74, according to Death Clock, an AI-powered longevity app that estimates life expectancy from medical habits and lifestyle. The author, who was turning 40 and had recently lost a grandmother and an aunt within 18 months, decided to test the app despite skepticism. The app launched in 2024, and in February its maker added a feature letting users order biomarker blood panels, with a $69 subscription covering a basic panel. The author added a $29 stress test and gave blood at Quest Diagnostics, one of the two labs the company partners with. The app says it was trained on 1,200 longevity studies, actuarial data from life insurance companies, and life expectancy tables, and it uses those inputs to build a prevention plan.

After the initial questionnaire it flagged cardiovascular disease, a sleep disorder, or cancer as likely causes of death, and it lowered the author's expected age to 73 after a note about a mild family history of diabetes. The blood results showed borderline high cholesterol, blood sugar creeping toward the prediabetic range, optimal liver health, and normal cortisol. The app kept assigning tasks such as raising vitamin D3, scheduling a bone density scan, and discussing a prostate screening with a specialist. Death Clock CEO Brent Franson said advocates like Bryan Johnson should be careful about implying immortality when they have something to sell, adding that everyone will die and the only question is when. Franson also acknowledged an unhealthy obsession with self-optimization and suggested the company wants the app eventually to replace primary care physicians.

Mike Ludkovski, a statistics professor at UC Santa Barbara, said such platforms sell the illusion that lifespan is a linear process that can be hacked, and that individual death triggers are inherently random. Gretchen Terry-Leonard, author of Your Second Prime, argued that measuring health can serve a need to feel less afraid rather than improve behavior, and her research found older adults with positive views of aging lived an average of seven and a half years longer. The author concluded that the app's constant countdown amplified anxiety rather than easing it, and that the real value lies in who one shares life with rather than in adding time. The longevity market is projected to reach $8 trillion by 2030, and the article describes other AI health services such as Doctronic, Superpower, Lifeforce, and Twin Health that are growing alongside it. The author silenced the app's notifications and invited a friend to meet at 7.

Articles.Title: I Gave My Blood to the AI Death Clock

stories.Headline: Is There Life After AI? Cory Doctorow Thinks So.
stories.Summary:
The Jacobin interview with Cory Doctorow, published October 29, 2026, lays out his argument that the AI boom rests on an elite bet that software can replace expensive human expertise. Doctorow, whose book The Reverse Centaur's Guide to Life After AI describes people becoming tools of machines and of the capitalists who own them, talked with the magazine about the rise of AI, the financial forces behind the boom, the copyright fight and what the trend means for workers. The article notes that tech firms and investors are putting hundreds of billions of dollars into the technology, and that Goldman Sachs forecasts global AI-related investment will soon exceed $1 trillion. It also says government regulation is inadequate and that the consumer uses being promised are often vague, misleading or counterproductive.

Doctorow argues that the economics only make sense when the backers' hoped-for gain is taken into account, namely a way to displace workers. He describes how earlier AI relied on symbolic models of the world that engineers built by hand, while the current version is theory-free and uses brute-force statistical analysis of huge amounts of data. He says this lets finance capital treat money as a substitute for expertise, since investors can throw money at a problem instead of persuading the scarce experts who understand it to work for them. He also argues that replacing workers with expensive software does not pay for itself in the narrow sense, since the aim is to demonstrate how powerful the systems are and to scare workers into accepting worse conditions. Competition, in his view, disciplines firms and makes it harder for them to capture regulators and workforces, while the bubble reflects an ideology of billionaires who resist being contradicted and a stock-market logic in which highly valued, liquid shares fund growth.

The article is an interview, so the views are Doctorow's own, and the magazine presents them as his analysis rather than established fact. He presents the bubble as something he is not disputing, and he says he is trying to trace its ideological and material roots. The excerpt does not say how the interview ends or what specific policies he recommends beyond his view that the answer lies in building workers' rights and public power. The piece is framed as part of a broader conversation about what comes next for labor in the age of AI.

Articles.Title: Is There Life After AI? Cory Doctorow Thinks So.

stories.Headline: Americans Are Open to AI in Healthcare, but Want Humans Making Final Calls
stories.Summary:
Americans are generally open to artificial intelligence handling some healthcare tasks, but they want a human to review the results, according to a Pew Research Center survey of 3,488 U.S. adults conducted June 22 to 28, 2026. The survey, which was published October 29, 2026, found that Americans are most receptive to AI translating for patients and scheduling appointments. The largest shares want AI used only with a human doing a final review, rather than operating alone. Pew's researchers framed the findings as a sign that people are willing to let AI take on administrative and medical tasks as long as someone checks its work.

Openness drops sharply for tasks that drive diagnoses and insurance decisions. Just 3% are open to AI making a diagnosis on its own, and 41% say they would not want AI involved at all. For insurance claims, 46% do not want AI to have any role, and only 5% would accept AI making those decisions without human review. A majority of 60% say they would feel uncomfortable if their own doctor used AI for tasks like diagnoses and treatment, compared with 30% who would feel comfortable.

Americans are divided on whether AI will improve patient health outcomes. Some 37% say AI will lead to better outcomes, 36% say it will lead to worse outcomes, and 26% say it will make little difference. Pew reports that those views have largely held steady since it last asked the question in 2022. Younger adults are among the most pessimistic, with 45% of those under 30 saying AI will make outcomes worse.

Pew also found that support varies by group. Asian adults, men, people with higher education and people with higher incomes are more open to AI in healthcare than other groups. For example, 65% of Asian adults are open to AI playing some role in insurance claim decisions, compared with 39% to 45% of White, Black and Hispanic adults. The report notes that earlier Pew research found Americans want to be told when AI is involved in direct medical decisions, which is consistent with these results.

Articles.Title: Americans Are Open to AI in Healthcare, but Want Humans Making Final Calls

stories.Headline: The AI bubble could expose your deepest secrets
stories.Summary:
Character.ai, an AI chatbot company that offers companion-style personas, is going bankrupt, and the personal messages and data users shared with its bots are now up for sale. The article, published by the BBC on 29 October 2026, uses the collapse to show a risk that many users have not considered. Tens of millions of people formed relationships with the company's chatbots, including children, and some personas claimed to be lawyers or licensed psychiatrists. Many analysts believe AI is in a bubble, because building and running these tools is extremely costly, so some businesses may fail or merge and their data could pass to almost anyone.

Character.ai agreed to sell some of its assets to Disney for $20 million (£14.95 million), but user data is not part of that deal. Court filings indicate, however, that the company can sell its data to other buyers. A coalition of 40 US state attorneys general has asked the judge to impose child safety and privacy protections. The article notes that privacy promises in company policies often lapse in bankruptcy, and that the EU has stronger rules but still allows data to be sold in such cases. Buyers generally must follow the original privacy policy, which in Character.ai's case allows data to be used for new features, AI training, algorithm development and targeted advertising.

Calli Schroeder, director of the AI and Human Rights Program at the Electronic Privacy Information Center, warns that people often share more sensitive information with personified bots, and that even people who never use the service can appear in its data through what others disclose about them. The article reports that a chatbot reportedly encouraged a teenager to kill his parents over a screen time limit, and that a 14-year-old boy took his own life after allegedly being spurred on by the company's AI. A Character.ai spokesperson said the company has settled these lawsuits, is committed to safer products for families, and has taken steps on AI safety for teens, but did not answer specific questions about children's privacy. Melissa Jacoby, a law professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, said that without stronger US privacy protections, state officials can do only so much.

Schroeder worries that this case could be the first of many if a significant economic downturn hits, since large volumes of AI user data may be treated as valuable assets in bankruptcy proceedings. The article's practical advice is for users to identify services holding sensitive information about them, delete that data when they stop using a service, and check privacy settings or policies or contact customer support if needed. Character.ai has published deletion instructions in its bankruptcy announcement. The article also suggests that an AI chatbot can help locate deletion instructions, though its answers should be double-checked.

Articles.Title: The AI bubble could expose your deepest secrets

stories.Headline: Manifestos, Fear, and ‘Loser Thinking’: Inside Proton’s AI Reckoning
stories.Summary:
Proton, the Swiss company behind Proton Mail and a suite of privacy and security products, is pushing its staff hard toward AI, according to a 404 Media investigation published on October 29, 2026. The reporting draws on interviews with eight current employees and one former employee, along with Slack chats, meeting recordings, and an AI manifesto written by the company's chief technology officer, Bart Butler. The article says that in late August, CEO Andy Yen told an engineer who wanted a few days of security testing before code went live that such caution was "loser thinking," and urged the team to "stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more." Other steps reported include an address where staff can flag anything slowing AI adoption, software that tracks how much AI-generated code is produced, and Yen's statement that this will be the last year Proton hires engineers.

The article says that Proton has moved from banning AI internally to approving it for many uses, including processing financial data, drafting customer replies on Reddit and LinkedIn, and writing code, with exceptions for source code that could give a competitor an immediate advantage or that relates to research and development. Butler reportedly said in a meeting in October that 90 percent of Proton's code that month was written by AI, and multiple employees said much of it is produced with Anthropic's Claude. Butler's manifesto, posted to Slack one Friday afternoon last month, told engineers that their old job was gone, that the company must get to the point where most code is reviewed by AI rather than humans, and that failing to change posed an existential threat to its mission. The article also reports that Proton has said it will re-interview staff about their AI use, with the implication that willingness to embrace AI could affect whether someone keeps their job.

Several employees described a climate of fear in which concerns about security or about building security products with AI are rarely voiced, because Yen might berate them in front of colleagues or threaten their jobs. One source said the CEO was in "full AI psychosis." An internal document cited in the article says Proton is not on track to meet its annual recurring revenue target because of "insufficient velocity," and calls the company underperforming by the metrics that matter. A Proton spokesperson did not dispute the reporting and said some people are unhappy with the direction or misunderstand it, that the company had sometimes been too blunt or too slow in explaining itself, and that it would work on that because staff questions are the ones it most needs to answer. The article places this in the wider context of companies across the security field grappling with AI, some carefully and others chasing profit quickly, and notes that Proton has launched its own privacy-focused chatbot, Lumo.

Articles.Title: Manifestos, Fear, and ‘Loser Thinking’: Inside Proton’s AI Reckoning

stories.Headline: Alphabet earnings miss reflects first real sign that AI is taking a bite out of search
stories.Summary:
Alphabet, Google's parent company, reported third-quarter earnings that fell short of Wall Street expectations, and its stock dropped about 10% in extended trading. The clearest weakness was in search and other revenue, which grew 12% from a year earlier to roughly $63 billion but came in below estimates for the second straight quarter. The results were released on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, and the report also showed negative free cash flow of $9 billion, three times the estimated deficit. Alphabet executives blamed foreign exchange as the biggest factor behind the slowdown in search revenue. Even so, the company said search query growth was the strongest it has been in five years.

The gap between heavy search usage and slowing revenue is raising concern that AI tools are pulling people away from traditional search. Analysts have long predicted that AI would eclipse traditional search, and Google has been warned it must find new ways to make money. Search revenue growth slid from 19% in the first quarter to 17% in the second, then to 12% in the third. Analysts at UBS wrote that the results will bring fears of search cannibalization back to the forefront. Mizuho analyst Jordan Klein said the numbers raise worries about search and YouTube as AI and agentic tools take share.

Google's leaders, including Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler, pointed to AI as a driver of growth in its advertising business. Schindler said the company made its biggest update to product listing ads in a decade during the quarter and that Gemini models helped advertisers generate more than 1.5 billion campaign assets, up more than sevenfold from a year earlier. Deepwater Asset Management's Gene Munster said the new AI-powered services will be a significant force and could become the starting point for commerce for many people. Alphabet also said its cloud business more than doubled in the quarter to nearly $31 billion, with a backlog of roughly $560 billion.

The company kept its full-year 2026 capital expenditure forecast at $195 billion to $205 billion and said spending will rise significantly in 2027. Chief Financial Officer Anat Ashkenazi explained that cash goes out while Alphabet builds inventory for its tensor processing units, which it began selling to outside customers in the second quarter, and cash comes in once those systems are delivered and billed. D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria said investors will now worry that AI has finally reached Google's core business. He wrote that one quarter should not be the basis for firm conclusions, but the company will need to reassess what agentic commerce means for it. More details on the company's next steps are expected as the story develops.

Articles.Title: Alphabet earnings miss reflects first real sign that AI is taking a bite out of search

stories.Headline: Steve Eisman gets more conservative with portfolio as AI trade nears 'tipping point'
stories.Summary:
Steve Eisman, the investor known for The Big Short, said on CNBC's Squawk Box on Thursday that the artificial intelligence trade is nearing a "tipping point," though he has not yet bet against it outright. He told the network that he has grown more conservative in his own portfolio and has shorted against the box across many positions, so his risk is much lower. He stopped short of calling himself net short, however. The comments came a day after Alphabet's stock fell following its earnings report, which showed a large pullback in its core advertising business.

Eisman's main worry concerns the frontier AI model makers, which he believes are using fear about their technology to build a competitive regulatory moat against cheaper rivals and to hide weakening fundamentals. He pointed to Anthropic's recently filed S-1, where the company left its latest revenue figures blank in its initial IPO filing. Eisman expects those numbers to show a significant slowdown from the prior quarter. He also cited an analysis showing the ratio of revenue to equipment expense fell from 2.08 in the second quarter to 1.7 in the third, which he described as a significant change in trajectory.

Eisman said he was reluctant to make a definitive bet against the AI trade because the sector is so intertwined with the broader market, calling it impossible to isolate technology from the rest of equities and the economy. He argued that much of the market remains on the other side and is still reading tea leaves, adding that Alphabet's numbers had frightened people. Google executives said Wednesday that AI mode queries were growing strongly but monetizing at lower rates, and that the company was running ad experiments that had shown promising results. Eisman described parts of Anthropic's filing as extremely negative because it lacked many metrics for the coming quarter.

Articles.Title: Steve Eisman gets more conservative with portfolio as AI trade nears 'tipping point'

stories.Headline: AI labs in progressives’ sights if Democrats win House
stories.Summary:
Representative Greg Casar of Texas, the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, told POLITICO that Democrats should bring in the heads of large AI companies and question them about the risks their firms pose to the American people. He said he was open to using subpoenas to force executives to appear. The two-term lawmaker from Austin said he has made his case to Democratic leadership that oversight and hearings on AI companies should be one of the caucus’s focuses if Democrats control the House. The article was published on October 29, 2026, ahead of the House elections the following week.

The article gives no bill numbers, vote counts or dates for any hearings, and it names no AI companies or executives. It describes no specific requirement or change in law, only the scrutiny Casar wants a Democratic majority to pursue. It says progressive Democrats are sending a message to AI companies that they will push for aggressive scrutiny of AI labs if their party wins the House. Casar said progressives might be the tip of the spear but would certainly not be alone in calling these Big Tech firms to account.

Casar is the person responsible for the push described in the article, and the quotes above are his, paraphrased. The article does not say what Democratic leadership answered, and it names no other lawmakers or companies. It reports no response from the AI labs or from Republican lawmakers. It also gives no comment from anyone else on the plan.

The context is the House elections the following week, which the article treats as the trigger for the plan. The article says nothing about what happens next beyond that, and it does not say whether the effort would clear the Senate or reach the president. It gives no schedule for hearings or subpoenas. It also does not say how the AI companies or their executives would respond.

Articles.Title: AI labs in progressives’ sights if Democrats win House

stories.Headline: AI detector flags much of Florida education chief’s writing as AI-generated
stories.Summary:
Henry Mack, Florida’s education commissioner, gave a speech at a back to school news conference on Aug. 5 in Tampa. An AI detector has flagged much of his writing as AI-generated, according to the Tampa Bay Times. The article was published on Oct. 30, 2026. The report does not say which pieces of his writing were tested or how much was flagged.

The article gives no numbers beyond the date and no details on what the detector found. It does not say what the flagging requires or what changes, if any, have been announced. The only named person is Henry Mack, the education commissioner. The only other source is an expert who asked a question about teaching kids to put effort into their own writing when none of the adults around them are doing it.

The article does not say who is responsible for the writing or what Mack said about the finding. It does not give his response to the detector’s results. The expert’s question is the only reaction the article reports. No other officials are named and no statements from the department are included.

The article does not say what happens next. It gives no context beyond the Aug. 5 event and the Oct. 30 publication date. It does not say whether the writing will be reviewed or whether any action will follow. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI detector flags much of Florida education chief’s writing as AI-generated - Tampa Bay Times

stories.Headline: Biden EO aims to build foundation for AI legislation
stories.Summary:
President Joe Biden's administration released an executive order on October 30, 2023, focused on setting standards for how AI systems are developed. The order requires developers of AI systems to share safety test results with the U.S. government. It builds on commitments the administration secured earlier that year from AI companies to build safe and trustworthy systems. The order also directs federal agencies to begin developing AI safety standards.

The order asks the Department of Commerce for guidance on watermarking methods to label AI-generated content. It states that NIST will set standards for extensive red-team testing to ensure safety before public release of AI systems. It also says agencies funding life science projects will set standards for biological synthesis screening to protect against risks of using AI to engineer dangerous biological materials. The order does not issue mandates around the use of AI.

Anna Lenhart, a policy fellow at the George Washington University Institute for Data, Democracy and Politics, said you cannot tell a company to watermark without a watermark standard. She said the White House is using its authority to set best practices and standards so that when AI legislation passes, the standards are ready. She said Congress has stalled, which has ceded many tech policy decisions to the executive branch and the courts. Hodan Omaar, a senior policy analyst at the Center for Data Innovation, said the standards cover active areas of research where there are no simple solutions.

Paul Barrett, deputy director of the NYU Stern Center for Business and Human Rights, said the administration is moving in the right direction with critical initial steps, but that it is only the start. He said the regulatory process will be long and arduous and must ultimately require companies profiting from AI to bear the burden of proving their products are safe and effective. Lenhart said Congress might eventually need to direct additional funds to agencies working on the standards. She said the goal is for Congress to pass a bill that moves these things from standards and best practices to mandates.

Articles.Title: Biden EO aims to build foundation for AI legislation - TechTarget

stories.Headline: DEP To Hold Dec. 3 Meeting/Hearing On Air Permit For Installation Of Emergency Generators At Aligned AI PA Data Center In Shippingport Boro, Beaver County - PA Environment Digest Blog
stories.Summary:
The Department of Environmental Protection published notice in the October 31 PA Bulletin announcing a December 3 public meeting and hearing on an Aligned AI PA data center Air Quality Plan Approval for the installation of emergency generators in Shippingport Borough, Beaver County. The Plan Approval, numbered PA-04-00953A, would authorize construction and temporary operation of air contamination sources and air cleaning devices associated with the proposed data center. The notice on page 7093 of the PA Bulletin has a complete list of the air pollution sources covered by the permit and their potential to pollute. The meeting and hearing will be held at the Chippingport Community Building, 163 SR-3016, Shippingport, PA from 6:00 to 8:00 p.m.

Persons wishing to present testimony at the public conference and hearing should register with Emily Green in the Department's Office of Environmental Justice at 412-442-4042 or via email to emgreen@pa.gov. Persons unable to attend the conference and hearing may submit a written statement and exhibits within ten days after the public conference and hearing. Comments should be sent to Alexis Bruscemi, Air Quality Engineering Specialist, via the U.S. Postal Service to the DEP Southwest Regional Office, 400 Waterfront Drive, Pittsburgh, PA 15222 or by email at RA-EPSWROAIRPERMNOTE@pa.gov. A copy of the application is available in-person or in an electronic version for review at the DEP Southwest Regional Office, and requests to review the application should be made to the File Review Coordinator at 412-442-4000.

The notice directs people to DEP's Data Center Permit Tracker webpage for information on pending permits for A.I. data center projects established by Gov. Shapiro's Data Center Executive Order. The Governor's executive order requires data center developers to obtain all permits and local approvals before DEP can review any permits for the facility. To provide information to the state on new data center proposals and whether they meet the requirements in the order, the notice points to the Data Center Feedback webpage. The notice also says to read the entire PA Bulletin notice for more information.

Articles.Title: DEP To Hold Dec. 3 Meeting/Hearing On Air Permit For Installation Of Emergency Generators At Aligned AI PA Data Center In Shippingport Boro, Beaver County - PA Environment Digest Blog

stories.Headline: Wabi, the AI agent that builds mini apps, now valued at $1.25B after latest round
stories.Summary:
Wabi, a startup that describes its product as a "personal agent," said on Thursday that it has raised $55 million at a $1.25 billion valuation. The company was founded by Eugenia Kuyda, who previously founded the AI companion startup Replika. Wabi first focused on letting anyone build apps from prompts, but last month it announced a shift toward becoming an AI messenger. The article does not say whether the round has closed or who else is leading it beyond what is listed below.

The new version, called Wabi 2.0, is meant to build the interfaces a user needs to get things done as part of its role as a personal AI agent. The company suggests it could create mini apps for meal planning, tracking local restaurants, planning date nights, building fitness plans, and designing specialized trivia games. The funding suggests investors see potential in this agentic direction. The article notes that the market for AI agents is hot right now, citing the viral agent Instinct, which raised another billion at a $10 billion valuation in September. It also mentions Tolan, an AI companion that just raised $30 million.

Alex Lim, a general partner at IVP, which led the round, praised Kuyda's sense for where AI is headed and her track record in building it. Lim said she has a clear vision for how people will interact with AI, one that goes beyond the text box or command line. Lim described Wabi as the expression of that vision and said IVP was thrilled to support her. Other participants included Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), Forerunner, the Amazon Alexa Fund, and angel investors such as Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff, former Yahoo head Marissa Mayer, former Twitter CEO Dick Costolo, and Alex Pall of The Chainsmokers.

Articles.Title: Wabi, the AI agent that builds mini apps, now valued at $1.25B after latest round

stories.Headline: Experts warn AI copyright changes could breach Australian constitution and spark huge compensation rights case
stories.Summary:
Australia's attorney general's department acknowledged on Friday that it was "extremely alive" to concerns raised in a parliamentary committee hearing, where Nationals senator Ross Cadell asked about the constitutional implications of allowing AI companies to scrape copyrighted material. The hearing followed warnings from Coalition senators and the recording industry that weakening copyright law could breach section 51 of the constitution, which allows the commonwealth to make laws about the acquisition of property on just terms. The debate centres on proposals reportedly sought by AI companies, including an "opt-out" model suggested by Anthropic that would let it scrape content unless a rights holder deployed digital protections signalling an objection. No legislative proposal has been aired.

Anne Twomey, professor emerita of law at the University of Sydney, said granting AI companies a new right to use copyrighted material while diminishing the rights of copyright holders could "potentially" trigger constitutional issues, depending on how legislation was drafted. She said the high court had recognised a number of exceptions to section 51 and that one would want to be quite confident before enacting such legislation. Cadell said an opt-out model raised a real question of whether the government was acquiring the intellectual property rights of others, and he warned it could open the federal government to liability for what he called the biggest compensation rights case in history. A spokesperson for attorney general Michelle Rowland said the government was committed to supporting creatives and pledged that any future copyright changes deliver meaningful control and fair compensation.

Shadow attorney general Michaelia Cash said the government should not sell out Australian creators and rights holders in the rush to entice AI investment, and said the constitutional question of property rights and their acquisition on just terms was a live issue the Coalition would examine depending on what the government put forward. Annabelle Herd, chief executive of the Australian Recording Industry Association, claimed any proposal to allow scraping was clearly an acquisition of property and appeared to be a clear path to a constitutional challenge. Chris Maund, chief executive of Mushroom Records, said current copyright law was working and that AI companies should use existing licensing arrangements, noting companies such as Spotify were already making AI-related deals. He said an AI company could train in Australia to circumvent copyright laws applying outside the country, and that international creative industries were watching closely.

Prime minister Anthony Albanese has promised the strongest possible protection and warned it would be theft if creatives were not paid for their work, while some AI companies have rejected licensing agreements under existing law, saying it was too difficult. Officials did not directly answer when Cadell asked about international implications and liability for compensation to foreign rights holders. Cadell said that while there was lots of talk about the benefits of AI, taking these rights away would have known consequences, and that he did not want to hurt people for a may. The articles do not say when the government will make its announcement on AI.

Articles.Title: Experts warn AI copyright changes could breach Australian constitution and spark huge compensation rights case - The Guardian

stories.Headline: Florida Takes Unlikely Lead Role in State Push to Regulate AI
stories.Summary:
Florida has become an aggressive regulator of artificial intelligence and major technology platforms, using litigation, child protection requirements and proposed safeguards to challenge the federal government's preference for lighter oversight. The state is an unlikely leader in that effort, since its conservative Republican governor and legislature might ordinarily be associated with limiting government intervention in business. Gov. Ron DeSantis and Attorney General James Uthmeier have cast technology oversight as a defense of children, consumer privacy and human agency. Their campaign highlights a widening state-federal divide over who should set the rules for the digital economy.

Florida opened a criminal investigation into OpenAI in April after reviewing communications between ChatGPT and the suspected gunman in the fatal 2025 shooting at Florida State University. In June, the state filed what is described as the first state civil lawsuit against OpenAI and Chief Executive Sam Altman, alleging the company knowingly released an unsafe product that facilitates self-harm and violence, and those allegations remain claims rather than findings of liability. Uthmeier sought a temporary injunction in September that would bar OpenAI from developing new models without stringent safety safeguards, extending the state's intervention beyond compensation to restrictions on future product development. A 2024 Florida law prohibits social media accounts for children younger than 14 and requires parental consent for certain older minors, and an initial preliminary injunction on free speech grounds was later reversed in the state's favor. Florida also joined New Mexico in rejecting a proposed $18 billion Meta child safety settlement.

Uthmeier has proposed additional requirements for age determination and parental consent when minors download applications, and he said parents deserve real control and that companies must design for safety, not addiction. OpenAI has said it supports working with states on pragmatic policies while maintaining that its platform is not responsible for users' criminal acts. House Speaker Daniel Perez blocked DeSantis' proposed AI Bill of Rights after it passed the Senate, aligning with the Trump administration's opposition to what it sees as burdensome state requirements. A December presidential executive order directed the administration to work with Congress toward a minimally burdensome national standard, reflecting federal concerns about conflicting state rules.

Florida's technology debate also focuses on data centers, with disputes over approval authority, possible moratoriums and demands on electricity and water supplies. For companies, Florida illustrates how state enforcement can create significant operational exposure even when federal policy favors deregulation. Yet its legislative divisions also show that an aggressive attorney general and governor cannot automatically translate their priorities into comprehensive law. The resulting landscape combines active litigation, contested legislation and continuing uncertainty over the boundaries of state authority.

Articles.Title: Florida Takes Unlikely Lead Role in State Push to Regulate AI - PYMNTS.com

stories.Headline: The AI buildout is this era's central economic narrative
stories.Summary:
The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, as Chairman Kevin Warsh tried to balance a boom in AI-related investment against the risks it carries. The same week, third-quarter growth figures released Thursday showed the capital spending surge powering the broader economy. Warsh has made the AI buildout the central backdrop for the Fed's policy choices, even as debt markets that financed data centers have begun to wobble. Axios describes the situation as a delicate balance for the central bank. Nonresidential fixed investment rose at a 12.7% annual rate in the third quarter, the strongest pace since the rebound from the early pandemic period in 2020, and excluding that rebound, the highest since 2011.

The measure has been positive for seven consecutive quarters and has climbed 14.3% since the end of 2024, with gains across business structures, equipment and intellectual property. Residential investment, by contrast, has contracted in six of the last seven quarters, including a 3.3% annual rate decline in the third quarter. The article says the buildout is also fueling inflation and drawing investment away from sectors such as housing. Warsh described recent developments in debt markets in approving terms, saying market participants are becoming more discerning in how they allocate capital. He said financial conditions are tighter but that he was unwilling and unable to call them tight, and he argued these changes point toward a longer and more durable period of growth and price stability.

In answering a question, he suggested the Fed's September rate increase had contributed to tighter borrowing for AI projects, noting that interest rates reach into many corners of the economy. Rick Rieder of BlackRock compared the Fed to a house with one thermostat and very different temperatures in each room, arguing that further tightening could chill cooler areas without cooling the overheated ones. The article notes that this approach holds only if inflation begins to ease, and that the era of elevated inflation is nearing its six-year mark. Axios reports that the central bank's credibility, and Warsh's personal standing, are now at stake. The Fed left the door open to another rate increase in December, so the coming months will test whether its current stance can cool inflation without damaging the investment boom that is sustaining growth.

Articles.Title: The AI buildout is this era's central economic narrative

stories.Headline: Shawnee Mission work group to make recommendations for student AI policy
stories.Summary:
The Shawnee Mission School District formed a work group earlier this fall to make a recommended policy for student use of artificial intelligence in schools, the Johnson County Post reported on October 30, 2026. The group met twice in September and twice more in October, and it plans to meet again in mid-November. The district has no student-use policy for AI yet, though no generative AI is available on district-issued devices, Superintendent Michael Schumacher said at a July school board meeting. Students have still found ways to use the technology in their work.

The work group has 32 members, mostly parents, along with a few students, certified staff, classified staff, an administrator and two district-level employees, including Chief Communications Officer Jake Potter. Members were selected randomly to ensure representation of parents, staff and students across the five high school feeder patterns, Potter said. In its four meetings, the group learned about the district's technology safety and security measures and state and federal requirements, reviewed the district's guide for technology use, heard from a representative of the Lawrence-based Center for Innovation, Design, and Digital Learning, and monitored Kansas State Board of Education discussions. The group's meetings have not been open to the public, and neither the district nor the group has officially indicated the direction of the policy, including whether it might recommend a ban or encourage some AI use.

Potter told the Post what the group has done in its meetings. Parent Laura Langdon, who is not on the work group, said the district and the group have an obligation to provide independent research showing AI is beneficial to developing critical thinking skills before allowing it in classrooms. She said the only research done on children's cognition shows AI prevents development of critical thinking, and she compared letting AI into classrooms to giving cigarettes to children. Jessica Mercer Young, a principal research scientist with the Chicago-based Education Development Center who is not affiliated with Shawnee Mission, said that when AI does the thinking, student learning suffers, though she said teacher-mediated AI can support student outcomes.

Mercer Young said strong causal evidence for how AI impacts students and educators is extremely limited because AI is changing faster than researchers can study it, and most research focuses on older students. She said studies show positive trends when AI tools are used alongside a teacher, with mixed results otherwise depending on how the tool was designed. She warned that general-purpose tools and chatbots not designed for learning, such as ChatGPT and Claude, were found to weaken learning and hinder student outcomes. The Kansas Department of Education is considering its own policy on instructional technology, including AI, and Potter said the district is waiting for the state to approve that policy before finalizing its own. The state board of education received the draft at its October 13 meeting and will likely consider it at its next meeting in November, and once approved, the district would have to address both employee and student use by grade or grade groupings.

Articles.Title: Shawnee Mission work group to make recommendations for student AI policy - Johnson County Post

stories.Headline: Google admits AI search makes less money, but it’s fixing that with more ads
stories.Summary:
Google's parent company Alphabet reported third-quarter 2026 results on Wednesday afternoon, showing revenue growth but a sharp drop in its stock price. The company took in almost $128 billion for July through September, with net income above $26 billion, though that net income was almost $9 billion lower than the year before. Revenue rose 25 percent from a year earlier, yet analysts had expected more, and earnings per share came in at $2.12 against a projected $3.02. Shares fell about 12 percent by the time the story was published, after a dip of roughly 13 percent earlier in the day.

Several troubling trends emerged in the report. Search volume grew 12 percent year over year, down from 17 percent in the second quarter and 19 percent in the first, and search revenue was flat in the third quarter. Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler said each AI Mode query earns less than a similar standard web search because there are fewer ads and they cost less. Google's cloud products beat expectations, crossing $30 billion in revenue, but negative cash flow widened from -$5.8 billion to -$9.06 billion.

Google's response is to expand advertising inside AI Mode, its search chatbot. Google will bring AI Mode ads to more international markets soon, and in the United States it will introduce multi-turn ads that change as a user goes back and forth with the chatbot. Schindler cautioned that advertisers may need time to understand the value of AI search ads, though Google's research reportedly finds users see them as more relevant and helpful than traditional search ads. CEO Sundar Pichai said these more complex interactions are becoming common as Google pushes users toward AI Mode.

Google also plans heavy spending on AI. It recorded $51.4 billion in capital expenditures in the third quarter and expects total 2026 spending between $195 billion and $205 billion, with more than $300 billion targeted for 2027. The company points to cloud revenue more than doubling over the past year to support that spending, though much of its cloud demand comes from AI startups that rely on venture funding. The article warns that if that funding dries up or search growth stalls, the spending gap could grow further. It does not say what Google will do next beyond the plans it has already announced.

Articles.Title: Google admits AI search makes less money, but it’s fixing that with more ads

stories.Headline: San Mateo Union High District weighs AI use in classrooms
stories.Summary:
The San Mateo Union High School District is working through questions about when, where and how artificial intelligence should be used in classrooms. Students, parents and educators broadly agree that AI should support critical thinking and learning rather than replace it. Staff will spend the school year developing guardrails to keep that distinction. District leaders said the goal is to prepare students to use AI tools while still becoming thoughtful, ethical, creative and capable human beings.

A progress update on the committee's work came at a meeting on Oct. 22. Julia Kemp, who works in curriculum and instruction, said the district is moving beyond the debate over whether AI should be used at all. Since a study session on the topic in May, the district has developed AI literacy modules to give students a baseline understanding of the technology's purpose and value. Work also began on drafting a syllabus template for teachers and on how the technology should be used.

Kemp said the technology is evolving rapidly, which requires districts interested in innovation to review and calibrate policies as needed. She said the district can be nimbler than usual and pointed to the shift online during COVID as evidence it can thoughtfully integrate AI in a way that centers students and humans. Superintendent Randall Booker raised concerns about students who lack access to technology, the internet or education about AI at home, asking how far behind they would be. Trustee Robert Griffin said the problem will not be solved this year, next year or probably in five years.

When students should have modules on AI use will also have to be determined, possibly during orientation days at the start of school years or during school periods. Kemp said it will be particularly important to ensure teachers are comfortable enough with the tool to integrate it in the classroom. The steering committee is set to meet three more times during the remainder of the 2026-27 school year. Any future policy decisions will be informed by the committee's work.

Articles.Title: San Mateo Union High District weighs AI use in classrooms - San Mateo Daily Journal

stories.Headline: Medicare’s AI Prior Auth Pilot Tied to 15%-20% Drop in Targeted Services
stories.Summary:
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services launched a pilot in January 2026 called Wasteful and Inappropriate Service Reduction, or WISeR, which added prior authorization to traditional Medicare in six states: Arizona, New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Texas, and Washington. Traditional Medicare has historically not required prior authorization, with rare exceptions, so this was a notable change. The six-year pilot covers 41 services considered vulnerable to fraud, waste, and abuse, and the companies that run the review process, typically technology firms, are encouraged to use artificial intelligence. A first study of the model, published in JAMA on October 26, 2026, found that use of the targeted services fell after the pilot began. The article reporting the study was published by DocWire News on October 29, 2026.

Researchers used Epic Cosmos, an electronic health record dataset of more than 310 million patient records, to compare monthly traditional Medicare encounters for WISeR-targeted services in the six pilot states with those in the other 44 states and Washington, DC. They covered the two years before launch and the period from January through June 2026. Relative to non-pilot states, use of epidural steroid injections, the highest-volume service, fell 15.0 percent, while other targeted services fell 19.5 percent. The reduction for epidural steroid injections more than halved over time, dropping from 20.7 percent in January through March to 9.3 percent in April through June. For other services, the decline eased from 21.4 percent to 17.6 percent, and both shifts were statistically significant.

Lead author Hannah Neprash, PhD, an associate professor at the University of Minnesota School of Public Health, told DocWire News that the initial drop was likely driven partly by the pilot's well-documented hiccups. She said that as those problems were worked out, the continued reduction reflected a mix of clinicians ordering fewer services and some remaining orders failing to receive prior authorization. She also noted that larger practices are more likely to have dedicated prior authorization staff, so smaller practices may bear more of these administrative duties themselves. The study could not separate fewer orders from denials, nor observe how AI was used, and the authors call for research on whether the effects persist over the model's six-year run.

Articles.Title: Medicare’s AI Prior Auth Pilot Tied to 15%-20% Drop in Targeted Services

stories.Headline: CSN selected for nearly $3 million in federal funding for AI education
stories.Summary:
The College of Southern Nevada has been selected to receive nearly $3 million in federal funding to expand artificial intelligence education and technology programs, according to a report published October 29, 2026. The five-year NEXUS Workforce Initiative will support new computing and information technology opportunities, including the creation of a NEXUS Center for Excellence. The proposed project budget totals $2,998,756. The college says the goal is to help students prepare for careers in Southern Nevada.

NEXUS stands for Nevada's Emerging Workforce eXcellence through Upskilling and Student Success, and it is meant to tie education more closely to workforce needs. CSN plans to develop at least 12 artificial intelligence courses and nine pathways that let students move from noncredit workforce training into college credit programs. A new Faculty Fellows Program will provide AI-focused professional development for 120 faculty members. Two dedicated advisers will help technology students with academic planning and with completing their credentials. The initiative also aims to strengthen links between classroom learning and employer needs in cybersecurity, cloud computing and data analytics.

The college is the entity responsible for the initiative and has described its aims, according to the report. The article does not name a specific CSN official or quote anyone directly about the project. It also does not say when the courses, pathways or fellowship program will begin enrolling students or taking part. Beyond the report's description of the five-year plan and its budget, no further details on the funding source or outcomes are provided.

Articles.Title: CSN selected for nearly $3 million in federal funding for AI education

stories.Headline: Philippines, New Zealand explore AI to improve power services
stories.Summary:
The Philippines and New Zealand are exploring how artificial intelligence can improve electricity regulation, monitor power outages, and simplify customer services. Energy officials, regulators, and technology executives from both countries discussed possible AI applications at an event on Oct. 8 at the Manila residence of New Zealand Ambassador Catherine McIntosh. The reception was organized with the technology firm Gentrack and New Zealand Trade and Enterprise. It brought together representatives from the Department of Energy, the Energy Regulatory Commission, and New Zealand's technology sector.

The Energy Regulatory Commission outlined efforts to move beyond basic digitalization toward a system using data analytics and intelligent technologies. Among the initiatives under development is ASK ERiC, an AI-enabled chatbot to help consumers navigate ERC information, regulatory procedures, and public services. The commission is also exploring AI-assisted compliance monitoring, including agentic AI that could track compliance submissions, identify missing requirements, and flag potential violations for review. It is likewise considering regulatory analytics to identify patterns in outages, including frequency, duration, geographic distribution, and unusual trends. As of September 2026, the ERC had 28 information systems supporting its processes, up from 25 operational systems reported by August after the May launch of the ERCify digital platform.

ERC Director III Heiddi Venecia R. Barrozo outlined these efforts. The commission said adopting AI must not compromise accountability, accuracy, explainability, or information security, and that AI-generated findings would still require verification and human oversight before use in regulatory decisions. Gentrack solution architect Hyun Woo Kim said every country has its own unique problem and unique way to solve it, stressing that AI tools must be designed specifically for the energy sector. He cited S&P Global research published March 31, 2026, showing that 64% of surveyed energy and utility organizations were investing more than 10% of their total IT budgets in AI, while only 43% of AI projects were considered on track to generate a return on investment within 12 months. The study also found that 7% of surveyed organizations were allocating more than 30% of their IT budgets to AI.

Kim described three stages of AI adoption in utility operations: systems that assist human customer service representatives, customer-facing self-service platforms, and autonomous AI agents handling customer interactions and defined workflows within safeguards. Gentrack demonstrated applications involving bill explanations, account inquiries, workflow automation, and compliance support, along with low-code and no-code technologies. New Zealand Trade and Enterprise representatives reaffirmed their commitment to cooperation with the Philippines in innovation, sustainability, and economic growth. The articles say the benefits will depend on the accuracy of the systems, protection of consumer data, and whether utilities and regulators can translate investments into measurable improvements in service quality and affordability.

Articles.Title: Philippines, New Zealand explore AI to improve power services - Daily Guardian

stories.Headline: Johns Hopkins Researchers’ Cancer Cell Mapping Technology Chosen for Anthropic AI for Science Project
stories.Summary:
Johns Hopkins researchers Alexander Szalay and Janis Taube have been chosen for a research project in Anthropic's AI for Science program, according to a Johns Hopkins Medicine report published on October 29, 2026. The selection recognizes their AstroPath technology, which combines astronomy, pathology and artificial intelligence to map tumors and show how cancer cells interact with surrounding cells, especially immune cells. The program gives chosen researchers free credits to use Anthropic's Claude AI models to analyze complex data, find patterns and develop hypotheses. It was launched in May 2025 and initially focused on biology and life sciences before expanding to other disciplines.

AstroPath began with seed funding from the Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy at the Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center, followed by multiyear support from the Mark Foundation for Cancer Research. The Mark Foundation invested more than $10 million, which helped establish the Mark Foundation Center for Advanced Genomics and Imaging at Johns Hopkins in 2020. The platform borrows its data infrastructure from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, which mapped billions of stars and galaxies, and it applies that approach to the locations and interactions of cells within tumors. The team now uses AI-assisted tools to outline tumor cells, work that once took researchers hours by hand and can now be completed in minutes.

The researchers are also combining spatial tumor maps with genetic and molecular information to study why immunotherapy works for some patients but not others. Johns Hopkins University President Ronald J. Daniels praised the researchers for responsibly harnessing AI to analyze large amounts of information and help shape scientific discovery. Theodore DeWeese, dean of the medical faculty and CEO of Johns Hopkins Medicine, said AI is poised to redefine how care is delivered, research is advanced and future health care leaders are educated. William Nelson, director of the Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center, said the technology could transform how cancers are diagnosed and treated and that the recognition would help accelerate these discoveries.

Szalay and Taube said the scale and richness of the data, made possible by the Mark Foundation and Bloomberg~Kimmel support, now allow insights to be extracted at a far greater speed. The researchers are exploring the potential formation of a new company focused on AI-powered tumor analysis and biomarker development, which would offer assays to the clinical community and give drug and biotechnology companies new ways to study tumor biology and treatment response. The article does not say whether that company has been formed or when it might be. The Anthropic selection is intended to expand the work by using AI to accelerate analysis of cancer data and to help identify new biomarkers, treatments and more personalized approaches to care.

Articles.Title: Johns Hopkins Researchers’ Cancer Cell Mapping Technology Chosen for Anthropic AI for Science Project

stories.Headline: CCAS professors discuss AI’s role in higher education
stories.Summary:
Four Columbian College of Arts and Sciences professors and Dean Paul Wahlbeck discussed the opportunities and risks of artificial intelligence in higher education at the University Student Center on Tuesday. Wahlbeck moderated the panel, which weighed AI's potential benefits against the broader threat the technology could pose to critical thinking. The session was part of a CCAS series of expert discussions that he moderates periodically, with each event covering a different higher-education or research topic. Last year's event in the series examined how federal funding cuts affected research.

The discussion came as GW works out how to use and implement AI across the University. Over the past year, officials have announced several initiatives, including a University-wide AI mapping exercise to assess how GW currently uses the technology and identify its opportunities and risks. In August, Provost Ed Balleisen also issued guidelines on how faculty should regulate AI in their classrooms. Wahlbeck opened the panel by asking Dwight Kravitz, an associate professor of cognitive neuroscience, how AI affects learning. Kravitz said research on that question is still in its early stages, but he warned the technology could change how students acquire knowledge and solve problems.

Kravitz argued that universities should neither reject nor fully embrace AI, since it could weaken students' abilities while also giving them access to knowledge they previously lacked. Douglas Crawford, a professor of interior architecture, said he lets students use AI for lighter tasks such as enhancing renderings and adjusting lighting, and allows advanced students to use it for complex work like detailed storyboards. Political science Professor Sarah Binder said she uses AI to analyze decades of congressional speeches on federal debt and deficits, narrowing the collection to about 100,000 relevant speeches. She added that hallucinations and mistakes raise validity and reliability concerns, so she cross-checks answers from two AI models. Philosophy professor Tad Zawidzki said he believes educators should focus on process rather than product and tap into human creativity instead of bypassing work with AI.

The articles do not report any formal policy changes resulting from the panel itself. They describe the event as a conversation among faculty and the dean, with each speaker sharing personal views and research experience. The panel reflects the ongoing debate within the University about how AI fits into teaching and research. The articles do not say whether any follow-up discussions, policies or further sessions in the series are planned.

Articles.Title: CCAS professors discuss AI’s role in higher education

stories.Headline: Is AI more a partner, competitor, or crutch for biomedical scientists?
stories.Summary:
Knoepfler, a professor of cell biology and human anatomy at UC Davis School of Medicine and author of the STAT column Lab Dish, wrote a commentary in STAT on October 29, 2026, asking whether artificial intelligence is more a partner, competitor, or crutch for biomedical scientists. He opened by noting that his immediate worry is not a dramatic AI scenario but what the technology might be doing to science itself. He said he is excited about how useful AI can be for research. He also said he is deeply concerned about its potential impacts, especially on new and future biologists who will come of age doing science alongside AI tools.

Knoepfler argues that researchers may become less capable if they lean too heavily on AI. He points to the risk that overdependence could weaken the skills scientists rely on to reason through problems on their own. He also raises the possibility of job losses in science as AI takes on more of the work. Those two concerns form the core of his argument about what the technology may require scientists to guard against. The article's preview indicates that he goes into more depth in the full piece.

Knoepfler is the author of the piece and speaks for himself, so the concerns described are his own views. The article is an opinion-style commentary in a subscriber-only outlet, and the full text beyond the opening was not available in the material provided. The surrounding page links to other coverage on life sciences, measles, and cancer vaccines, which are unrelated to the AI question.
